- **Main goal:** Extends ENSO prediction lead time and reduces the spring predictability barrier while providing physically interpretable insights.
- **Architecture:** CTEFNet: a hybrid convolutional neural network and transformer using multiple oceanic and atmospheric predictors, with gradient-based sensitivity analysis.
- **Data:** Multivariate oceanic and atmospheric predictor fields; training and evaluation datasets are not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Extends effective ENSO forecast lead to 20 months, outperforming dynamical models and prior deep learning methods, and identifies inter-basin precursors.
- **Open work:** Further explore Pacific-Atlantic-Indian inter-basin interactions and apply the model to other climate modes.
- **Issues:** Long-lead skill evaluated on limited historical ENSO events; gradient-based sensitivities may not imply causality.
- *Basis: abstract*

### Forecasting El Niño with Convolutional and Recurrent Neural Networks
Mahesh et al. (2019), *Venue not recorded*. 17 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts El Nino-Southern Oscillation with deep learning to extend ENSO predictability beyond conventional methods.
- **Architecture:** Convolutional neural network (CNN) and recurrent neural network models, as stated in the title; the recurrent cell type is not specified here.
- **Data:** Not reported (abstract missing); likely gridded ocean fields with a Nino index target, but sources are not stated.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Not reported; natural next steps include longer leads and interpretability of learned predictors.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; details of data, evaluation and skill cannot be verified from the record.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [An expert system‐based approach to prediction of year‐to‐year climatic variations in the North Atlantic region](https://doi.org/10.1002/(sici)1097-0088(199907)19:9<951::aid-joc372>3.0.co;2-j)
Rodionov et al. (1999), *International Journal of Climatology*. 16 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts year-to-year climate variations, such as winter anomalies, in the North Atlantic region using an expert system.
- **Architecture:** Expert system (rule-based knowledge-based system) built on known circulation regimes and teleconnections.
- **Data:** Historical atmospheric circulation and climate records for the North Atlantic region; specifics not reported here.
- **Main result:** Reports skill of the expert system for interannual prediction; quantitative scores are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Updating the rule base with new data and comparing its skill with dynamical and other statistical seasonal forecasts.
- **Issues:** Rules rest on historical circulation relationships that may be nonstationary; short records limit independent verification of skill.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Predicting the Onset of Australian Winter Rainfall by Nonlinear Classification](https://doi.org/10.1175/jcli-3291.1)
Firth et al. (2005), *Journal of Climate*. 16 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts the onset date of winter rainfall in southwest Australia, which matters for crop sowing decisions.
- **Architecture:** Nonlinear classification of onset timing from predictors; the specific classifier type is not specified in the available metadata.
- **Data:** Rainfall records and large-scale climate predictors for Australia; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Operational forecasting of onset and testing with additional predictors.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; card is based on the title only.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Combined dynamical-deep learning ENSO forecasts](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59173-8)
Chen et al. (2025), *Nature Communications*. 15 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves ENSO prediction by combining the strengths of deep learning and dynamical model forecasts.
- **Architecture:** Convolutional neural network and 3D-Geoformer (transformer) ENSO forecasts combined with dynamical model forecasts through two combination strategies.
- **Data:** Dynamical model ensemble forecasts and DL forecasts; specific datasets are not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** DL forecasts match the dynamical multi-model mean, and both combined dynamical-DL strategies significantly outperform individual DL or dynamical forecasts across lead times.
- **Open work:** Extend the combination approach to other climate forecasting problems.
- **Issues:** Gains depend on the specific dynamical and DL members; limited historical verification sample.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Projection of ENSO using observation-informed deep learning](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63157-z)
Zhu et al. (2025), *Nature Communications*. 14 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reduces the large inter-model spread in projected 21st-century ENSO SST variability by constraining projections with observed ENSO physics.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural networks (ANN, MLP-type) trained to map tropical Pacific warming patterns to ENSO SST variability response, with interpretability analysis and a model-as-truth test.
- **Data:** Climate model simulations (CMIP-class) and observations; projections under a high-emission scenario.
- **Main result:** Reduces ENSO projection uncertainty by 54%, from a range of 0.59 °C to 0.27 °C; warming in the far-eastern and central equatorial Pacific is key to ENSO change.
- **Open work:** Integrate machine learning with observational constraints for other climate projection uncertainties.
- **Issues:** Relies on short observational records and on the assumption that the observed ENSO-warming-pattern relationship holds in future; constraint conditional on projected warming patterns.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Explained predictions of strong eastern Pacific El Niño events using deep learning](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-45739-3)
Tello et al. (2023), *Scientific Reports*. 12 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predict ENSO diversity, particularly the onset of strong eastern Pacific El Nino events, and explain predictions.
- **Architecture:** Deep learning model (IGP-UHM AI model v1.0) predicting E and C indices with a classification output, plus XAI analysis.
- **Data:** Not detailed in abstract; tropical Pacific and global fields; real-time forecast initialized May 2023.
- **Main result:** Higher ENSO nonlinearity associated with better skill; forecasts El Nino persistence into 2024 with weakening; XAI identifies western Pacific precursors.
- **Open work:** Verification of the 2023-2024 forecast and implications for predictability in a warming climate.
- **Issues:** Limited strong El Nino samples; real-time forecast verification pending.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [OmniCast: A Masked Latent Diffusion Model for Weather Forecasting Across Time Scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18707)
Nguyen et al. (2025), *Neural Information Processing Systems*. 12 citations.

- **Main goal:** Unifies probabilistic weather forecasting from medium range to subseasonal-to-seasonal scales, where autoregressive models suffer error accumulation.
- **Architecture:** OmniCast: a VAE encoding weather into a latent space and a masked diffusion transformer (per-token diffusion head) generating future latent token sequences jointly across space and time.
- **Data:** Global reanalysis data (ERA5); evaluated on medium-range and subseasonal-to-seasonal benchmarks.
- **Main result:** Competitive with leading probabilistic medium-range methods while 10x to 20x faster; state of the art at S2S scales across accuracy, physics-based and probabilistic metrics; stable rollouts up to 100 years.
- **Open work:** Extend to coupled components and higher resolutions for seasonal and climate-scale forecasting.
- **Issues:** Latent compression may lose fine-scale detail; trained on reanalysis so inherits its biases; 100-year stability does not imply correct climate response to forcing.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Advancing seasonal prediction of tropical cyclone activity with a hybrid AI-physics climate model](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/adf864)
Zhang et al. (2025), *Environmental Research Letters*. 11 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explores whether hybrid ML-physics atmospheric models can deliver useful seasonal predictions of large-scale circulation and Northern Hemisphere tropical cyclone activity.
- **Architecture:** NeuralGCM, a hybrid model combining a differentiable dynamical core with neural network physics, run with persisted-anomaly SST and sea ice boundary conditions.
- **Data:** Seasonal hindcasts for July–November 1990–2023 verified against observed TC records; NeuralGCM was trained on ERA5 reanalysis.
- **Main result:** Simulates 100 days in about 8 minutes on one GPU; predicted North Atlantic and East Pacific TC frequency correlates with observations at r of about 0.7, comparable to physical GCMs, with significant skill for ACE and sub-basin tracks.
- **Open work:** Coupling to ocean models or better boundary forcing, higher resolution, and seamless weather-climate prediction of TC risk.
- **Issues:** Coarse resolution limits TC representation; simplified persisted-anomaly SST forcing; skill assessed on a modest number of seasons.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Retrieval Non‐Linear Dynamic Forecast Model Of El Nino/ La Nina Index Based on Genetic Algorithm Optimization](https://doi.org/10.1002/cjg2.1290)
Zhang et al. (2008), *Chinese Journal of Geophysics*. 11 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds a nonlinear dynamic forecast model of El Niño/La Niña indices from observed data.
- **Architecture:** Genetic algorithm used to retrieve a nonlinear dynamical model from the index time series.
- **Data:** ENSO index time series; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The retrieved model is reported to forecast the index with reasonable skill; numbers are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Longer lead forecasts and multivariate models.
- **Issues:** Low-dimensional model; limited validation.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Testing the reliability of interpretable neural networks in geoscience using the Madden–Julian oscillation](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-14-4495-2021)
Toms et al. (2021), *Geoscientific Model Development*. 10 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether NN interpretation methods reliably recover known geophysical structure, using the MJO as test case.
- **Architecture:** Neural network classifying MJO phase, interpreted with backward optimization and layerwise relevance propagation.
- **Data:** Observed/reanalysis tropical atmospheric fields (e.g. OLR and winds) with MJO phase labels.
- **Main result:** NN identifies MJO phase twice as accurately as linear regression; interpretations recover known spatial structure and suggest extended seasons should shift one month later.
- **Open work:** Applying interpretable NNs to test other geoscientific hypotheses.
- **Issues:** Interpretation reliability shown for one well-known phenomenon; methods may behave differently where truth is unknown.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [The AI Weather Quest: an international competition for sub-seasonal forecasting with AI](https://doi.org/10.1088/3049-4753/adf649)
Loegel et al. (2025), *Machine Learning: Earth*. 9 citations.

- **Main goal:** Launches an open international competition to evaluate AI and ML methods for sub-seasonal forecasting under operational-like real-time conditions.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark competition description (AI Weather Quest by ECMWF with WMO support), not a single model; teams submit weekly probabilistic forecasts scored on live leaderboards.
- **Data:** Real-time weekly probabilistic forecasts of 2 m temperature, accumulated precipitation and mean sea level pressure, verified globally against ECMWF reference data.
- **Main result:** Establishes the competition framework, submission tools and evaluation using global ranked probability skill scores; no competition results reported.
- **Open work:** Reporting quarterly and yearly results and identifying which methods advance reliable sub-seasonal prediction.
- **Issues:** Describes the setup only; leaderboard metrics focus on RPSS for three variables and may not capture extremes or regional skill.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Data-driven seasonal climate predictions via variational inference and transformers](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01320-z)
Palma et al. (2025), *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*. 5 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides data-driven global seasonal predictions of temperature and rainfall anomalies comparable to operational products while separating skill from climate-change trends.
- **Architecture:** Transformer combined with variational inference for probabilistic seasonal prediction.
- **Data:** Trained on CMIP6 model output; tested against ERA5 reanalysis; benchmarked against ECMWF SEAS5.
- **Main result:** Temperature forecasts show skill beyond climatology and trend, outperforming SEAS5 in some ocean and land areas; precipitation skill is more limited.
- **Open work:** Improve precipitation skill and investigate shared predictability sources with dynamical systems.
- **Issues:** Limited precipitation skill; trained on CMIP6 so inherits model biases and domain shift to ERA5; short verification record.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Using Deep Learning to Identify Initial Error Sensitivity for Interpretable ENSO Forecasts](https://doi.org/10.1175/aies-d-24-0045.1)
Toride et al. (2024), *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth Systems*. 5 citations.

- **Main goal:** Creates interpretable ENSO forecasts while identifying regions where initial errors matter most.
- **Architecture:** Optimized model-analog method in which a convolutional neural network estimates state-dependent weights for selecting analogs from a model simulation library.
- **Data:** CESM2 Large Ensemble as analog library and training data; evaluation also against a reanalysis dataset at seasonal-to-annual leads.
- **Main result:** Significantly improves on unweighted model-analogs and matches a standalone neural network; El Niño forecasts are sensitive to winter tropical Pacific SST, La Niña to summer zonal wind stress.
- **Open work:** Apply to other phenomena such as regional temperature and precipitation.
- **Issues:** Limited by the analog library's model biases; reanalysis verification record is short.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Predicting Atlantic and Benguela Niño events with deep learning](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ads5185)
Bachèlery et al. (2025), *Science Advances*. 3 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predict Atlantic and Benguela Niño events, which dynamical forecasting systems predict poorly, and test tropical Atlantic predictability.
- **Architecture:** Simple convolutional neural network (CNN) forecasting the event indices from ocean-state precursors.
- **Data:** Not specified in the abstract; likely ocean reanalysis or model output of sea surface and subsurface fields.
- **Main result:** Atlantic/Benguela Niños predicted 3–4 months ahead and peak-season events up to 5 months; the model exploits known precursors such as long-wave ocean dynamics.
- **Open work:** Extending lead times, probabilistic forecasts and use for process understanding of tropical Atlantic variability.
- **Issues:** Few events in the observational record limit robust skill assessment; training data details not given in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Prediction Beyond the Medium Range With an Atmosphere‐Ocean Model That Combines Physics‐Based Modeling and Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024ms004480)
Patel et al. (2024), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 2 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether a hybrid physics–machine learning atmosphere-ocean model can deliver useful weather and climate-variability prediction beyond the medium range, extending earlier hybrid SPEEDY work.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid model coupling the low-resolution SPEEDY atmospheric general circulation model with reservoir computing (a recurrent neural network variant), plus purely ML prognostic variables for 6 h precipitation, SST and upper-300 m ocean heat content.
- **Data:** Trained on reanalysis (ERA5) and ocean data; evaluated on hindcasts of ENSO, equatorial waves, MJO and tropical precipitation.
- **Main result:** Predicts the El Niño cycle and its precipitation teleconnections for 3–7 months depending on season; equatorial precipitation skill reaches 15 days in the East Pacific and 11.5 days in the West Pacific, comparable to high-resolution operational models.
- **Open work:** Increasing resolution, adding further ML-based Earth system components and extending toward seasonal-to-subseasonal operational use are natural next steps.
- **Issues:** Low spatial resolution and simplified physics of SPEEDY; ocean is represented only by ML-predicted SST and heat content rather than full ocean dynamics; comparison with operational models relies on published scores.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11126-x)
Guan et al. (2026), *Nature*. 1 citations.

- **Main goal:** Counters the sharp drop of forecast skill at subseasonal (2–6 week) leads caused by compounding errors and systematic model biases.
- **Architecture:** Probabilistic bias correction: a machine learning framework that learns to correct historical probabilistic forecasts of dynamical and AI models; specific network family not stated in the abstract.
- **Data:** Historical probabilistic forecasts from ECMWF's dynamical ensemble and AI Forecasting System (AIFS); evaluated on pressure, temperature and precipitation targets and in ECMWF's 2025 real-time subseasonal forecasting competition.
- **Main result:** Doubles AIFS subseasonal skill and improves the operationally debiased dynamical model for 91% of pressure, 92% of temperature and 98% of precipitation targets; best global forecasts for all variables and leads in the 2025 ECMWF competition.
- **Open work:** Applying the framework to other centres' models and translating gains into extreme-event and sector-specific decision support.
- **Issues:** Skill remains modest in absolute terms at subseasonal leads; correction depends on long, consistent hindcast archives; methodological details are not given in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Deep learning reveals enhanced ENSO predictability under historical anthropogenic forcing](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aec9518)
Lin et al. (2026), *Science Advances*. 1 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates how ENSO predictability changes under historical anthropogenic forcing, relevant for future climate projections.
- **Architecture:** Convolutional neural network (CNN) forecast model with a leave-one-model-out strategy, used as a predictability diagnostic.
- **Data:** CMIP6 historical and preindustrial control simulations.
- **Main result:** ENSO predictability is enhanced by 14.0 ± 1.8% under historical forcing, linked to a shoaling equatorial Pacific thermocline that strengthens advective and thermocline feedbacks.
- **Open work:** Extending the analysis to future scenarios and observations, and checking robustness to model choice.
- **Issues:** Relies on CMIP6 models with known ENSO biases; CNN-derived predictability may reflect model-specific dynamics rather than the real climate system.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Tropical basin interactions reduce spring predictability barrier of ENSO in a deep learning model](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeb0901)
Zhou et al. (2026), *Science Advances*. 1 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates whether tropical basin interactions among the Indian, Atlantic and Pacific Oceans can reduce the ENSO spring predictability barrier in a deep learning model.
- **Architecture:** GL-Geoformer: a transformer-based deep learning model for global tropical ocean-atmosphere prediction of wind and three-dimensional temperature anomalies, with pacemaker experiments.
- **Data:** Tropical ocean-atmosphere wind and 3D temperature anomaly fields; specific training and evaluation products not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Including tropical basin interactions substantially reduces the spring predictability barrier, giving skillful ENSO predictions up to 16 months ahead from spring initializations; quantifies IOD and Atlantic Niño contributions via subsurface heat transport and Walker circulation.
- **Open work:** Extending to other modes of variability and using the framework to further diagnose interbasin mechanisms.
- **Issues:** Attribution via pacemaker experiments within a data-driven model may not reflect true causality; training data source and length not stated in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Deep learning with spatio-temporal conditioning improves global subseasonal precipitation forecasts](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01430-8)
Noh et al. (2026), *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*. 1 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves global subseasonal (1–5 week) precipitation forecasts by correcting systematic NWP biases with geographic and seasonal conditioning.
- **Architecture:** ReST: U-Net backbone with spatio-temporal adaptive modulation combining SPADE and FiLM conditioning layers; compared with quantile mapping, random forest and Res34-Unet.
- **Data:** GEFSv12 reforecasts 2000–2019 for training; evaluated against a global station precipitation dataset from 63,588 stations.
- **Main result:** Consistently improves skill over raw forecasts and conventional post-processing and yields more spatially coherent fields; gains largest in weeks 1–2, with predictability declining rapidly beyond week 2.
- **Open work:** Extending conditioning to probabilistic outputs and other variables or models.
- **Issues:** Limited gains beyond week 2; station-based verification is uneven globally; single forecast system (GEFSv12).
- *Basis: abstract*

### [On the importance of historical context and bias correction in deep learning MJO prediction models](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01459-9)
Virji et al. (2026), *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Examines whether extended historical context and bias correction improve deep learning forecasts of the Madden-Julian Oscillation.
- **Architecture:** Deep learning MJO prediction models with varying historical input context plus bias-correction methods; specific network family not stated in the abstract.
- **Data:** Not reported in the abstract; MJO indices and atmospheric fields presumably from reanalysis.
- **Main result:** MJO predictability is governed by the current state rather than prior propagation; bias correction helps DL models only beyond 3 weeks, cutting errors by 11% in weeks 5–6 and extending skill from 37 to 40 days.
- **Open work:** Developing correction methods that target model deficiencies rather than dataset inconsistencies.
- **Issues:** Data sources and architecture are unclear from the abstract; conclusions may depend on the specific DL models tested.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Skillful and interpretable ENSO prediction via a glass-box dynamical-deep learning model](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01513-6)
Wang et al. (2026), *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Aims at skillful and interpretable ENSO prediction by combining dynamical modeling with deep learning, as implied by the title.
- **Architecture:** Glass-box hybrid dynamical–deep learning model for ENSO; exact network family not known without the abstract.
- **Data:** Not reported; abstract not available.
- **Main result:** Not reported; abstract not available.
- **Open work:** Likely further interpretability analysis and extension of lead times.
- **Issues:** Content not verifiable without the abstract.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Exascale Hybrid Numerical-AI Ensembles for Operational Flood-Season Forecasting in East Asia: 15-km Decadal Hindcasts and 1-km High-Resolution Capability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24896)
Chen et al. (2026), *arXiv*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves seasonal summer rainfall forecasts for the East Asian flood season, limited by the spring predictability barrier.
- **Architecture:** CAPES, a hybrid ensemble combining a kilometer-resolution coupled regional atmosphere–land–ocean model with a data-driven AI seasonal forecasting system, run on exascale computing.
- **Data:** Ten annual 1,774-member hindcasts for 2016–2025 at 15 km (174 numerical plus 1,600 AI members); training data of the AI system not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Hindcasts complete in 14.6 hours, improving mean prediction score from ECMWF's 71.8 to 75.9; 1-km configuration enables fine-scale typhoon simulation.
- **Open work:** Operationalize the 1-km fused ensemble and extend beyond one-week fine-scale runs.
- **Issues:** Prediction score metric is specific to Chinese operations; ten-year hindcast is short; AI component details not given.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [El Niño-Southern Oscillation forecasting using complex networks analysis of LSTM neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10015-019-00540-2)
Broni-Bedaiko et al. (2019), *Artificial Life and Robotics*. 0 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts El Niño-Southern Oscillation by combining complex network analysis with recurrent neural networks.
- **Architecture:** LSTM neural networks combined with complex network analysis of climate data, as stated in the title.
- **Data:** Not reported (no abstract); presumably ENSO indices and climate fields.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Not reported; extending lead time and comparing with dynamical ENSO forecasts would follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; card is based on the title only and should be checked.
- *Basis: assessment*

## Climate emulation & detection

### [Climatic Reconstruction in Europe for 18,000 YR B.P. from Pollen Data](https://doi.org/10.1006/qres.1997.1961)
Peyron et al. (1998), *Quaternary Research*. 443 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs European climate at the Last Glacial Maximum, about 18,000 years before present, from fossil pollen.
- **Architecture:** Modern analogue (nearest-neighbour) technique based on plant functional type scores, constrained by vegetation modelling; not a neural network.
- **Data:** Fossil pollen records from European sites and a modern pollen dataset with climate.
- **Main result:** Indicates a much colder and drier glacial climate in Europe than today, with strong cooling in winter temperature.
- **Open work:** Comparison with climate model simulations and more sites.
- **Issues:** Lack of good modern analogues for glacial vegetation; sparse site coverage; CO2 effects on vegetation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Using Self-Organizing Maps to Investigate Extreme Climate Events: An Application to Wintertime Precipitation in the Balkans](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0442(2000)013<1718:usomti>2.0.co;2)
Cavazos (2000), *Journal of Climate*. 261 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates the large-scale circulation and humidity patterns associated with extreme wintertime precipitation in the Balkans.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing maps (SOM) used to classify daily atmospheric circulation and humidity patterns.
- **Data:** NCEP reanalysis daily circulation and humidity fields and station precipitation in the Balkans, winter seasons.
- **Main result:** SOMs identify a continuum of synoptic patterns and link extreme precipitation events to specific circulation and moisture configurations.
- **Open work:** Applying the classification to climate-model output for downscaling and future extremes.
- **Issues:** Diagnostic study; results depend on SOM size and reanalysis quality.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Climate change now detectable from any single day of weather at global scale](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-019-0666-7)
Sippel et al. (2020), *Nature Climate Change*. 229 citations.

- **Main goal:** Detect externally forced climate change from a single day of global weather rather than from decades of data.
- **Architecture:** Statistical learning (regularized linear regression, ridge-type) linking spatial patterns of daily temperature and humidity to global climate metrics, trained on climate model simulations; observations projected onto the fingerprint.
- **Data:** CMIP5 climate model simulations for training; observational daily temperature and humidity datasets for detection.
- **Main result:** Forced climate change is detected from any single day in the observed record since early 2012 and from any year since 1999, robust even when the global mean trend is removed.
- **Open work:** Use the framework for communicating regional weather events in a climate context and for extending detection to other variables.
- **Issues:** Depends on climate models correctly representing internal variability; detection is global, not attributing individual local events.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Probabilistic climate change projections using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-003-0345-1)
Knutti et al. (2003), *Climate Dynamics*. 212 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides probabilistic climate change projections, addressing large uncertainties and expert-based uncertainty estimates.
- **Architecture:** Neural network (MLP) based climate model substitute (emulator) for large ensemble runs, with ensemble members constrained by observations.
- **Data:** Observed surface warming over the industrial period, estimates of global ocean heat uptake, and carbon cycle model outputs.
- **Main result:** The NN substitute speeds up ensembles by at least an order of magnitude; indirect aerosol forcing below about -1.2 W m-2 is excluded; almost half of members exceed the IPCC warming range.
- **Open work:** Adding further observational constraints, regional projections and more emission scenarios to narrow projection uncertainty.
- **Issues:** The emulator inherits the structure and limitations of the underlying intermediate-complexity climate model; projections depend strongly on the assumed upper limit of climate sensitivity.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Glacial Mediterranean sea surface temperatures based on planktonic foraminiferal assemblages](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.quascirev.2004.02.018)
Hayes et al. (2005), *Quaternary Science Reviews*. 209 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs Last Glacial Maximum sea surface temperatures in the Mediterranean to understand ice-age climate and provide boundary conditions for models.
- **Architecture:** Transfer functions relating planktonic foraminiferal assemblages to temperature, including artificial neural networks; the exact set of transfer-function methods is not reported here.
- **Data:** Planktonic foraminiferal census counts from Mediterranean sediment cores and core-top calibration datasets.
- **Main result:** Reconstructed glacial sea surface temperatures show cooling relative to present with marked spatial differences across the basin; specific values are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Comparing with other temperature proxies and with glacial climate model simulations.
- **Issues:** Transfer-function calibration uncertainty and possible no-analogue assemblages; dating and coverage limited by core availability; abstract unavailable.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Artificial intelligence reconstructs missing climate information](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-020-0582-5)
Kadow et al. (2020), *Nature Geoscience*. 204 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstruct missing values in historical observational surface temperature records to reduce coverage gaps that bias climate trend estimates.
- **Architecture:** Image inpainting CNN (U-Net with partial convolutions) adapted to climate fields, transfer-learning knowledge from model data to observations.
- **Data:** Trained on climate model output (20th Century Reanalysis and CMIP5 historical simulations); applied to HadCRUT4 gridded temperature anomalies.
- **Main result:** Inpainting reconstructions outperform conventional methods such as kriging and PCA-based infilling in tests, and recover large-scale patterns in sparse periods, e.g. the 1877-78 El Nino.
- **Open work:** Applying the method to other variables and datasets and quantifying uncertainty of reconstructions.
- **Issues:** Reconstruction learns model-based spatial structure that may not hold in reality; uncertainty not fully quantified; abstract unavailable, so details rely on knowledge of the paper.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [North Atlantic climate variability from a self-organizing map perspective](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006jd007460)
Reusch et al. (2007), *Journal of Geophysical Research*. 157 citations.

- **Main goal:** Characterises North Atlantic atmospheric circulation variability, including the North Atlantic Oscillation, with a nonlinear pattern-based method.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing map (SOM) applied to sea level pressure fields and compared with principal component (EOF) analysis.
- **Data:** Monthly winter sea level pressure from the NCEP/NCAR reanalysis over the North Atlantic.
- **Main result:** The SOM captures a continuum of circulation patterns, including NAO-like states and asymmetries that linear EOF analysis does not resolve.
- **Open work:** Linking SOM states to ice core and proxy records and to climate model output.
- **Issues:** SOM size and training choices are subjective; reanalysis biases are inherited.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Predicted changes in synoptic forcing of net precipitation in large Arctic river basins during the 21st century](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006jg000332)
Cassano et al. (2007), *Journal of Geophysical Research*. 140 citations.

- **Main goal:** Projects how changes in synoptic circulation will alter net precipitation (P-E) over large Arctic river basins in the 21st century.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing maps (SOM) classify daily sea level pressure into synoptic patterns; changes in pattern frequency are related to basin net precipitation.
- **Data:** Sea level pressure and precipitation fields from IPCC AR4 / CMIP3 global climate model simulations and reanalysis for the Lena, Mackenzie, Ob and Yenisei basins.
- **Main result:** Shifts in synoptic pattern frequency explain part of the projected increase in net precipitation, with the remainder due to within-pattern changes.
- **Open work:** Reducing inter-model spread and attributing within-pattern thermodynamic changes.
- **Issues:** Relies on GCM output with biases and coarse resolution; SOM node choice is subjective.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Data-driven predictions of the time remaining until critical global warming thresholds are reached](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2207183120)
Diffenbaugh et al. (2023), *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*. 139 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predict the time remaining until global warming thresholds (1.5 C and 2 C) are reached from observed temperature patterns.
- **Architecture:** Neural network trained to predict years-to-threshold from spatial maps of annual temperature anomalies, using transfer learning from climate models to observations.
- **Data:** CMIP6 simulations for training; historical temperature observations for out-of-sample prediction.
- **Main result:** 1.5 C is likely to be reached around the early-to-mid 2030s, even with reduced forcing; there is a possibility of exceeding 2 C even with substantial mitigation.
- **Open work:** Updating predictions as observations accumulate and testing other forcing pathways.
- **Issues:** Dependent on CMIP6 training and scenario assumptions; uncertainty in observational datasets.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Changes in synoptic weather patterns in the polar regions in the twentieth and twenty‐first centuries, part 2: Antarctic](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.1305)
Lynch et al. (2006), *International Journal of Climatology*. 139 citations.

- **Main goal:** Describes Antarctic synoptic weather patterns and how their frequency changes between the 20th and 21st centuries.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing maps (SOM) classify daily sea level pressure fields into a set of synoptic patterns.
- **Data:** ERA-40 reanalysis sea level pressure and IPCC AR4 / CMIP3 climate model simulations for the Antarctic.
- **Main result:** Models reproduce observed patterns with biases and project shifts toward deeper circumpolar trough patterns consistent with a positive Southern Annular Mode trend.
- **Open work:** Linking pattern changes to precipitation and temperature impacts.
- **Issues:** GCM biases in Antarctic sea level pressure; reanalysis quality is limited in data-sparse regions.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Statistical emulation of climate model projections based on precomputed GCM runs](https://doi.org/10.1175/jcli-d-13-00099.1)
Castruccio et al. (2014), *Journal of Climate*. 137 citations.

- **Main goal:** Emulates climate model projections for arbitrary forcing scenarios cheaply, reusing existing GCM runs instead of new simulations.
- **Architecture:** Statistical emulator (not ML) that models regional temperature and precipitation as a function of past CO2 forcing trajectories, fitted to precomputed GCM runs.
- **Data:** Precomputed GCM simulations under multiple CO2 scenarios (CCSM3); regional annual temperature and precipitation.
- **Main result:** The emulator reproduces GCM regional temperature and precipitation responses for scenarios not used in fitting; exact errors are not reproduced here.
- **Open work:** Extending to other GCMs, variables, extremes and finer spatial scales.
- **Issues:** Only CO2 forcing; single model; emulates the GCM including its biases; abstract unavailable.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [ACE2: accurately learning subseasonal to decadal atmospheric variability and forced responses](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-025-01090-0)
Watt‐Meyer et al. (2024), *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*. 134 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds an ML atmosphere emulator that responds to external forcings (SST, greenhouse gases) and reproduces variability from days to decades.
- **Architecture:** ACE2: 450M-parameter autoregressive emulator (Spherical Fourier Neural Operator based) with 6 h steps, 1 degree resolution, and eight vertical layers; exactly conserves dry air mass and moisture.
- **Data:** ERA5 reanalysis over about 80 years, forced by SST and CO2.
- **Main result:** Stable for arbitrarily long runs at about 1500 simulated years per day; produces tropical cyclones, the MJO, and sudden stratospheric warmings; reproduces ENSO responses and 80-year temperature trends.
- **Open work:** Fixing unrealistic separate sensitivities to SST and CO2, and coupling to ocean models.
- **Issues:** Sensitivities to SST and CO2 changes individually are not realistic; coarse vertical resolution; inherits reanalysis biases.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [ACE: A fast, skillful learned global atmospheric model for climate prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02074)
Watt‐Meyer et al. (2023), *arXiv*. 113 citations.

- **Main goal:** Create a stable, physically consistent ML atmospheric model suitable for climate prediction rather than only weather.
- **Architecture:** ACE: a 200M-parameter autoregressive emulator based on Spherical Fourier Neural Operators with 6-hour steps.
- **Data:** Output of a comprehensive 100-km global atmospheric model (FV3GFS); tested also with an unseen historical SST dataset (AMIP-style).
- **Main result:** Stable for 100 years, nearly conserves column moisture, outperforms a challenging baseline on over 90% of variables, and is ~100x faster and more energy efficient.
- **Open work:** Coupling with ocean, responding to CO2 and forcings, and training on observations or reanalysis.
- **Issues:** Emulates one model, so inherits its biases; prescribed SST, no forcing change; climate change response untested.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Predicting global patterns of long-term climate change from short-term simulations using machine learning](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-020-00148-5)
Mansfield et al. (2020), *npj Climate and Atmospheric Science*. 113 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether long-term regional temperature responses to forcing can be predicted from short-term climate model simulations, to cut scenario computation costs.
- **Architecture:** Statistical learning (ridge regression and Gaussian process regression) mapping short-term temperature responses to long-term response patterns across forcing scenarios.
- **Data:** An existing ensemble of GCM simulations with different forcing perturbations (greenhouse gases, aerosols), providing paired short- and long-term responses.
- **Main result:** ML predictions of long-term regional temperature change patterns outperform simple baselines (e.g., pattern scaling) and reveal early indicators of long-term responses.
- **Open work:** Use larger multi-model datasets and data sharing between institutes to build stronger climate response emulators.
- **Issues:** Small training set of scenarios from limited models; emulator only reproduces modelled responses and is not validated against observations.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Climate Zonation in Puerto Rico Based on Principal Components Analysis and an Artificial Neural Network](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0442(1999)012<0977:cziprb>2.0.co;2)
Malmgren et al. (1999), *Journal of Climate*. 109 citations.

- **Main goal:** Defines climate zones of Puerto Rico objectively from station climate data.
- **Architecture:** Principal components analysis combined with an artificial neural network classifier for climate zonation.
- **Data:** Station temperature and precipitation climatologies across Puerto Rico.
- **Main result:** PCA and neural network classification identify distinct climate zones that reflect the island's temperature and rainfall gradients; exact skill not reported here.
- **Open work:** Using denser station networks and assessing zone changes over time.
- **Issues:** Limited number of stations; zonation depends on chosen variables and classification thresholds.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Anthropogenic fingerprints in daily precipitation revealed by deep learning](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06474-x)
Ham et al. (2023), *Nature*. 104 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether anthropogenic climate change is already detectable in daily precipitation variability despite large natural fluctuations.
- **Architecture:** CNN trained to predict annual global mean surface air temperature from daily precipitation fields, analyzed with an explainable AI framework.
- **Data:** Ensemble of present-day and future climate model simulations for training; applied to observed daily precipitation records.
- **Main result:** Observed daily precipitation predicts planetary warming and departs clearly from natural variability since the mid-2010s; sub-10-day variability over the tropical eastern Pacific and midlatitude storm tracks is most sensitive.
- **Open work:** Regional attribution of extremes and testing robustness across observational datasets and models.
- **Issues:** Relies on climate models to represent forced and natural precipitation variability correctly; observational dataset uncertainties; detection is indirect via temperature prediction.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Cool‐season precipitation in the southwestern USA since AD 1000: comparison of linear and nonlinear techniques for reconstruction](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.804)
Ni et al. (2002), *International Journal of Climatology*. 101 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs cool-season precipitation in the southwestern USA back to AD 1000 from tree-ring chronologies, testing whether nonlinear techniques improve on linear regression for paleoclimate reconstruction.
- **Architecture:** Compares multiple linear regression with a nonlinear artificial neural network (feedforward MLP) transfer function from tree-ring predictors to seasonal precipitation.
- **Data:** Tree-ring width chronologies from the southwestern USA as predictors; instrumental climate-division cool-season precipitation for calibration and verification.
- **Main result:** Both approaches yield skilful reconstructions with broadly similar verification statistics; the reconstruction documents multi-decadal droughts and wet periods over the past millennium.
- **Open work:** Extend nonlinear calibration to larger tree-ring networks and quantify reconstruction uncertainty for extremes.
- **Issues:** Short instrumental calibration period limits nonlinear model training; the nonlinear method's added value is modest and stationarity of the tree-ring–climate relation is assumed.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A regime view of northern hemisphere atmospheric variability and change under global warming](https://doi.org/10.1029/1999gl011111)
Monahan et al. (2000), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 99 citations.

- **Main goal:** Examines whether Northern Hemisphere atmospheric variability is organized in regimes and how these change under global warming.
- **Architecture:** Nonlinear principal component analysis implemented with an autoassociative neural network.
- **Data:** Northern Hemisphere fields from control and greenhouse-warming integrations of the CCCma coupled climate model.
- **Main result:** Nonlinear modes reveal regime-like behaviour; under warming, regime occupancy shifts, reflecting changes in the Arctic Oscillation-like variability.
- **Open work:** Confirm regime changes in observations and other models.
- **Issues:** Single climate model; NLPCA results sensitive to overfitting and network choices.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Emulating Earth system model temperatures with MESMER: from global mean temperature trajectories to grid-point-level realizations on land](https://doi.org/10.5194/esd-11-139-2020)
Beusch et al. (2018), *Earth System Dynamics*. 98 citations.

- **Main goal:** Generates large ensembles of spatially resolved land temperature at negligible cost to emulate Earth system model (ESM) runs for uncertainty propagation.
- **Architecture:** MESMER: modular statistical emulator with global mean temperature, local temperature response, and local residual variability modules (not deep learning).
- **Data:** Yearly land temperature 1870–2100 from 40 CMIP5 models; single-model initial-condition ensembles for validation.
- **Main result:** Training on one ESM run suffices to mimic initial-condition ensembles at grid-point to regional scales; a superensemble of 40 CMIP5 emulators is built and suggests investing in multi-model rather than large single-model ensembles.
- **Open work:** Extension to other variables (e.g. precipitation), sub-annual timescales, ocean, and CMIP6.
- **Issues:** Yearly land temperature only; separate calibration per ESM; statistical assumptions on residual variability may miss nonlinear changes.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Uncovering the Forced Climate Response from a Single Ensemble Member Using Statistical Learning](https://doi.org/10.1175/jcli-d-18-0882.1)
Sippel et al. (2019), *Journal of Climate*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Separate the forced climate response from internal circulation-driven variability, enabling forced-signal estimates from few ensemble members or a single realization.
- **Architecture:** Statistical-learning dynamical adjustment using regularized linear models (e.g. ridge-type regression) mapping circulation fields to temperature and precipitation.
- **Data:** CESM large-ensemble simulations; training on around 30 years of record.
- **Main result:** Circulation explains on average 83% and 78% of European monthly winter temperature and precipitation variability at grid-cell level and about 80% of global mean temperature and hemispheric precipitation variability; 3–5 times fewer members needed.
- **Open work:** Application to observations for detection and attribution, and handling forced changes in circulation.
- **Issues:** Assumes forced circulation changes are gradual; demonstrated mainly in one climate model, so transfer to observations needs care.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Constraints on Model Response to Greenhouse Gas Forcing and the Role of Subgrid-Scale Processes](https://doi.org/10.1175/2008jcli1869.1)
Sanderson et al. (2008), *Journal of Climate*. 91 citations.

- **Main goal:** Constrains climate model response to greenhouse gas forcing (climate sensitivity) using a perturbed-physics ensemble and identifies key subgrid-scale parameters.
- **Architecture:** Neural network emulator of model climatology and response as a function of perturbed parameters, combined with comparison to observations.
- **Data:** Perturbed-physics ensemble from the climateprediction.net project (HadSM3 slab model) and observational climatologies.
- **Main result:** Observational constraints narrow plausible climate sensitivity, with subgrid-scale parameters such as entrainment strongly controlling the response; exact ranges not reported here.
- **Open work:** Extending to fully coupled models and more parameters and observations.
- **Issues:** Results tied to one model structure; emulator error and choice of observational metrics affect constraints.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Synoptic Forcing of Precipitation over Greenland: Climatology for 1961–99](https://doi.org/10.1175/2008jhm1014.1)
Schuenemann et al. (2009), *Journal of Hydrometeorology*. 87 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds a climatology of the synoptic circulation patterns that drive precipitation over Greenland, relevant to ice-sheet mass balance.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing maps (SOM) classify daily sea-level pressure fields into a set of synoptic patterns, which are then linked to precipitation; unsupervised neural clustering.
- **Data:** ERA-40 reanalysis sea-level pressure and precipitation over Greenland and the surrounding North Atlantic, 1961–99.
- **Main result:** Distinct synoptic patterns, notably cyclones positioned near southern and southeastern Greenland, account for much of the precipitation; pattern frequencies explain seasonal and spatial precipitation variability.
- **Open work:** Applying the SOM pattern framework to climate model simulations to assess future changes in Greenland precipitation.
- **Issues:** Relies on reanalysis precipitation, which carries model biases over the ice sheet where observations are sparse.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Classification of rainfall variability by using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.702)
Michaelides et al. (2001), *International Journal of Climatology*. 86 citations.

- **Main goal:** Classifies patterns of rainfall variability to characterize rainfall regimes using neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network classification of rainfall series; the specific network type is not specified in the available metadata.
- **Data:** Rainfall records from a regional station network; locations and periods are not reported here (no abstract available).
- **Main result:** Not reported; no abstract is available for this paper.
- **Open work:** Linking identified rainfall classes to large-scale circulation and testing stability over longer records.
- **Issues:** Card based on the title only; dataset, classes and validation are unknown.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Changes in synoptic weather patterns and Greenland precipitation in the 20th and 21st centuries](https://doi.org/10.1029/2009jd011706)
Schuenemann et al. (2009), *Venue not recorded*. 80 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses how changes in synoptic weather patterns drive changes in Greenland precipitation through the 20th and 21st centuries.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing maps (SOM) of sea-level pressure define synoptic patterns; precipitation changes are decomposed into pattern-frequency and within-pattern components.
- **Data:** ERA-40 reanalysis for the historical SOM training, and CMIP3 (IPCC AR4) global climate model simulations for the 20th century and a 21st-century emissions scenario.
- **Main result:** Projected Greenland precipitation increases, with changes arising mostly from changes within patterns rather than from changes in pattern frequency.
- **Open work:** Higher-resolution regional modeling and links to ice-sheet mass balance.
- **Issues:** Coarse GCM resolution and model biases over Greenland; card partly relies on knowledge.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Attribution of Projected Changes in Atmospheric Moisture Transport in the Arctic: A Self-Organizing Map Perspective](https://doi.org/10.1175/2009jcli2645.1)
Skific et al. (2009), *Journal of Climate*. 76 citations.

- **Main goal:** Attributes projected 21st-century changes in Arctic atmospheric moisture transport to changes in circulation-pattern frequency versus changes within the patterns themselves.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing map classifying daily sea-level pressure patterns, with moisture transport changes decomposed into pattern-frequency and within-pattern contributions; not a predictive ML model.
- **Data:** Coupled climate model simulations (CCSM3) for late 20th-century and projected 21st-century climate; Arctic moisture flux fields.
- **Main result:** Projected increases in poleward moisture transport into the Arctic come mostly from changes within circulation patterns, chiefly higher atmospheric moisture, rather than shifts in pattern frequency.
- **Open work:** Extending to multi-model ensembles and linking moisture transport changes to Arctic precipitation and sea-ice changes.
- **Issues:** Relies on a single climate model and emission scenario; SOM node count and domain choices affect the decomposition.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Dimensionally reduced emulation of an AOGCM for application to integrated assessment modelling](https://doi.org/10.1029/2010gl045137)
Holden et al. (2010), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 70 citations.

- **Main goal:** Providing fast, nonlinear spatio-temporal climate change estimates for integrated assessment models as an alternative to pattern scaling.
- **Architecture:** Non-neural statistical emulator: decomposition of climate change fields into dominant spatial patterns (principal components) with regression of their dependence on model inputs.
- **Data:** Ensemble of simulations from an intermediate complexity AOGCM (GENIE-1) across greenhouse gas concentration profiles and model parameters.
- **Main result:** The emulator rapidly reconstructs a good approximation to simulated change for arbitrary concentration profiles without further simulation.
- **Open work:** Incorporating improved climate change calculations and location-dependent uncertainty into integrated assessment.
- **Issues:** Inherits limitations of the intermediate complexity model.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Changes in synoptic weather patterns and Greenland precipitation in the 20th and 21st centuries: 1. Evaluation of late 20th century simulations from IPCC models](https://doi.org/10.1029/2009jd011705)
Schuenemann et al. (2009), *Journal of Geophysical Research*. 70 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates how well IPCC AR4 climate models reproduce late-20th-century synoptic circulation patterns and associated precipitation over Greenland.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing map (SOM) classification of daily sea level pressure fields into synoptic patterns, used to compare pattern frequencies between models and reanalysis.
- **Data:** ERA-40 reanalysis daily sea level pressure and precipitation, and late-20th-century simulations from multiple IPCC AR4 (CMIP3) models.
- **Main result:** Models generally reproduce the main synoptic patterns, but pattern frequencies and associated precipitation biases differ among models; better models are identified for later projection analysis.
- **Open work:** Part 2 applies the SOM framework to 21st-century projections of Greenland precipitation.
- **Issues:** Reanalysis precipitation over Greenland is itself uncertain; SOM pattern counts depend on map size choice.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Projection of future climate change conditions using IPCC simulations, neural networks and Bayesian statistics. Part 1: Temperature mean state and seasonal cycle in South America](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-006-0134-8)
Boulanger et al. (2006), *Climate Dynamics*. 70 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces weighted multi-model projections of South American temperature by weighting IPCC models according to their skill in reproducing observed climate.
- **Architecture:** Neural network combined with Bayesian statistics to estimate model weights and combine IPCC model simulations; not a single-model emulator.
- **Data:** 20th-century and scenario simulations from IPCC AR4 (CMIP3) models with observed/reanalysis temperature climatology over South America.
- **Main result:** The weighted ensemble reproduces the observed mean temperature and seasonal cycle better than individual models and projects warming over South America with model-dependent spread.
- **Open work:** Part 2 extends the method to precipitation; further work on weighting robustness.
- **Issues:** Weights based on present-day skill may not reflect projection reliability; observational uncertainty affects weights.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Learning to Correct Climate Projection Biases](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021ms002509)
Pan et al. (2021), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 66 citations.

- **Main goal:** Corrects climate model biases beyond low-order statistics while keeping spatiotemporal consistency and dependence on the model's resolved dynamics.
- **Architecture:** Regularized Adversarial Domain Adaptation (RADA): discriminative neural networks separate simulation from observation samples, guiding domain-adaptation networks regularized by cycle-consistent statistical and dynamical constraints, a GAN-style adversarial setup.
- **Data:** Historical climate simulations and observations of daily precipitation over the contiguous United States at about 1° resolution; specific model and observation products are not named in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Corrects all considered moments of daily precipitation, preserves spatiotemporal consistency and inter-field correlations, and discriminates between dynamical conditions.
- **Open work:** Apply to other variables and regions and use it to disentangle parameterization biases from chaotic climate variability in projections.
- **Issues:** Demonstrated on a single variable and region; correcting future projections assumes the learned bias mapping holds under climate change; adversarial training can be unstable.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Neural network modelling for the analysis of forcings/temperatures relationships at different scales in the climate system](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2005.08.012)
Pasini et al. (2006), *Ecological Modelling*. 64 citations.

- **Main goal:** Analyses relationships between natural and anthropogenic forcings and temperatures at global and regional scales in the climate system using neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural network (MLP) models with ensemble training, used as nonlinear attribution tools relating forcings and circulation indices to temperature.
- **Data:** Global mean temperature records with natural (solar, volcanic) and anthropogenic (greenhouse gases, aerosols) forcing series, plus regional temperatures and circulation indices such as ENSO and NAO.
- **Main result:** Anthropogenic forcings are needed to reproduce the recent global temperature behaviour, while regional temperatures are more tied to circulation patterns.
- **Open work:** Extending the neural attribution approach to other regions, variables and to comparison with GCM-based detection and attribution.
- **Issues:** Short annual records limit training; statistical attribution may be confounded by collinear forcings.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Projection of future climate change conditions using IPCC simulations, neural networks and Bayesian statistics. Part 2: Precipitation mean state and seasonal cycle in South America](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-006-0182-0)
Boulanger et al. (2007), *Climate Dynamics*. 60 citations.

- **Main goal:** Projects future changes in South American precipitation mean state and seasonal cycle by weighting IPCC climate model simulations according to their skill.
- **Architecture:** Neural network (MLP) based method to characterise model errors combined with Bayesian statistics to weight IPCC AR4 (CMIP3) models into a multi-model projection.
- **Data:** IPCC AR4 / CMIP3 20th-century and scenario simulations and observed precipitation climatology over South America.
- **Main result:** Weighted projections indicate changes in mean precipitation and seasonal cycle over South America, with differences from equal-weight ensemble means; numbers not reported in the available metadata.
- **Open work:** Extension to other variables and to newer model ensembles.
- **Issues:** Weights based on present-climate skill may not reflect projection reliability; observational uncertainty.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Clustering and upscaling of station precipitation records to regional patterns using self-organizing maps (SOMs)](https://doi.org/10.3354/cr025095)
Crane et al. (2003), *Climate Research*. 58 citations.

- **Main goal:** Upscales station precipitation records to regional patterns to bridge point observations and the grid scales of climate models for downscaling studies.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing maps (SOMs) used to cluster daily station precipitation records into characteristic regional patterns.
- **Data:** Daily precipitation records from a network of rain gauge stations in a United States region; period is not reported here.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract; SOM clustering yields coherent regional precipitation patterns suitable for comparing with climate model output.
- **Open work:** Linking SOM precipitation patterns to atmospheric circulation for statistical downscaling of climate change scenarios.
- **Issues:** Results depend on SOM size and station density; clustering is descriptive rather than predictive.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Machine learning–based extreme event attribution](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adl3242)
Trok et al. (2024), *Science Advances*. 55 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides rapid, low-cost extreme event attribution by generating counterfactual versions of historical events at different global mean temperature levels.
- **Architecture:** Convolutional neural networks (CNN) that learn the relationship between daily temperature, global mean temperature and daily meteorological conditions, then generate counterfactual events.
- **Data:** Climate model simulations for training and observation-based fields for application (CMIP6 and ERA5 per knowledge; spot-check); southcentral North America 2023 heat event and previously analysed historical events.
- **Main result:** The 2023 southcentral North America event was 1.18–1.42 °C warmer due to global warming; similar events will occur 0.14–0.60 times per year at 2.0 °C warming. Results broadly agree with established attribution methods.
- **Open work:** Extending to precipitation and other extremes and operational rapid attribution.
- **Issues:** Relies on climate-model-learned relationships, so model biases in forced response propagate; uncertainty quantification depends on training ensembles.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Artificial neural networks and dendroclimatic reconstructions: an example from the Front Range, Colorado, USA](https://doi.org/10.1191/095968399667128516)
Woodhouse (1999), *The Holocene*. 52 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests artificial neural networks for reconstructing past climate from tree rings, compared with traditional regression.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (multilayer perceptron) versus linear regression for transfer functions from tree-ring chronologies to climate.
- **Data:** Tree-ring chronologies and instrumental precipitation records from the Front Range, Colorado, USA.
- **Main result:** Neural network reconstructions perform broadly similarly to regression-based ones; exact calibration and verification scores not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing in other regions and with more predictors.
- **Issues:** Short calibration periods favour overfitting; little gain over regression.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Detecting Climate Signals Using Explainable AI With Single‐Forcing Large Ensembles](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021ms002464)
Labe et al. (2021), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 51 citations.

- **Main goal:** Disentangle the influences of aerosols and greenhouse gases on regional surface temperature trends.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network predicting the year from near-surface temperature maps, explained with layer-wise relevance propagation plus a simple uncertainty metric to mask noise.
- **Data:** CESM1 single-forcing initial-condition large ensembles with different aerosol and greenhouse gas forcing; observational temperature maps.
- **Main result:** North Atlantic, Southern Ocean and Southeast Asia are key regions; observations correlate better with the year after training on the ensemble with aerosols fixed at 1920 levels.
- **Open work:** Further use of XAI to understand nonlinear combinations of anthropogenic forcings across models.
- **Issues:** Single climate model; LRP relevance depends on network and method choice; attribution is indirect.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Emulation and interpretation of high-dimensional climate model outputs](https://doi.org/10.1080/02664763.2015.1016412)
Holden et al. (2015), *Journal of Applied Statistics*. 51 citations.

- **Main goal:** Emulates and interprets high-dimensional climate model outputs to make expensive simulations tractable for analysis, as the title implies.
- **Architecture:** Statistical emulator for high-dimensional climate model output; the specific method is not stated here (no abstract available).
- **Data:** Not reported (no abstract available); climate model ensemble output is implied.

- **Open work:** Not reported; extension to more complex models would follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Details unknown without the abstract.

Chen et al. (2006), *Journal of Climate*. 49 citations.

Monahan et al. (2003), *Journal of Climate*. 49 citations.

Anderson et al. (2018), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 48 citations.

### [Data-model comparison using fuzzy logic in paleoclimatology](https://doi.org/10.1007/s003820050301)
Guiot et al. (1999), *Climate Dynamics*. 47 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares palaeoclimate model simulations with proxy-based reconstructions in a way that accounts for the uncertainties of both.
- **Architecture:** Fuzzy logic comparison method using membership functions to measure agreement between simulated and reconstructed climate variables; non-neural method.
- **Data:** Mid-Holocene (6 ka) climate model simulations and pollen-based palaeoclimate reconstructions, mainly over Europe.
- **Main result:** Fuzzy-logic distances give a more nuanced, uncertainty-aware assessment of model-data agreement than crisp comparisons; specific scores are not reproduced here.
- **Open work:** Applying the approach to more models, periods and proxy types, and to model evaluation in multi-model intercomparisons.
- **Issues:** Results depend on the chosen membership functions and on proxy reconstruction uncertainties; spatial coverage of proxies is uneven.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A Deep Learning Earth System Model for Efficient Simulation of the Observed Climate](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025av001706)
Cresswell-Clay et al. (2024), *AGU Advances*. 46 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds an efficient deep learning Earth system model that simulates the current climate stably for long periods.
- **Architecture:** DLESyM: coupled atmosphere and ocean deep learning model (convolutional networks on a HEALPix mesh) for atmosphere state and SST.
- **Data:** Historical reanalysis and satellite observations; compared with historical simulations from four CMIP6 models.
- **Main result:** Stable 1000-year simulations with little smoothing or drift; matches or beats CMIP6 models for tropical cyclogenesis, the Indian summer monsoon cycle, and mid-latitude blocking climatology.
- **Open work:** Use for subseasonal and seasonal forecasting and extension to forced climate change.
- **Issues:** Simulates current climate only, not forced changes; limited set of variables; inherits reanalysis biases.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Dendroclimatic transfer functions revisited: Little Ice Age and Medieval Warm Period summer temperatures reconstructed using artificial neural networks and linear algorithms](https://doi.org/10.5194/angeo-27-1097-2009)
Helama et al. (2009), *Annales Geophysicae*. 46 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares linear and nonlinear transfer functions for reconstructing past summer temperatures from tree-ring chronologies.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural networks compared with multiple linear regression, linear scaling and a hybrid timescale-separated MLR model.
- **Data:** Regional tree-ring chronology and instrumental temperatures from Lapland (northern Finland and Sweden), AD 1802–1998 instrumental, reconstruction AD 802–1801.
- **Main result:** MLR and ANN reconstruct reliably; linear scaling fails. MLR shows ~0.5 °C cooling from the Medieval Warm Period to the Little Ice Age, ANNs 0.2–0.5 °C.
- **Open work:** Applying ANNs to proxies and environments with more complex, noisier climate relationships.
- **Issues:** Larger model disagreement outside the calibration period; ANNs give no clear benefit for this timberline dataset.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Synoptically forced hydroclimatology of major Arctic watersheds in general circulation models; Part 1: the Mackenzie River Basin](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.1753)
Finnis et al. (2009), *International Journal of Climatology*. 46 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates how general circulation models represent synoptically forced precipitation in the Mackenzie River Basin and how it changes in the future.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing maps classify synoptic sea level pressure patterns, used to diagnose precipitation by pattern in reanalysis and GCMs; climate diagnosis rather than prediction.
- **Data:** Reanalysis atmospheric fields and precipitation with CMIP3 (IPCC AR4) GCM simulations for present and future climates.
- **Main result:** GCMs reproduce the main synoptic patterns; projected precipitation increases arise mainly from changes within patterns (more moisture) rather than circulation frequency changes.
- **Open work:** Applying the framework to other Arctic watersheds (subsequent parts) and to newer model generations.
- **Issues:** Coarse GCM resolution and reanalysis precipitation uncertainty; SOM node choice affects attribution.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### Data Mining for the Discovery of Ocean Climate Indices
Steinbach et al. (2002), *Venue not recorded*. 45 citations.

- **Main goal:** Uses data mining to discover ocean climate indices that explain land climate variability.
- **Architecture:** Shared nearest neighbour (SNN) clustering of ocean time series to identify candidate climate indices.
- **Data:** Global gridded sea surface temperature and sea level pressure from reanalysis, with land climate variables for correlation.
- **Main result:** Clusters reproduce known indices such as SOI and NAO and suggest new candidate indices correlated with land climate.
- **Open work:** Physical interpretation and validation of new candidate indices.
- **Issues:** Clustering results depend on parameters; candidate indices may be spurious correlations.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Nonlinear atmospheric teleconnections](https://doi.org/10.1029/2005gl025471)
Hsieh et al. (2006), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 43 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reveals nonlinear winter atmospheric teleconnection patterns over the Northern Hemisphere associated with ENSO and the Arctic Oscillation.
- **Architecture:** Neural network (multilayer perceptron) nonlinear regression of climate fields onto ENSO and AO indices, compared with linear regression teleconnections.
- **Data:** Winter surface air temperature, precipitation, sea level pressure and 500 hPa geopotential height over the Northern Hemisphere with ENSO and AO indices; source dataset not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Nonlinear teleconnections relate quadratically to the ENSO and AO indices and propagate perturbations farther, into regions where linear teleconnections are insignificant.
- **Open work:** Physical explanation of the quadratic response and use of nonlinear teleconnections in seasonal forecasting.
- **Issues:** Limited record length for fitting nonlinear models; risk of overfitting; seasonal means only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Toward machine-assisted tuning avoiding the underestimation of uncertainty in climate change projections](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adf2758)
Hourdin et al. (2023), *Science Advances*. 42 citations.

- **Main goal:** Addresses the underestimation of uncertainty in climate projections caused by selecting a single tuned parameter configuration per climate model.
- **Architecture:** Machine-assisted tuning via history matching with statistical emulators of the climate model, used to explore free parameter space; the emulator type is not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** Perturbed-parameter simulations of a climate model (IPSL model family) constrained by present-day observations of the climate system.
- **Main result:** Automatic selection yields multiple parameter configurations all consistent with present-day observations but producing different warming worlds.
- **Open work:** Integrate parametric uncertainty quantification into CMIP contributions and accelerate model improvement.
- **Issues:** Quantitative details not given in the abstract; results depend on chosen metrics and tolerance to observational error.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Constraining Uncertainty in Projected Gross Primary Production With Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019jg005619)
Schlund et al. (2020), *Journal of Geophysical Research - Biogeosciences*. 42 citations.

- **Main goal:** Constrains the large spread in Earth system model projections of gross primary production (GPP) under CO2 fertilization.
- **Architecture:** Emergent constraint on CO2 fertilization combined with a machine learning regression trained on CMIP5 models; the ML model family is not specified in the abstract.
- **Data:** CMIP5 ESMs under RCP8.5, observed CO2 seasonal cycle changes at Cape Kumukahi, and observational diagnostics as ML inputs.
- **Main result:** Constrains 2091–2100 global GPP to 171 ± 12 Gt C/yr versus an unconstrained 156–247; ML beats the CMIP5 mean in leave-one-model-out cross-validation and predicts larger GPP gains at high northern latitudes.
- **Open work:** Apply to CMIP6 and to other carbon cycle variables.
- **Issues:** Relies on CMIP5 structural assumptions and the validity of the emergent constraint; cross-validation uses models, not observed futures.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Challenges of learning multi-scale dynamics with AI weather models: Implications for stability and one solution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07029)
Chattopadhyay et al. (2023), *arXiv*. 41 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explain why AI weather models become unstable or unphysical on long integrations and propose a remedy.
- **Architecture:** Theoretical and numerical analysis linking instability to spectral bias of deep networks, plus a mitigation approach targeting small-scale learning.
- **Data:** Quasi-geostrophic turbulence simulations and ERA5 reanalysis.
- **Main result:** Identifies spectral bias as a universal cause of instability; the proposed solution gives accurate short-term forecasts and stable centuries-long integration with realistic mean and variability.
- **Open work:** Applying the mitigation to full-scale AI weather models and assessing climate change responses.
- **Issues:** Demonstrated on QG and limited ERA5 setting; mitigation may not generalize to all architectures.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Fldgen v1.0: an emulator with internal variability and space–time correlation for Earth system models](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-12-1477-2019)
Link et al. (2019), *Geoscientific Model Development*. 40 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides a cheap emulator of Earth system model temperature fields with realistic internal variability so large ensembles and many scenarios can be explored.
- **Architecture:** Non-ML statistical emulator: a deterministic pattern-scaling mean response to global temperature plus stochastic residual variability fields with space-time correlation (EOF and Fourier phase randomization), released as an R package.
- **Data:** Gridded temperature output of Earth system models (CMIP5-era ESM runs) used to fit the mean response and residual variability.
- **Main result:** Generated fields have spatially and temporally coherent variability and statistically reproduce the target ESM properties; arbitrarily many realisations can be produced.
- **Open work:** Extending to other variables such as precipitation and joint multivariate fields, and coupling to human-Earth system models.
- **Issues:** Variability statistics are assumed stationary and tied to the mean-response relation; only temperature is emulated and fidelity is limited to properties the method is built to capture.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Towards ice‐core‐based synoptic reconstructions of west antarctic climate with artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.1143)
Reusch et al. (2005), *International Journal of Climatology*. 39 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs West Antarctic synoptic climate from ice-core records using neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing maps linking ice-core chemistry to atmospheric circulation patterns.
- **Data:** West Antarctic ice-core records and ERA-40 reanalysis atmospheric fields.
- **Main result:** The approach shows promise for synoptic reconstructions from ice cores.
- **Open work:** More cores and longer reconstructions.
- **Issues:** Weak and noisy relationships; reanalysis biases in Antarctica.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [LUCIE: A Lightweight Uncoupled Climate Emulator With Long‐Term Stability and Physical Consistency](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025ms005152)
Guan et al. (2024), *Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems*. 37 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds a lightweight data-driven climate emulator that remains stable and physically consistent over century-long autoregressive runs, unlike most AI weather models.
- **Architecture:** Low-resolution SFNO-based emulator with a hard-constrained first-order integrator, spectral regularization for fine scales, and a training strategy for data-limited settings.
- **Data:** 6-hourly ERA5 at coarse resolution; can be trained on as little as 2 years of data.
- **Main result:** Stable for 100-year simulations with 100 ensemble members; climatology and variability of temperature, wind, precipitation and humidity match ERA5; trains in 2.4 hours on one A100.
- **Open work:** Using large ensembles to study extremes, responses to external forcing, and variable importance; adding forcing to represent climate change.
- **Issues:** Coarse resolution and no ocean coupling or time-varying forcing, so it reproduces present-day climate rather than projections; inherits ERA5 biases.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*
