### [Predicting monthly streamflow using data‐driven models coupled with data‐preprocessing techniques](https://doi.org/10.1029/2007wr006737)
Wu et al. (2009), *Water Resources Research*. 414 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves monthly streamflow prediction by coupling data-driven models with data-preprocessing techniques.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of ARMA, k-nearest neighbour (KNN) and artificial neural network models, coupled with moving average, singular spectrum analysis and wavelet multiresolution preprocessing.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow series from several catchments in China.
- **Main result:** Data preprocessing improves forecasts substantially, with the neural network combined with moving average preprocessing performing best.
- **Open work:** Assessing other preprocessing methods and the practical lag introduced by smoothing.
- **Issues:** Preprocessing with centred filters can leak future information and introduce lags; limited sites.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Artificial neural network modeling of water table depth fluctuations](https://doi.org/10.1029/2000wr900368)
Coulibaly et al. (2001), *Water Resources Research*. 401 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models and forecasts water table depth fluctuations in an aquifer to support groundwater management in a data-scarce region.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of input delay neural networks, recurrent neural networks and radial basis function networks.
- **Data:** Water table depth, precipitation and temperature records from the Gondo aquifer, Burkina Faso.
- **Main result:** Neural networks reproduce water table fluctuations well, with the recurrent network giving the most accurate forecasts.
- **Open work:** Testing longer horizons and other aquifers, and including pumping information.
- **Issues:** Short records from one aquifer; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Model trees as an alternative to neural networks in rainfall—runoff modelling](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.48.3.399.45291)
Solomatine et al. (2003), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 396 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests model trees as an interpretable alternative to neural networks for rainfall-runoff forecasting.
- **Architecture:** M5 model trees (piecewise linear regression trees) compared with artificial neural networks (MLP).
- **Data:** Hourly rainfall and discharge data from the Sieve catchment, Italy, with forecasts several hours ahead.
- **Main result:** Model trees achieve accuracy similar to neural networks while being faster to train and more transparent.
- **Open work:** Testing on other catchments and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; performance degrades for longer horizons as for ANNs.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Process‐Guided Deep Learning Predictions of Lake Water Temperature](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr024922)
Read et al. (2019), *Water Resources Research*. 394 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts depth-specific lake water temperature with a hybrid model that integrates physical theory with deep learning.
- **Architecture:** Process-Guided Deep Learning (PGDL): LSTM recurrent neural network with an energy-conservation penalty in the loss and pretraining on outputs of a process-based lake model.
- **Data:** In situ lake temperature observations and process-based (General Lake Model) simulations for two detailed study lakes and 68 additional lakes.
- **Main result:** PGDL beats DL and process-based models; across 68 lakes median test RMSE is 1.65 °C versus 1.78 °C (DL) and 2.03 °C (PB).
- **Open work:** Applying process-guided deep learning to other environmental variables and larger lake populations.
- **Issues:** Gains depend on pretraining data having more variability than the training period; in some lakes PB or DL is more accurate.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A review of the artificial intelligence methods in groundwater level modeling](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2018.12.037)
Rajaee et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 386 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews artificial intelligence methods for groundwater level modelling and forecasting to provide practical guidelines.
- **Architecture:** Review of 67 papers (2001–2018) on AI methods such as artificial neural networks, neuro-fuzzy, support vector machines and hybrid models for groundwater level.
- **Data:** Reviewed studies on groundwater level time series in various aquifers; no new data.
- **Main result:** Properly developed AI methods can simulate and forecast groundwater level, though many modelling steps rely on trial and error.
- **Open work:** Proposes new ideas for innovative methods and improved modelling quality.
- **Issues:** Qualitative synthesis; predates widespread deep learning use.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Streamflow Forecasting Using Different Artificial Neural Network Algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2007)12:5(532))
Kisi (2007), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 383 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts streamflow with artificial neural networks and compares different network training algorithms.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural networks trained with different algorithms; the network family beyond ANN is not specified in the available metadata.
- **Data:** Streamflow time series; the river and period are not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Compares forecast skill across training algorithms; specific results are not available here.
- **Open work:** Testing on other basins and with additional inputs.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single-variable time series forecasting.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Interpretable spatio-temporal attention LSTM model for flood forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2020.04.110)
Ding et al. (2020), *Neurocomputing*. 377 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds an accurate and interpretable deep learning flood forecasting model, addressing low robustness of hydrological models and opacity of ML.
- **Architecture:** Spatio-temporal attention long short-term memory (STA-LSTM) network with dynamic spatial and temporal attention, trained with Adam.
- **Data:** Hydrological data from three small and medium basins in China.
- **Main result:** STA-LSTM outperforms HA, FCN, CNN, GCN, LSTM, SA-LSTM and TA-LSTM in most cases, and attention weights are physically reasonable.
- **Open work:** Testing on larger basins and more systematic interpretability evaluation.
- **Issues:** Attention weights are a limited form of interpretation; only three basins.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Drought forecasting using feed-forward recursive neural network](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2006.04.017)
Mishra et al. (2006), *Ecological Modelling*. 377 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts drought, measured by the Standardized Precipitation Index, at several lead times to aid drought planning.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural networks applied with recursive multistep and direct multistep forecasting strategies.
- **Data:** SPI series from a river basin in India (Kansabati basin); details should be checked.
- **Main result:** Neural network approaches give useful drought forecasts, with differences between recursive and direct strategies by lead time; numbers not available here.
- **Open work:** Hybrid stochastic–neural models and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single-basin study.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Improved weighting methods, deterministic and stochastic data-driven models for estimation of missing precipitation records](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.02.015)
Teegavarapu et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrology*. 375 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates missing daily precipitation records at rain gauges, a common gap-filling problem for hydrological analysis.
- **Architecture:** Compares improved inverse-distance and correlation-based weighting schemes with data-driven models, including an artificial neural network (MLP) and kriging-type stochastic interpolation.
- **Data:** Long-term daily precipitation records from a rain gauge network in Kentucky, USA.
- **Main result:** Modified weighting methods and the neural network improve on the classical inverse distance weighting method for filling missing records.
- **Open work:** Testing in other climates and gauge densities and handling of dry/wet day classification remain open.
- **Issues:** Single regional gauge network; performance depends on correlation between neighbouring stations and may degrade for extremes.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Application of ANN for Reservoir Inflow Prediction and Operation](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9496(1999)125:5(263))
Jain et al. (1999), *Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management*. 371 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts reservoir inflow and derives operating rules to improve reservoir management.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural network (multilayer perceptron) for inflow forecasting and for releases, compared with time series models.
- **Data:** Inflow and operation records of the Indravati reservoir, India.
- **Main result:** The neural network forecasts inflows better than conventional time series models, notably for high flows, and helps model operation rules.
- **Open work:** Integration with optimization and broader validation.
- **Issues:** Single reservoir; network design by trial and error.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Multi-criteria calibration of a conceptual runoff model using a genetic algorithm](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-4-215-2000)
Seibert (2000), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 371 citations.

- **Main goal:** Calibrates a conceptual runoff model against several output variables to obtain reliable simulations of internal catchment processes and reduce parameter uncertainty.
- **Architecture:** Non-ML optimisation: a genetic algorithm combined with local optimisation for automatic single- and multi-criteria calibration of the HBV conceptual runoff model.
- **Data:** Observed runoff and groundwater level time series in two catchments with different geology, plus a synthetic error-free test case.
- **Main result:** The algorithm usually recovers true parameters in the synthetic case; calibrating on runoff and groundwater levels together constrains parameters much more than runoff alone, and motivated a model-structure change in one catchment.
- **Open work:** Extending multi-criteria calibration to other internal variables and catchments, and refining model structure where calibration reveals inconsistencies.
- **Issues:** Only two catchments; parameter equifinality remains when only runoff is used; groundwater data are point measurements compared with a lumped storage.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Statistical downscaling of GCM simulations to streamflow using relevance vector machine](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2007.07.005)
Ghosh et al. (2008), *Advances in Water Resources*. 370 citations.

- **Main goal:** Downscales general circulation model simulations to basin-scale streamflow to assess climate change impacts on hydrology.
- **Architecture:** Relevance vector machine (sparse Bayesian kernel regression), with PCA and fuzzy clustering of predictors, compared with a support vector machine.
- **Data:** Reanalysis predictors for training and CGCM2 GCM simulations, with observed streamflow of the Mahanadi River, India.
- **Main result:** The relevance vector machine performs comparably or better than SVM with fewer relevance vectors and projects decreasing streamflow in the basin.
- **Open work:** Multi-GCM uncertainty and other basins.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single GCM and basin, stationarity assumption of downscaling.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [PRECIPITATION-RUNOFF MODELING USING ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORKS AND CONCEPTUAL MODELS](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2000)5:2(156))
Tokar et al. (2000), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 365 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses whether artificial neural networks can model precipitation-runoff as well as conceptual hydrological models.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) compared with conceptual rainfall-runoff models such as the Sacramento soil moisture accounting model.
- **Data:** Precipitation, temperature and streamflow records from three US watersheds (Fraser River, Colorado; Raccoon Creek, Iowa; Little Patuxent River, Maryland).
- **Main result:** The neural networks give comparable or better runoff simulations than the conceptual models.
- **Open work:** Combining physical understanding with neural networks and testing generalisation to other basins.
- **Issues:** Black-box model with limited physical interpretability; performance on extremes and outside the training range is uncertain.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Groundwater Level Forecasting in a Shallow Aquifer Using Artificial Neural Network Approach](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-006-4007-z)
Nayak et al. (2006), *Water Resources Management*. 363 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater levels in a shallow unconfined aquifer to support water management.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) trained with backpropagation, using past groundwater levels, rainfall and canal releases as inputs.
- **Data:** Observation-well groundwater levels with rainfall and canal release data from the Central Godavari Delta, Andhra Pradesh, India.
- **Main result:** The neural network forecasts groundwater levels with reasonable accuracy up to several months ahead.
- **Open work:** Extending to more wells, spatial forecasting and coupling with physically based groundwater models.
- **Issues:** Site-specific wells; data-driven model cannot represent aquifer physics or changing pumping regimes.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A Multivariate ANN-Wavelet Approach for Rainfall–Runoff Modeling](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-009-9414-5)
Nourani et al. (2009), *Water Resources Management*. 356 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves rainfall-runoff modelling by capturing multiscale features of the input time series.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid wavelet-ANN: discrete wavelet transform decomposes rainfall and runoff series into subseries that feed a multivariate artificial neural network (MLP).
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from the Ligvanchai watershed near Tabriz, Iran.
- **Main result:** The wavelet-ANN model outperforms a plain neural network and a linear ARIMAX-type model, especially for peak flows.
- **Open work:** Choice of wavelet type and decomposition level and extension to other catchments.
- **Issues:** Single small watershed; wavelet decomposition can leak future information if not applied causally; extremes are few.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Neural-Network Models of Rainfall-Runoff Process](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9496(1995)121:6(499))
Smith et al. (1995), *Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management*. 343 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explores neural networks as rainfall-runoff models, predicting peak discharge and full hydrographs.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward backpropagation neural network (multilayer perceptron); hydrographs represented through Fourier series coefficients.
- **Data:** Synthetic rainfall-runoff data generated on a grid of cells representing a watershed.
- **Main result:** The network predicts peak discharge and timing and reconstructs hydrographs well for the synthetic cases.
- **Open work:** Application to real watersheds with observed data.
- **Issues:** Synthetic data only; idealized watershed representation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Comparison of Several Flood Forecasting Models in Yangtze River](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2005)10:6(485))
Chau et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 342 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares data-driven flood forecasting models for a large river to identify accurate and practical options.
- **Architecture:** Compares linear regression, an artificial neural network (MLP), a genetic-algorithm-trained neural network and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS).
- **Data:** Water level or discharge records from stations in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, China.
- **Main result:** The genetic-algorithm-based neural network and ANFIS outperform the linear model and standard neural network, with ANFIS needing fewer parameters.
- **Open work:** Testing longer lead times and other reaches and combining with hydrodynamic models.
- **Issues:** Single river reach; limited number of flood events; short lead times.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Deep learning rainfall-runoff predictions of extreme events](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-2021-423)
Frame et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 341 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether deep learning rainfall-runoff models remain reliable for extreme, high return-period events not seen in training.
- **Architecture:** LSTM recurrent neural network and a mass-conserving LSTM (MC-LSTM) variant architecturally constrained to conserve water mass.
- **Data:** CAMELS US basins with daily forcing and streamflow; benchmarks are the Sacramento conceptual model and the US National Water Model.
- **Main result:** LSTM and MC-LSTM remain relatively accurate for extreme events, even when extremes are excluded from training; adding mass-balance constraints reduced skill during extremes.
- **Open work:** Understanding why mass constraints hurt extremes and improving data-driven extrapolation.
- **Issues:** Limited to US basins and daily resolution; few truly extreme events available for evaluation.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A non-linear rainfall–runoff model using an artificial neural network](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(98)00273-x)
Sajikumar et al. (1999), *Journal of Hydrology*. 340 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models monthly rainfall-runoff with limited data using neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Temporal backpropagation neural network (feedforward network with time-delay connections), compared with a Volterra-type functional series model.
- **Data:** Monthly rainfall and runoff from catchments including the River Lee (UK) and the Thuthapuzha (Kerala, India).
- **Main result:** The neural network models rainfall-runoff well even with short calibration records and outperforms the functional series model.
- **Open work:** Daily scale and more catchments.
- **Issues:** Monthly resolution; few catchments; black-box structure.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Drought forecasting using artificial neural networks and time series of drought indices](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.1498)
Morid et al. (2007), *International Journal of Climatology*. 338 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts drought indices months ahead to support drought early warning.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) predicting the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Effective Drought Index (EDI) from past rainfall, index values and climate indices such as SOI and NAO.
- **Data:** Rainfall records from stations in Tehran Province, Iran, with SOI and NAO indices.
- **Main result:** The neural networks forecast drought indices with useful skill at lead times up to about 12 months, with EDI better predicted than SPI.
- **Open work:** Including more large-scale climate predictors and extending to other regions.
- **Issues:** Limited station set; skill decreases with lead time; relatively few drought events.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [River flow forecasting: use of phase-space reconstruction and artificial neural networks approaches](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(02)00112-9)
Sivakumar et al. (2002), *Journal of Hydrology*. 332 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares chaos-based and neural network approaches for forecasting daily river flow.
- **Architecture:** Phase-space reconstruction with local approximation (nonlinear dynamics, non-ML) compared with a feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP).
- **Data:** Daily river flow series from the Chao Phraya River, Thailand.
- **Main result:** Phase-space reconstruction gives better flow forecasts than the neural network at the tested lead times.
- **Open work:** Combining both approaches and testing other rivers and time scales.
- **Issues:** Single river; univariate inputs; conclusions sensitive to embedding parameter choices.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A comparative analysis of training methods for artificial neural network rainfall-runoff models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asoc.2005.02.002)
Srinivasulu et al. (2006), *Applied Soft Computing*. 329 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares training methods for neural network rainfall-runoff models to improve their accuracy.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network trained by backpropagation versus a real-coded genetic algorithm, among other training approaches.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall and streamflow data from the Kentucky River basin, USA.
- **Main result:** Genetic-algorithm training gives better rainfall-runoff models than backpropagation, especially for high flows.
- **Open work:** Testing hybrid and evolutionary training schemes on more catchments.
- **Issues:** Single basin; computational cost of genetic training; limited assessment of uncertainty.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [FLOOD STAGE FORECASTING WITH SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES 1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-1688.2002.tb01544.x)
Liong et al. (2002), *JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association*. 328 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts flood stage at a river location to improve flood warning.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine regression compared with an artificial neural network (MLP).
- **Data:** Daily water level records from gauging stations upstream of and at Dhaka, Bangladesh.
- **Main result:** The support vector machine forecasts flood stage accurately for lead times of up to about seven days and outperforms the neural network.
- **Open work:** Kernel and parameter selection and extension to other river systems.
- **Issues:** Single river system; skill decreases with lead time; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Evaluation of global terrestrial evapotranspiration using state-of-the-art approaches in remote sensing, machine learning and land surface modeling](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-24-1485-2020)
Pan et al. (2019), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 325 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates global terrestrial evapotranspiration estimates from remote sensing, machine learning and land surface models, since ET cannot be measured directly globally.
- **Architecture:** Review and intercomparison of 4 remote-sensing physical models, 2 machine-learning upscaling algorithms and 14 land surface models (TRENDY ensemble); not a new ML model.
- **Data:** Global gridded ET products and land surface model simulations, 1982-2011.
- **Main result:** Ensemble means agree at 589.6-617.1 mm/yr; remote sensing and ML ensembles show significant increasing trends (0.62 and 0.38 mm/yr2) while LSMs do not; greening increases ET.
- **Open work:** Better water stress and canopy parameterization, new satellite retrievals, deep learning and model-data fusion.
- **Issues:** Large uncertainties in the Amazon and arid/semiarid regions; ML products inherit flux tower sampling biases.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A comparison between neural-network forecasting techniques-case study: river flow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1109/72.750569)
Atiya et al. (1999), *IEEE Trans. Neural Networks*. 325 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares neural network forecasting approaches for river flow, using the Nile River as a case study, to identify which input representations and forecast set-ups work best.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron forecasters with different input preprocessing and forecasting strategies, compared against one another and simpler baselines.
- **Data:** Historical Nile River flow records at an upstream gauging station; record length and split not reported here.
- **Main result:** Finds that the choice of input representation strongly affects accuracy and that suitably configured neural networks forecast flow well; exact error statistics not reproduced here.
- **Open work:** Testing on other rivers and including upstream rainfall or climate indices as inputs.
- **Issues:** Single-river case study; lacks uncertainty estimates and comparisons with physically based hydrological models.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Optimal division of data for neural network models in water resources applications](https://doi.org/10.1029/2001wr000266)
Bowden et al. (2002), *Water Resources Research*. 325 citations.

- **Main goal:** Examines how data are divided into training, testing and validation sets for neural network models in water resources.
- **Architecture:** Data-division methods using a genetic algorithm and a self-organizing map (SOM) to create statistically similar subsets for MLP neural network models.
- **Data:** Salinity forecasting case study for the River Murray, South Australia, plus a synthetic data example.
- **Main result:** Both the genetic algorithm and SOM-based divisions produce representative subsets and improve the reliability of neural network performance evaluation compared with arbitrary splits.
- **Open work:** Testing on more applications and accounting for temporal dependence in division.
- **Issues:** Random-like splits of time series can inflate apparent skill; results tied to one case study.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Drought assessment and monitoring through blending of multi-sensor indices using machine learning approaches for different climate regions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2015.10.011)
Park et al. (2016), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*. 324 citations.

- **Main goal:** Monitors drought by blending multiple satellite drought indices with machine learning for different climate regions.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning models including random forest, boosted regression trees and Cubist used to combine multi-sensor drought indices.
- **Data:** Satellite indices from MODIS (vegetation and land surface temperature) and TRMM precipitation, evaluated against in situ drought indices and US Drought Monitor in arid and humid US regions.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the abstract (unavailable); random forest is reported to perform best and blended indices outperform individual indices.
- **Open work:** Extending to other regions and to drought forecasting.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; quantitative results and exact regions not verified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Particle Swarm Optimization Training Algorithm for ANNs in Stage Prediction of Shing Mun River](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2006.02.025)
Chau (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 322 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves the training of neural networks for river stage prediction.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network trained with particle swarm optimization instead of backpropagation.
- **Data:** Water level records from the Shing Mun River, Hong Kong.
- **Main result:** Particle swarm optimization training converges faster and gives more accurate stage predictions than backpropagation.
- **Open work:** Applying swarm-based training to other networks and hydrological problems.
- **Issues:** Single river; short lead times; limited comparison with other optimisers.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Rainfall-Runoff Prediction at Multiple Timescales with a Single Long Short-Term Memory Network](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-2020-540)
Gauch et al. (2020), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 319 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts discharge at multiple timescales (daily and hourly) with one model, since sub-daily flood peaks are missed by daily models.
- **Architecture:** Two multi-timescale LSTM (MTS-LSTM) architectures that process long-past inputs at coarse resolution and recent inputs at fine resolution.
- **Data:** 516 basins across the contiguous US with hourly and daily forcings and discharge; benchmark is the US National Water Model.
- **Main result:** MTS-LSTMs achieve significantly higher NSE than the National Water Model and match per-timescale LSTMs with lower computational cost.
- **Open work:** Operational use with forcings of differing lead times and resolutions.
- **Issues:** US basins only; simulation with observed forcing rather than true forecasting; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [M5 Model Trees and Neural Networks: Application to Flood Forecasting in the Upper Reach of the Huai River in China](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2004)9:6(491))
Solomatine et al. (2004), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 317 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares data-driven models for flood forecasting in a Chinese river basin.
- **Architecture:** M5 model trees (piecewise linear regression trees) compared with artificial neural networks (MLP).
- **Data:** Daily rainfall and discharge records from the upper reach of the Huai River, China.
- **Main result:** M5 model trees and neural networks give similar forecast accuracy, with model trees being more transparent and faster to train.
- **Open work:** Combining models in committees or modular schemes and extending lead times.
- **Issues:** Single basin; short lead times; few extreme flood events in the record.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Neural networks and M5 model trees in modelling water level-discharge relationship](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2004.04.016)
Bhattacharya et al. (2005), *Neurocomputing*. 314 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models the water level-discharge (rating curve) relationship, including hysteresis effects, using data-driven methods.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) and M5 model trees compared with conventional rating curves.
- **Data:** Stage and discharge measurements from a river gauging station in India.
- **Main result:** Both neural networks and M5 model trees reproduce discharge more accurately than the traditional rating curve.
- **Open work:** Applying to other stations and including additional hydraulic inputs.
- **Issues:** Single station; limited high-flow measurements; data-driven models may extrapolate poorly.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Groundwater level forecasting with artificial neural networks: a comparison of long short-term memory (LSTM), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and non-linear autoregressive networks with exogenous input (NARX)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-25-1671-2021)
Wunsch et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 313 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares shallow and deep neural networks for groundwater level forecasting using only widely available meteorological inputs.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of NARX (non-linear autoregressive network with exogenous input), LSTM recurrent networks and convolutional neural networks for seq2val and seq2seq forecasting.
- **Data:** Groundwater level time series from wells with meteorological inputs (precipitation, temperature); 4-year test period; well locations not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** NARX performs best on average, CNNs are much faster and slightly worse; with small training data NARX clearly beats LSTM and CNN.
- **Open work:** Testing with larger datasets where deep learning may excel.
- **Issues:** NARX is sensitive to initialization (handled by ensembles); conclusions depend on the small data typical of groundwater.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Monthly runoff forecasting based on LSTM–ALO model](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00477-018-1560-y)
Yuan et al. (2018), *Stochastic environmental research and risk assessment (Print)*. 313 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts monthly runoff with a deep learning model whose parameters are optimized automatically.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) network with parameters tuned by the ant lion optimizer (ALO).
- **Data:** Monthly runoff records; the basin and period are not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Reports that LSTM-ALO improves monthly runoff forecasting over comparison models; numbers not available here.
- **Open work:** Testing other basins and inputs.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; single-variable monthly series, small data.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Methods for combining the outputs of different rainfall–runoff models](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(96)03259-3)
Shamseldin et al. (1997), *Journal of Hydrology*. 311 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates whether combining discharge forecasts from several rainfall-runoff models yields better simulations than any single model.
- **Architecture:** Three combination methods: simple averaging, weighted averaging with least-squares weights, and a neural network (multilayer perceptron) combiner of the individual model outputs.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall-runoff records from multiple catchments with differing climates, each simulated by several rainfall-runoff models.
- **Main result:** Combined outputs generally outperform the best individual model, with the neural network combination performing best overall.
- **Open work:** Testing combination schemes with more diverse models and in real-time forecasting with updating.
- **Issues:** Gains depend on the diversity and quality of the member models; the neural combiner adds parameters and risks overfitting on short records.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A deep convolutional neural network model for rapid prediction of fluvial flood inundation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125481)
Kabir et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 310 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides rapid prediction of fluvial flood inundation because 2D hydraulic models are too slow for real-time use.
- **Architecture:** Deep convolutional neural network (CNN) trained to predict water depths, benchmarked against support vector regression.
- **Data:** LISFLOOD-FP 2D hydraulic model outputs for Carlisle, UK, evaluated on the January 2005 and December 2015 floods.
- **Main result:** CNN agrees well with LISFLOOD-FP and beats SVR; maximum-depth errors are 0–0.2 m (2005) and 0–0.5 m (2015) at over 99% of cells.
- **Open work:** Real-time flood forecasting deployment and other sites.
- **Issues:** Trained on and evaluated against its own hydraulic model, inheriting its errors; single town.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [SOIL MOISTURE PREDICTION USING SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES 1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-1688.2006.tb04512.x)
Gill et al. (2006), *JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association*. 310 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts soil moisture several days ahead to support irrigation and water management decisions, using a data-driven alternative to physically based soil water models.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine (support vector regression) using lagged soil moisture and meteorological inputs, compared with a multilayer perceptron (MLP) artificial neural network.
- **Data:** Point soil moisture and meteorological observations from monitoring sites in the western United States; exact sites and record lengths are not given here.
- **Main result:** Support vector machines give soil moisture forecasts a few days ahead that are as good as or better than the neural network benchmark.
- **Open work:** Testing other sites, soil types and longer lead times, and adding uncertainty estimates to the forecasts.
- **Issues:** Point-scale study with limited sites; no abstract available, so details of inputs and skill scores are not verified here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Automated Mapping of Montane Snow Cover at Subpixel Resolution from the Landsat Thematic Mapper](https://doi.org/10.1029/95wr02718)
Rosenthal et al. (1996), *Water Resources Research*. 307 citations.

- **Main goal:** Maps fractional snow-covered area in mountainous terrain at subpixel resolution from Landsat TM imagery, needed for snowmelt hydrology.
- **Architecture:** Spectral mixture analysis combined with a binary regression (decision) tree that predicts snow fraction from TM band reflectances.
- **Data:** Landsat Thematic Mapper scenes over montane terrain in the Sierra Nevada, with higher-resolution reference data for validation.
- **Main result:** Produces automated subpixel snow-cover maps with good agreement with reference snow fractions; exact error values not reproduced here.
- **Open work:** Extension to other sensors with more frequent revisit and to other mountain ranges.
- **Issues:** Accuracy is affected by illumination, terrain shading, vegetation and cloud; the tree is trained on specific scenes and may not transfer.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [River Flow Modeling Using Artificial Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2004)9:1(60))
Kisi (2004), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 307 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts monthly river flow with neural networks as an alternative to stochastic time series models.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) compared with autoregressive (AR) time series models.
- **Data:** Monthly river flow records from a river in Turkey.
- **Main result:** The neural network gives better monthly flow forecasts than the AR models.
- **Open work:** Testing other network types and inputs such as precipitation.
- **Issues:** Single river; univariate inputs; limited record length.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Prolongation of SMAP to Spatiotemporally Seamless Coverage of Continental U.S. Using a Deep Learning Neural Network](https://doi.org/10.1002/2017gl075619)
Fang et al. (2017), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 304 citations.

- **Main goal:** Extends the short and irregular SMAP soil moisture record into a spatiotemporally seamless product over the continental US.

- **Main result:** Test RMSE below 0.035 and correlation above 0.87 over more than 75% of CONUS, removing most bias of model simulations, robust in temporal and spatial extrapolation.
- **Open work:** Hindcasting, data assimilation and weather forecasting applications.
- **Issues:** Short SMAP training record; inherits SMAP retrieval errors; surface layer only.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

Deo et al. (2015), *Atmospheric Research*. 304 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts the monthly Effective Drought Index (EDI) in eastern Australia to support drought early warning and water resource planning.

- **Data:** Monthly hydrometeorological variables (e.g., rainfall, temperature, evaporation) and large-scale climate indices as predictors at stations in eastern Australia; exact stations and periods not given here.
- **Main result:** The extreme learning machine predicts monthly EDI with accuracy better than or comparable to the ANN benchmark while training much faster.
- **Open work:** Extending to longer lead times, more regions and hybrid or ensemble models, and quantifying predictive uncertainty.

### [Comparison of artificial neural network models and empirical and semi-empirical equations for daily reference evapotranspiration estimation in the Basque Country (Northern Spain)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agwat.2007.12.011)
Landeras et al. (2008), *Agricultural Water Management*. 303 citations.

- **Main result:** Neural networks outperform the empirical and semi-empirical equations that use the same inputs.

### [Modeling of the daily rainfall-runoff relationship with artificial neural network](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2003.08.011)
Rajurkar et al. (2004), *Journal of Hydrology*. 301 citations.

- **Main result:** The coupled neural network model simulates daily runoff well, including during flood events.

### Wavelet Network Model and Its Application to the Prediction of Hydrology
Wang et al. (2003), *Venue not recorded*. 299 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a wavelet network model to improve prediction of hydrological time series.

- **Main result:** The wavelet network model gives better predictions than a conventional neural network for the tested series.

### [From calibration to parameter learning: Harnessing the scaling effects of big data in geoscientific modeling](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-26107-z)
Tsai et al. (2020), *Nature Communications*. 298 citations.

- **Main goal:** Replaces inefficient, non-unique per-site calibration of process-based geoscientific models with a learned global mapping from inputs to spatially varying parameters.
- **Architecture:** Differentiable parameter learning (dPL): a neural network (LSTM or MLP parameter network) coupled end-to-end with a differentiable process-based model, trained by backpropagation through the physics.
- **Data:** Soil moisture (SMAP satellite retrievals with the VIC land surface model) and streamflow (CAMELS basins with the HBV hydrologic model) across the contiguous United States.
- **Main result:** dPL drastically outperforms evolutionary calibration and regionalization, improves with more training data, generalizes better to unseen locations and uncalibrated variables, and matches performance with only ~12.5% of the data at orders-of-magnitude lower cost.
- **Open work:** Extend dPL to more complex process models and Earth system components, and use it to learn missing physics rather than only parameters.
- **Issues:** Requires process models to be rewritten or wrapped as differentiable code; results inherit structural deficiencies of the backbone model; demonstrated mainly over CONUS.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [River Stage Forecasting Using Artificial Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(1998)3:1(26))
Thirumalaiah et al. (1998), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 297 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river stage in real time for flood warning using artificial neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward multilayer perceptron trained with different algorithms (error backpropagation, conjugate gradient and cascade correlation), compared with each other and a statistical model.
- **Data:** Hourly or daily river stage records from a river in India; period not reported here.
- **Main result:** Neural networks forecast river stage well for short lead times, outperforming the statistical benchmark; training algorithm choice affects speed more than accuracy.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times, inclusion of rainfall inputs and testing on more rivers.
- **Issues:** Single-basin study; accuracy degrades with lead time and for extreme floods outside the training range.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [ESTIMATION AND FORECASTING OF DAILY SUSPENDED SEDIMENT DATA BY MULTI-LAYER PERCEPTRONS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2003.10.003)
Cigizoglu (2004), *Advances in Water Resources*. 291 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates and forecasts daily suspended sediment concentrations, which are costly to measure.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network compared with sediment rating curves and multiple linear regression.

- **Main result:** The MLP estimates and forecasts suspended sediment better than rating curves and regression.
- **Open work:** Adding rainfall and other inputs and testing on more rivers.
- **Issues:** Limited extrapolation for extreme sediment events; few rivers.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Caravan - A global community dataset for large-sample hydrology](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-01975-w)
Kratzert et al. (2023), *Scientific Data*. 290 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides a globally standardized large-sample hydrology dataset, since existing regional CAMELS datasets differ in format and content and hinder global studies.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark dataset and open-source software: harmonizes seven CAMELS-style datasets and provides cloud-based (Google Earth Engine) code to extract forcings and catchment attributes for new basins. Not an ML model itself.
- **Data:** 6830 catchments with streamflow, ERA5-Land meteorological forcing and static attributes (HydroATLAS geophysical, sociological and climatological attributes) aggregated from CAMELS (US, GB, BR, CL, AUS), LamaH-CE and HYSETS.
- **Main result:** Delivers a consistent global dataset of forcing, streamflow and attributes plus tooling that lets the community add catchments, supporting global training of models such as LSTMs.

- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Short-Term Water Demand Forecast Modelling at IIT Kanpur Using Artificial Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1014415503476)
Jain et al. (2001), *Water Resources Management*. 289 citations.

### [Multivariate modelling of water resources time series using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626669509491401)
Raman et al. (1995), *Hydrological Sciences Journal-journal Des Sciences Hydrologiques*. 288 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models and synthesizes multivariate water resources time series such as reservoir inflows with artificial neural networks.

### [Two decades of anarchy? Emerging themes and outstanding challenges for neural network river forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1177/0309133312444943)
Abrahart et al. (2012), *Progress in Physical Geography*. 287 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews two decades of neural network rainfall-runoff and streamflow modelling ('river forecasting') to identify emerging themes and outstanding challenges.
- **Architecture:** Review of artificial neural network (mostly MLP) river forecasting, covering input selection, physical interpretation, modular designs, ensembles and hybridization with conventional hydrological models.
- **Data:** Literature review; no new data. Discusses the need for agreed benchmark data sets for intermodel comparison.
- **Main result:** The field is established but fragmented; it needs consistent protocols for inputs, interpretation and benchmarking, and confidence intervals before operational use.
- **Open work:** Agreed benchmark data sets, better diagnostics, uncertainty characterization and a coordinated international research effort instead of isolated incremental studies.

### [Comparing neural network and autoregressive moving average techniques for the provision of continuous river flow forecasts in two contrasting catchments](https://doi.org/10.1002/1099-1085(20000815/30)14:11/12<2157::aid-hyp57>3.0.co;2-s)

- **Main goal:** Compares neural network and ARMA models for continuous river flow forecasting in contrasting catchments.

### [A non-linear combination of the forecasts of rainfall-runoff models by the first-order Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy system](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-1694(01)00349-3)
Xiong et al. (2001), *Journal of Hydrology*. 287 citations.

- **Main goal:** Combines forecasts from several rainfall-runoff models to obtain better discharge forecasts.

- **Main result:** The Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy combination performs comparably to the neural network combination and better than simple averaging.

Asefa et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 287 citations.

Chang et al. (2001), *Journal of Hydrology*. 278 citations.

Dawson et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 276 citations.

Bougadis et al. (2005), *Hydrological Processes*. 269 citations.

### [Machine learning algorithms for modeling groundwater level changes in agricultural regions of the U.S.](https://doi.org/10.1002/2016wr019933)
Sahoo et al. (2017), *Water Resources Research*. 265 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts seasonal groundwater level change and quantifies the relative importance of climate, pumping and surface-water drivers in agricultural aquifers without expensive physical models.

### [Developing reservoir monthly inflow forecasts using artificial intelligence and climate phenomenon information](https://doi.org/10.1002/2017wr020482)
Yang et al. (2017), *Water Resources Research*. 264 citations.

### [Machine learning methods for empirical streamflow simulation: a comparison of model accuracy, interpretability, and uncertainty in seasonal watersheds](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-20-2611-2016)
Shortridge et al. (2016), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 264 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares machine learning methods for monthly streamflow simulation not only on accuracy but also on interpretability and uncertainty, which matter for planning and management.

- **Main result:** Data-driven models reduce errors relative to regional physical models, with relative ranking varying by basin; random forests and GAMs aid interpretation, but GAMs and MARS become highly variable under high temperatures.

Cho et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 264 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves streamflow predictions of the physically based WRF-Hydro model, which carry systematic errors, by combining it with deep learning.

- **Open work:** Testing in more basins and coupling strategies, and adding uncertainty quantification.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; coupling design, basin and skill numbers are not verified here.

### [Differentiable, Learnable, Regionalized Process‐Based Models With Multiphysical Outputs can Approach State‐Of‐The‐Art Hydrologic Prediction Accuracy](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022wr032404)
Feng et al. (2022), *Water Resources Research*. 263 citations.

- **Main goal:** Shows that differentiable, learnable process-based hydrologic models can approach LSTM accuracy for streamflow while remaining interpretable and predicting untrained physical variables.
- **Architecture:** Differentiable (δ) model: the HBV conceptual hydrologic model implemented in a differentiable programming framework with embedded neural networks (LSTM/MLP) that regionalize parameters and enhance or replace process modules.

- **Issues:** No abstract available; data set, baselines and scores are not verified here.

### [HESS Opinions: Incubating deep-learning-powered hydrologic science advances as a community](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-22-5639-2018)
Shen et al. (2018), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 261 citations.

- **Main goal:** Argues that deep learning can open a complementary route to knowledge discovery in hydrologic science and outlines how the community can foster it.
- **Architecture:** Opinion/perspective paper on deep learning in hydrology: competing data-consistent hypotheses from DL, interpretation methods, and integration with process-based models.
- **Data:** No new data; discusses data limitations, heterogeneity and the need to share data and baseline models.
- **Main result:** Hydrology is ripe for DL breakthroughs, but progress needs coordinated community effort, process-DL integration, shared data and baselines, and open competitions.
- **Open work:** Building shared datasets, baseline models and competitions, interpretable DL, and grassroots DL education in hydrology.
- **Issues:** Perspective without quantitative evaluation; recommendations are not tested.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Self‐organizing linear output map (SOLO): An artificial neural network suitable for hydrologic modeling and analysis](https://doi.org/10.1029/2001wr000795)
Hsu et al. (2002), *Water Resources Research*. 261 citations.

- **Main goal:** Overcomes training difficulties of conventional neural networks for hydrologic prediction while giving insight into underlying processes.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing linear output map (SOLO): a self-organizing map classification layer combined with local linear regression outputs.
- **Data:** Classic rainfall-runoff forecasting case (Leaf River basin, Mississippi, daily data).
- **Main result:** SOLO estimates structure and parameters rapidly and precisely and performs competitively against multilayer feedforward ANNs, linear time-series and conceptual rainfall-runoff models.
- **Open work:** Applying SOLO to other hydrologic variables and exploiting its interpretability for process studies.
- **Issues:** Demonstrated on a single classic basin; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Drought Forecasting Using a Hybrid Stochastic and Neural Network Model](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2007)12:6(626))
Mishra et al. (2007), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 260 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts drought conditions at several lead times to support drought preparedness.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid model combining a linear stochastic ARIMA model with an artificial neural network.
- **Data:** Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) series derived from rainfall in the Kansabati River basin, India.
- **Main result:** The hybrid stochastic-neural model forecasts SPI more accurately than either ARIMA or ANN alone, especially at longer leads.
- **Open work:** Including climate indices as predictors and probabilistic forecasts.
- **Issues:** Single basin and SPI-only inputs; skill decreases with lead time.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Long lead-time daily and monthly streamflow forecasting using machine learning methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125376)
Cheng et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 259 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses long lead-time daily and monthly streamflow forecasting with machine learning for water resources planning, where systematic short- versus long-term comparisons are scarce.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) and long short-term memory (LSTM) network, both run recursively by feeding one-step-ahead forecasts back as inputs.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff data from the Nan and Ping River Basins, Thailand, 1974-2014.
- **Main result:** Both models give accurate daily forecasts up to 20 days ahead; LSTM is better at long-lead daily forecasts but worse for multi-monthly forecasts due to small monthly training sets; time lag and epoch count are key settings.
- **Open work:** Larger training sets for monthly forecasting, additional predictors and uncertainty quantification.
- **Issues:** Recursive forecasting accumulates errors; two basins only; monthly data too short for LSTM; no probabilistic output.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Prediction of droughts over Pakistan using machine learning algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2020.103562)
Khan et al. (2020), *Advances in Water Resources*. 256 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops seasonal drought prediction models for Pakistan to support early warning for vulnerable communities.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine, artificial neural network (MLP) and k-nearest neighbour models, with recursive feature elimination for predictor selection.
- **Data:** SPEI-based moderate, severe and extreme drought for the Rabi and Kharif seasons; predictors from NCEP/NCAR reanalysis.
- **Main result:** SVM best captures temporal and spatial drought characteristics; KNN performs worst; relative humidity, temperature and wind over the Mediterranean, Caspian, Indian Ocean and Arabian Sea are key predictors.
- **Open work:** Using climate model projections for future drought, and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Trained on reanalysis predictors and inherits its biases; skill numbers not reported in the abstract; limited sample of drought events.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Estimation, forecasting and extrapolation of river flows by artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.48.3.349.45288)
Cigizoglu (2003), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 256 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests neural networks for estimating, forecasting and extrapolating river flows.

- **Data:** River flow records from rivers in Turkey.
- **Main result:** Neural networks estimate and forecast flows better than stochastic models, but extrapolation beyond the training range is limited.

- **Issues:** Poor extrapolation beyond observed ranges; no abstract available, so error figures are not reported here.

### [Generalization performance of support vector machines and neural networks in runoff modeling](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2008.09.053)
Behzad et al. (2009), *Expert systems with applications*. 253 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares the generalization of support vector machines and neural networks for runoff modeling.

- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff data from a river basin in Iran (Bakhtiyari); details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Support vector machines generalize better than neural networks for runoff prediction.
- **Open work:** Testing on more basins and with longer records.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; single basin and error statistics not reported here.

### [Simulation and forecasting of streamflows using machine learning models coupled with base flow separation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2018.07.004)
Tongal et al. (2018), *Journal of Hydrology*. 246 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves machine learning streamflow simulation from meteorological inputs alone, which struggles because of weak, lagged links between streamflow and weather.
- **Architecture:** Support vector regression, artificial neural networks (MLP) and random forest coupled with a base flow separation method; both simulation (no antecedent flow) and forecasting (with antecedent flow) schemes.
- **Data:** Precipitation, temperature and potential evapotranspiration with streamflow for four rivers in the United States.
- **Main result:** Base flow separation improves the simulation performance of all three models to a degree; performance depends on model type, input structure and catchment dynamics.
- **Open work:** Testing more catchments and other flow separation or hybrid approaches.
- **Issues:** Only four catchments; improvements described as modest; numbers not reported in the abstract.

### [Nonstationary hydrological time series forecasting using nonlinear dynamic methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2004.10.008)
Coulibaly et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrology*. 246 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts nonstationary hydrological time series such as streamflow and lake levels.
- **Architecture:** Recurrent neural network (dynamic, nonlinear) compared with other nonlinear and linear models.
- **Data:** Nonstationary hydrological series (streamflow and lake water levels); sites not reported here.
- **Main result:** Dynamic recurrent networks forecast nonstationary series better than the comparison models.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times and uncertainty estimation.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; data sets and scores are not reported here.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Flood forecasting with machine learning models in an operational framework](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-2021-554)
Nevo et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 245 citations.

- **Main goal:** Describes Google's operational riverine flood forecasting and warning system, aiming to deliver accurate real-time flood alerts for large gauged rivers.
- **Architecture:** Operational system with four subsystems; stage forecasting uses Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and linear models, and inundation uses a Thresholding model and a new machine-learning Manifold model as an alternative to hydraulic modeling.
- **Data:** Historical river stage gauge data and inundation information for flood-prone rivers in India and Bangladesh; operational evaluation during the 2021 monsoon season.
- **Main result:** All models meet operational performance thresholds; LSTM beats the linear model; Thresholding and Manifold are similar for extent. In 2021 the system covered 287,000 km² and over 350M people, sending more than 100M alerts.
- **Open work:** Extend coverage to more flood-prone and ungauged locations and improve modeling skill and accuracy.
- **Issues:** Limited to large gauged rivers; evaluation on historical data with operational-metric framing rather than independent benchmarks; inundation depth validation is limited.

### [River Flow Forecasting using Recurrent Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1023/b:warm.0000024727.94701.12)
Kumar et al. (2004), *Water Resources Management*. 245 citations.

### [Interpretable and explainable AI (XAI) model for spatial drought prediction.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.149797)
Dikshit et al. (2021), *Science of the Total Environment*. 243 citations.

- **Main result:** The model predicts drought with good accuracy and the XAI analysis identifies the most influential predictors.

Rahimzad et al. (2021), *Water resources management*. 241 citations.

### [Intelligent control for modelling of real‐time reservoir operation](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.226)
Chang et al. (2001), *Hydrological Processes*. 241 citations.

Humphrey et al. (2016), *Journal of Hydrology*. 238 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves monthly streamflow forecasting by combining a conceptual hydrological model with a data-driven model, to exploit both physical knowledge and statistical learning.

- **Data:** Monthly rainfall, evapotranspiration and streamflow for catchments in Australia; details not given here.
- **Main result:** The hybrid gives better monthly forecasts and uncertainty estimates than either the conceptual model or the Bayesian ANN alone.
- **Open work:** Testing in more catchments and with seasonal climate forecasts as inputs.
- **Issues:** No abstract available; catchments and scores are not verified here.

### [Suspended sediment load simulation by two artificial neural network methods using hydrometeorological data](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2005.09.009)
Alp et al. (2007), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 237 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates suspended sediment load in a river from hydrometeorological data, since sediment transport is hard to describe physically and rating curves are often inaccurate.
- **Architecture:** Compares two artificial neural network types: a feedforward backpropagation MLP and a radial basis function (RBF) network, using rainfall and flow as inputs.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall, river flow and suspended sediment records from a river basin in the USA (Juniata River basin); exact periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** Both neural networks simulate sediment load satisfactorily and outperform conventional approaches such as sediment rating curves and regression; the RBF network trains without iterative weight optimization.

### [River Stage Forecasting in Bangladesh: Neural Network Approach](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0887-3801(2000)14:1(1))
Liong et al. (2000), *Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering*. 237 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river stages in Bangladesh several days ahead to support flood warning in a large, flood-prone delta river system.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural network (MLP) trained with backpropagation, using water levels at upstream gauging stations as inputs; sensitivity analysis is used to reduce the number of input stations.
- **Data:** Daily water level records from gauging stations on the Bangladesh river network (Dhaka region forecast point); exact periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** The network forecasts stages with high accuracy at short lead times, with accuracy decreasing for longer horizons up to about a week; few key upstream stations suffice as inputs.
- **Open work:** Including rainfall and upstream transboundary information, and extending to multiple forecast points and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single forecast location and station-based inputs only; performance degrades with lead time; no probabilistic output; abstract unavailable.

### [Machine learning for hydrologic sciences: An introductory overview](https://doi.org/10.1002/wat2.1533)
Xu et al. (2021), *WIREs Water*. 236 citations.

- **Main goal:** Introduces machine learning to hydrologists new to the field, motivated by growing hydrologic data and ML success elsewhere.
- **Architecture:** Review: non-technical overview of common machine learning algorithms and deep learning architectures in historical context, and their hydrologic applications including hybrid process-based modelling.
- **Data:** Literature review; no new data.
- **Main result:** Summarizes applications in pattern/event detection, approximation of hydrologic variables (e.g., rainfall-runoff), relationship mining, parameterization, surrogate modelling and bias correction.
- **Open work:** Improving extrapolation robustness, physical interpretability and learning from small samples in hydrology.
- **Issues:** Introductory overview without quantitative comparison.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Development of effective and efficient rainfall‐runoff models using integration of deterministic, real‐coded genetic algorithms and artificial neural network techniques](https://doi.org/10.1029/2003wr002355)
Jain et al. (2004), *Water Resources Research*. 233 citations.

- **Main goal:** Builds effective and efficient rainfall-runoff models by combining conceptual (deterministic) components with data-driven learning, aiming to better reproduce both low and high flows.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid approach integrating deterministic/conceptual modelling, a real-coded genetic algorithm for training, and artificial neural networks (feedforward MLP); compared with backpropagation-trained ANNs and conceptual models.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall and streamflow from the Kentucky River basin, USA; exact training and testing periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** The integrated models, particularly ANNs trained with real-coded genetic algorithms, improve the simulation of low-magnitude flows relative to backpropagation-trained networks while keeping good peak-flow performance.
- **Open work:** Decomposing the hydrograph into segments with separate models and testing the integration in other basins and with uncertainty estimates.
- **Issues:** Single basin; genetic-algorithm training is computationally heavier; deterministic components embed simplifying assumptions; no uncertainty quantification; abstract unavailable.

### [Estimating daily reference evapotranspiration based on limited meteorological data using deep learning and classical machine learning methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125286)
Chen et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 232 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates deep learning for estimating daily reference evapotranspiration (ETo) from limited meteorological inputs and tests transferability beyond training stations.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of deep neural network (MLP), temporal convolutional network (TCN) and LSTM with support vector machine and random forest, against temperature-, radiation- and humidity-based empirical equations; K-means clustering groups stations.
- **Data:** Weather station data from the Northeast Plain, China, with FAO-56 Penman–Monteith ETo as target; local per-station and cross-station (leave-station-out within clusters) strategies.
- **Main result:** TCN and RF beat modified Hargreaves locally (RMSE lower by ~0.10 and ~0.07 mm/d); across stations TCN and LSTM performed best with temperature inputs, and all ML models beat radiation- and humidity-based equations.
- **Open work:** Test in other climates and with other input combinations, and assess operational use with forecast inputs.
- **Issues:** Single region; target is computed Penman–Monteith ETo rather than lysimeter measurements; improvements over empirical formulas are modest in absolute terms.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Physics‐Constrained Machine Learning of Evapotranspiration](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019gl085291)
Zhao et al. (2019), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 232 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates ecosystem evapotranspiration (latent heat flux) while conserving the surface energy budget, to improve generalization of machine learning models.
- **Architecture:** Physics-constrained hybrid model: a neural network (MLP) predicts surface resistance that is fed into the Penman-Monteith equation, compared with a pure ML model.
- **Data:** Eddy covariance flux observations at 82 tower sites (FLUXNET).
- **Main result:** The hybrid model matches the pure ML model on mean metrics, conserves the energy balance, and extrapolates much better; vegetation height and soil moisture are main regulators of ET and surface resistance.
- **Open work:** Extending physics constraints to other fluxes and to global upscaling.
- **Issues:** Site-level evaluation; relies on Penman-Monteith assumptions; energy balance closure issues in eddy covariance data.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Hydrological Forecasting Using Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2000)5:2(180))
Thirumalaiah et al. (2000), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 232 citations.

- **Main goal:** Applies neural networks to hydrological forecasting of river flows or stages in real time, as an alternative to physically based or statistical models.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural networks (MLP); training algorithm details are not reported here.
- **Data:** Observed hydrological time series from an Indian river basin; details not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Neural networks produce forecasts of satisfactory accuracy for short lead times, comparable or superior to traditional statistical approaches.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times, comparison of training schemes and integration of rainfall inputs.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; data, lead times and metrics are not reported here; card is a general assessment.

### [Comparison of static-feedforward and dynamic-feedback neural networks for rainfall -runoff modeling](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2003.12.033)
Chiang et al. (2004), *Journal of Hydrology*. 232 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares static-feedforward and dynamic-feedback neural networks for rainfall-runoff modelling, to see which handles limited data and flood dynamics better.

### [Identification of Support Vector Machines for Runoff Modelling](https://doi.org/10.2166/hydro.2004.0020)
Bray et al. (2004), *Journal of Hydroinformatics*. 231 citations.

Wilby et al. (2003), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 231 citations.

Berkhahn et al. (2019), *Journal of Hydrology*. 227 citations.
