### [Deep Learning Data-Intelligence Model Based on Adjusted Forecasting Window Scale: Application in Daily Streamflow Simulation](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2020.2974406)
Fu et al. (2020), *IEEE Access*. 153 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses long short-term memory networks for daily streamflow forecasting in a tropical river and how data choices affect performance.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) network compared with a classic backpropagation neural network (MLP).
- **Data:** Historical daily streamflow of the Kelantan River, north-east Peninsular Malaysia.
- **Main result:** LSTM outperforms the backpropagation network, performing well in steady dry-season flows and capturing rapidly fluctuating rainy-season flows; no metrics are given in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Adding meteorological inputs and testing on other basins and longer horizons.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; streamflow-only inputs; quantitative results not reported in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [The potential of different ANN techniques in evapotranspiration modelling](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.6837)
Kisi (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 153 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates several artificial neural network types for modelling reference evapotranspiration.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron, radial basis function and generalized regression neural networks compared with empirical evapotranspiration equations.
- **Data:** Daily climatic data from California Irrigation Management Information System (CIMIS) stations.
- **Main result:** The neural networks reproduce Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration better than empirical formulas, with differences among network types.
- **Open work:** Testing in other climates and with reduced inputs.
- **Issues:** Target is a computed reference ET; few stations.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A note on leveraging synergy in multiple meteorological data sets with deep learning for rainfall–runoff modeling](https://doi.org/10.31223/osf.io/pjm5a)
Kratzert et al. (2020), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Shows that a deep learning rainfall-runoff model can exploit multiple meteorological forcing products together rather than relying on a single product.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory network (LSTM) taking several precipitation and meteorological forcing products simultaneously as input.
- **Data:** CAMELS basins in the continental US with forcings from NLDAS, Maurer and Daymet.
- **Main result:** Combining forcing products in a single LSTM significantly improves streamflow simulation accuracy over any individual product; the LSTM blends precipitation products differently by location and by hydrograph part.
- **Open work:** Extending to more forcing products and regions, and to operational forecasting with forecast inputs.
- **Issues:** US-only with gridded products that are themselves correlated; benefit relies on all products being available at prediction time.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Flood frequency analysis at ungauged sites using artificial neural networks in canonical correlation analysis physiographic space](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006wr005142)
Shu et al. (2007), *Water Resources Research*. 152 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates flood quantiles at ungauged sites, a key need for design where no streamflow records exist.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network regional model operating in the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) physiographic space, compared with other regional flood frequency approaches.
- **Data:** Flood quantiles and physiographic/climatic catchment attributes for gauging stations in Quebec, Canada.
- **Main result:** The ANN in CCA space gives more accurate flood quantile estimates than standard CCA-based regionalization.
- **Open work:** Combining with other region-of-influence methods and quantifying uncertainty.
- **Issues:** Jackknife evaluation on one region; flood quantiles themselves are uncertain at sites with short records.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A comprehensive study of deep learning for soil moisture prediction](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-28-917-2024)
Wang et al. (2024), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 151 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically compares deep learning architectures for soil moisture prediction to identify network design principles and understand how models use data.
- **Architecture:** Ten deep learning structures (three basic feature extractors such as LSTM, CNN-type and MLP-type networks, plus seven hybrids including feature-attention LSTM and GAN-based LSTM), interpreted with SHAP and t-SNE; three classical ML baselines.
- **Data:** Soil moisture observations across different soil textures and depths with meteorological drivers; specific sites and products not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** LSTM's temporal modelling suits soil moisture forecasting; feature-attention LSTM and GAN-LSTM further improve accuracy, showing benefits of attention and adversarial training. Code for 13 models is open source.
- **Open work:** Applying the design principles to other hydrology problems and testing transfer across regions.
- **Issues:** Site and dataset details are not given in the abstract; skill gains are modest and interpretability analyses are qualitative.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Experimental investigation of the predictive capabilities of data driven modeling techniques in hydrology - Part 2: Application](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-14-1943-2010)
Elshorbagy et al. (2009), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 151 citations.

- **Main goal:** Systematically compares data-driven modelling techniques across hydrological problems to guide technique selection.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark of neural networks (ANN), genetic programming, evolutionary polynomial regression, support vector machines, M5 model trees, k-nearest neighbours and multiple linear regression, with the Gamma test for guidance.
- **Data:** Five case studies: half-hourly actual evapotranspiration, daily peat and till soil moisture, and two daily rainfall-runoff data sets, each resampled into 12 realizations.
- **Main result:** Genetic programming is most successful overall; ANNs are sub-optimal for evapotranspiration and rainfall-runoff; M5 suits linear data; k-nn performs well in linear and nonlinear cases; SVM is kernel-sensitive.
- **Open work:** Extending the experiment to more data sets and better guidance for model choice from data characteristics.
- **Issues:** Results depend on the five data sets and tuning choices; random resampling ignores temporal dependence.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Integration of artificial neural networks with conceptual models in rainfall-runoff modeling](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.06.017)
Chen et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 149 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves rainfall-runoff modelling by combining conceptual hydrological models with artificial neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid approach in which an artificial neural network is integrated with conceptual rainfall-runoff models, for example to combine or route sub-catchment outputs.
- **Data:** Not reported in the abstract (no abstract available).
- **Main result:** The integrated ANN-conceptual models give better runoff simulations than the conceptual models alone.
- **Open work:** Testing in other basins and with distributed models.
- **Issues:** Limited case studies; interpretability of the ANN component remains limited.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Artificial Neural Networks for Forecasting Watershed Runoff and Stream Flows](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2005)10:3(216))
Wu et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 149 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts watershed runoff and stream flows with artificial neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network models with rainfall and flow inputs; network type not specified here.
- **Data:** Not reported in the abstract (no abstract available).
- **Main result:** The ANN models forecast runoff and stream flows with acceptable accuracy.
- **Open work:** Longer horizons and comparison with physically based models.
- **Issues:** Limited data and watersheds; generality unclear.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Forecasting Groundwater Table in a Flood Prone Coastal City with Long Short-term Memory and Recurrent Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.3390/w11051098)
Bowes et al. (2019), *Water*. 148 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater table response to storms in a flood-prone coastal city, where shallow groundwater amplifies flooding under sea level rise.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks compared with simple recurrent neural networks (RNN).
- **Data:** Observed groundwater table, rainfall and sea level in Norfolk, Virginia, 2010–2018, as continuous series or storm-only datasets; forecast rainfall and sea level for real-time tests.
- **Main result:** LSTM beats RNN (RMSE 0.09 m versus 0.14 m); in real-time forecasting, storm-trained models reach RMSE 0.07 m versus 0.66 m for continuous-trained models.
- **Open work:** Operational real-time deployment and coupling with coastal flood and stormwater models.
- **Issues:** Few wells in one city; skill depends on quality of rainfall and sea level forecasts; continuous-series models fail with forecast inputs.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Modelling the dynamics of the evapotranspiration process using genetic programming](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.52.3.563)
Parasuraman et al. (2007), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 148 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models evapotranspiration dynamics with an interpretable data-driven method.
- **Architecture:** Genetic programming to derive explicit evapotranspiration equations, compared with artificial neural networks and Penman-Monteith.
- **Data:** Eddy covariance evapotranspiration and meteorological measurements from field sites in Canada.
- **Main result:** Genetic programming models estimate evapotranspiration comparably or better than ANNs and Penman-Monteith while giving explicit expressions.
- **Open work:** Testing on more sites and vegetation types.
- **Issues:** Site-specific data; equations may not transfer.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Multi-model data fusion for river flow forecasting: an evaluation of six alternative methods based on two contrasting catchments](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-6-655-2002)
Abrahart et al. (2002), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 147 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates data fusion strategies to combine multiple hydrological model forecasts into better river flow forecasts.
- **Architecture:** Six fusion methods: arithmetic averaging, a probabilistic best-last-model method, two neural network fusion schemes and two soft computing (fuzzy) methods.
- **Data:** Single-model river level and discharge forecasts for the River Ouse and Upper River Wye, UK.
- **Main result:** Fusion outperforms individual models; neural network fusion of differenced data is best in a stable regime and a fuzzified probabilistic method in a volatile one.
- **Open work:** A data fusion research agenda for hydrology.
- **Issues:** Two catchments only; results depend on the input forecast set.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [On the relevance of using artificial neural networks for estimating soil moisture content](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2008.08.012)
Elshorbagy et al. (2008), *Journal of Hydrology*. 147 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses whether artificial neural networks are appropriate for estimating soil moisture content.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network models compared with alternative modelling approaches.
- **Data:** Soil moisture and meteorological data from reconstructed watersheds in Alberta, Canada.
- **Main result:** ANNs capture soil moisture dynamics only to a limited extent, raising questions about their relevance for this task.
- **Open work:** Combining data-driven and physically based approaches.
- **Issues:** Site-specific; limited data length.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Development of a fuzzy logic-based rainfall-runoff model](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626660109492832)
Hundecha et al. (2001), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 147 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a rainfall-runoff model based on fuzzy logic for simulating catchment discharge.
- **Architecture:** Fuzzy rule-based (fuzzy logic) rainfall-runoff model that relates rainfall, snowmelt and soil moisture states to runoff components.
- **Data:** Daily meteorological and discharge data from a catchment in Germany; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The fuzzy model simulates runoff with accuracy comparable to a conceptual model while being simple to set up.
- **Open work:** Application to more catchments and regionalisation of fuzzy rules.
- **Issues:** Rule construction requires expert judgement; extrapolation to extremes is uncertain.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Nearest‐neighbor methods for nonparametric rainfall‐runoff forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1029/wr023i007p01300)
Karlsson et al. (1987), *Water Resources Research*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops nonparametric forecasting of streamflow from rainfall without specifying a physical or parametric model.
- **Architecture:** Nearest-neighbour (k-nearest neighbour) nonparametric regression for rainfall-runoff forecasting.
- **Data:** Historical rainfall and runoff records from river basins; specific catchments not reported here.
- **Main result:** Nearest-neighbour forecasts perform comparably to or better than parametric time series models for the tested data.
- **Open work:** Larger data sets and multi-step forecasting with additional predictors.
- **Issues:** Requires long records to find similar past states and cannot extrapolate to unprecedented events.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Bayesian neural network for rainfall‐runoff modeling](https://doi.org/10.1029/2005wr003971)
Khan et al. (2006), *Water Resources Research*. 146 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides rainfall-runoff predictions with quantified uncertainty, which standard deterministic neural networks do not give.
- **Architecture:** Bayesian neural network: a multilayer perceptron (MLP) trained with Bayesian learning so that weights have posterior distributions and predictions carry confidence intervals.
- **Data:** Daily precipitation, temperature and streamflow from a Canadian catchment; exact record lengths are not reported here.
- **Main result:** The Bayesian neural network gives forecasts comparable to or better than a standard ANN and a conceptual hydrological model, while also providing predictive uncertainty bounds.
- **Open work:** Testing on more basins, longer lead times and with input uncertainty would strengthen the approach.
- **Issues:** Uncertainty bounds reflect parameter uncertainty mainly; computational cost of Bayesian training is higher; single-region evaluation.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Near-Real-Time Forecast of Satellite-Based Soil Moisture Using Long Short-Term Memory with an Adaptive Data Integration Kernel](https://doi.org/10.1175/jhm-d-19-0169.1)
Fang et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrometeorology*. 145 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides near-real-time forecasts of satellite-based surface soil moisture, using recent observations to correct a data-driven model.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) network with an adaptive data integration kernel that ingests the latest available SMAP observations.
- **Data:** SMAP Level-3 soil moisture over the contiguous United States with meteorological forcings and static attributes.
- **Main result:** Data integration markedly reduces forecast error compared with LSTM without integration and with the land surface model; exact metrics are not reproduced here.
- **Open work:** Extending to root-zone soil moisture, longer lead times and other satellite products.
- **Issues:** Target is SMAP retrievals, so it inherits their errors and shallow sensing depth; truncated abstract.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Prediction of Flow Based on a CNN-LSTM Combined Deep Learning Approach](https://doi.org/10.3390/w14060993)
Li et al. (2022), *Water*. 144 citations.

- **Main goal:** Computes downstream runoff directly from two-dimensional rainfall radar maps rather than one-dimensional rainfall series.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid CNN-LSTM: a convolutional neural network processes radar rainfall maps and an LSTM combines its features with upstream runoff.
- **Data:** Rainfall radar maps and runoff for the Elbe River basin in Saxony, Germany; high-water periods 2006, 2011, 2013 and low-water periods 2015, 2018.
- **Main result:** With fivefold validation, NSE 0.46–0.97 and KGE 0.47–0.92 for high-water periods and NSE 0.63–0.86, KGE 0.68–0.93 for low-water periods.
- **Open work:** Forecasting with predicted rather than observed rainfall and testing on other basins.
- **Issues:** Large spread across folds indicates sensitivity to training split; few events; relies on upstream gauge data.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Stream hydrological and ecological responses to climate change assessed with an artificial neural network](https://doi.org/10.4319/lo.1996.41.5.0857)
Poff et al. (1996), *Limnology and Oceanography*. 144 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses how climate change could alter stream hydrology and ecologically relevant flow characteristics.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (multilayer perceptron) rainfall-runoff model driven by precipitation and temperature.
- **Data:** Daily precipitation, temperature and streamflow records from contrasting US streams, with climate change scenarios applied to inputs.
- **Main result:** Simulated changes in precipitation and temperature produce substantial shifts in flow regime metrics relevant to stream ecology, differing between streams.
- **Open work:** Physically based comparison models and links to biological response data.
- **Issues:** Scenarios are simple perturbations; an empirical neural model may not extrapolate to climates outside training conditions.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [The strategy of building a flood forecast model by neuro‐fuzzy network](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.5942)
Chen et al. (2006), *Hydrological Processes*. 144 citations.

- **Main goal:** Proposes a systematic strategy for constructing flood forecasting models from limited flood-event data.
- **Architecture:** Neuro-fuzzy network (adaptive network-based fuzzy inference system, ANFIS) with a strategy for selecting inputs and training data.
- **Data:** Hourly rainfall and river stage or discharge records from flood events in a Taiwanese basin.
- **Main result:** The neuro-fuzzy model gives accurate short lead-time flood forecasts; quantitative scores are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Applying the strategy to other basins and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Few flood events for training; abstract unavailable so details are uncertain.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Enhancing predictive skills in physically-consistent way: Physics Informed Machine Learning for Hydrological Processes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.128618)
Bhasme et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 143 citations.

- **Main goal:** Combines conceptual hydrological models and machine learning so streamflow predictions are both skilful and physically consistent.
- **Architecture:** Physics-informed machine learning hybrid in which the abcd conceptual water-balance model structure is coupled with ML regressors that predict intermediate (evapotranspiration) and target (streamflow) variables.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow and actual evapotranspiration for the Narmada river basin, India.
- **Main result:** The PIML model outperforms both the purely conceptual abcd model and standalone ML algorithms while preserving water-balance consistency.
- **Open work:** Extending to daily time steps, more basins and flood risk assessment applications.
- **Issues:** Single basin at monthly resolution; specific ML algorithms and quantitative gains not detailed in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [ANN and Fuzzy Logic Models for Simulating Event-Based Rainfall-Runoff](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9429(2006)132:12(1321))
Tayfur et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydraulic Engineering*. 143 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops data-driven models for event-based rainfall-runoff and tests them against a physically based kinematic wave approximation.
- **Architecture:** Three-layer feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP) with sigmoid activation and backpropagation, and a fuzzy logic model with triangular membership functions and data-derived rules.
- **Data:** Measured event peak discharges and hydrographs from a laboratory flume, experimental plots and a small 8.44 km2 watershed.
- **Main result:** ANN, fuzzy logic and kinematic wave models all satisfactorily predict peak discharge and hydrographs with comparable error measures.
- **Open work:** Testing on larger watersheds and more varied rainfall events.
- **Issues:** Mainly laboratory and plot-scale data; only one small watershed hydrograph for field validation.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Flow forecasting for a Hawaii stream using rating curves and neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.05.008)
Sahoo et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrology*. 143 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts streamflow in a flashy Hawaiian stream, where rating curves are imperfect for converting stage to flow.
- **Architecture:** Neural networks compared with rating-curve estimates; the specific network type is not specified here.
- **Data:** Stage, discharge and possibly precipitation records from a stream in Hawaii.
- **Main result:** Neural networks provide flow estimates competitive with or better than rating curves; specific numbers are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing on other small tropical island streams and on extreme floods.
- **Issues:** Single stream; abstract unavailable so details are uncertain.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Using oceanic‐atmospheric oscillations for long lead time streamflow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1029/2008wr006855)
Kalra et al. (2007), *Water Resources Research*. 141 citations.

- **Main goal:** Uses large-scale ocean-atmosphere oscillations to forecast streamflow with lead times of up to several years for water planning.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machine (SVM) regression with climate indices as predictors, compared with artificial neural network and multiple linear regression models.
- **Data:** PDO, NAO, AMO and ENSO indices and annual streamflow volumes from gauges in the Upper Colorado River Basin.
- **Main result:** SVM gives skilful long-lead streamflow volume forecasts and outperforms the comparison models; detailed scores are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Adding other indices or seasonal predictands and testing in other basins.
- **Issues:** Short annual records limit training; teleconnection relations may be nonstationary. Card based on the authors' published SVM study; year listed differs, so worth spot-checking.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Short-term streamflow forecasting with global climate change implications – A comparative study between genetic programming and neural network models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2008.01.023)
Makkeasorn et al. (2008), *Journal of Hydrology*. 141 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts short-term streamflow under changing climate conditions and compares two machine learning approaches.
- **Architecture:** Genetic programming (GP) compared with feed-forward neural network models.
- **Data:** Streamflow, NEXRAD radar rainfall and climatic variables for the Choctawhatchee River basin, Florida.
- **Main result:** Genetic programming forecasts streamflow better than the neural network models; specific scores are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Linking to climate change projections and testing other basins.
- **Issues:** Single basin; climate change implications inferred from short records.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A soil moisture index as an auxiliary ANN input for stream flow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2003.09.006)
Anctil et al. (2004), *Journal of Hydrology*. 141 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether a soil moisture state from a conceptual model improves neural network streamflow forecasts.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network with an auxiliary soil moisture index derived from the GR4J conceptual rainfall-runoff model.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall, evapotranspiration and streamflow from several catchments.
- **Main result:** Adding the soil moisture index improves multi-day-ahead streamflow forecasts relative to MLPs without it.
- **Open work:** Exploring other conceptual state variables as inputs and more catchments.
- **Issues:** Few catchments; index quality depends on the conceptual model calibration.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Evaluation of random forests for short-term daily streamflow forecasting in rainfall- and snowmelt-driven watersheds](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-25-2997-2021)
Pham et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 140 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates random forests for 1-day-ahead streamflow forecasting in watersheds driven by both rainfall and snowmelt, beyond the usual rainfall-dominated settings.
- **Architecture:** Random forest regression benchmarked against naive persistence and multiple linear regression.
- **Data:** 86 watersheds in the Pacific Northwest, classified as rainfall-dominated, transient or snowmelt-dominated.
- **Main result:** Random forests perform better in snowmelt-driven watersheds, but improvements over benchmarks are largest in rainfall-driven ones; skill degrades with steeper slopes and sandier soils.
- **Open work:** Jointly considering variable importance measures with physical processes and testing longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Only 1-day lead time; two variable importance measures disagree, limiting inference; regional study.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [The classification of hydrologically homogeneous regions](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626669909492268)
Hall et al. (1999), *Hydrological Sciences Journal-journal Des Sciences Hydrologiques*. 139 citations.

- **Main goal:** Classifies catchments into hydrologically homogeneous regions for regional flood frequency estimation.
- **Architecture:** Self-organizing map (Kohonen neural network) clustering catchments by their characteristics.
- **Data:** Catchment characteristics and flood statistics for gauged catchments in the UK (southwest England and Wales).
- **Main result:** The self-organizing map yields groupings that are reasonably homogeneous in flood statistics, supporting regionalization.
- **Open work:** Testing regions in flood estimation for ungauged catchments and comparing with other clustering methods.
- **Issues:** Number of clusters and inputs is subjective; homogeneity testing is limited.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Treatment of precipitation uncertainty in rainfall-runoff modelling: a fuzzy set approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2004.07.001)
Maskey et al. (2004), *Advances in Water Resources*. 139 citations.

- **Main goal:** Represents imprecise precipitation inputs in rainfall-runoff modelling and propagates that uncertainty to runoff.
- **Architecture:** Fuzzy set approach using fuzzy numbers and the extension principle with alpha-cuts, compared with Monte Carlo propagation; not a machine learning model.
- **Data:** Precipitation and runoff data for a case-study catchment; details are not reported here.
- **Main result:** Fuzzy propagation gives runoff uncertainty envelopes comparable to probabilistic methods at lower cost.
- **Open work:** Combining precipitation with parameter uncertainty and comparison with probabilistic frameworks.
- **Issues:** Membership functions are subjective; does not give probabilistic interpretation.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Deep learning, hydrological processes and the uniqueness of place](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.13805)
Beven (2020), *Hydrological Processes*. 138 citations.

- **Main goal:** Comments on whether deep learning changes hydrological modelling and understanding, responding to Nearing et al. (2020).
- **Architecture:** Commentary and opinion on deep learning in hydrology; not an ML method paper.
- **Data:** Not applicable; discusses large-sample catchment studies such as LSTM work by Kratzert et al.
- **Main result:** Argues that DL may outperform conceptual models by compensating for data anomalies and epistemic uncertainty, but this does not necessarily yield process understanding.
- **Open work:** Handling epistemic uncertainty in observations, the uniqueness of place and how DL can contribute to hydrological theory.
- **Issues:** Opinion piece without new experiments; conservation constraints may not help where observations do not close water and energy balances.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Water, Energy, and Carbon with Artificial Neural Networks (WECANN): A statistically-based estimate of global surface turbulent fluxes and gross primary productivity using solar-induced fluorescence.](https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-14-4101-2017)
Alemohammad et al. (2017), *Biogeosciences*. 138 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces a joint global estimate of latent heat flux, sensible heat flux and gross primary production informed by solar-induced fluorescence.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) trained on a target dataset merged from three independent products weighted by triple collocation.
- **Data:** Satellite solar-induced fluorescence (GOME-2) and other radiative and meteorological variables; 2007–2015 at 1° monthly; evaluated against FLUXNET eddy covariance towers.
- **Main result:** WECANN typically outperforms other products against eddy covariance, especially for sensible and latent heat, and captures droughts, heatwaves and the 2015 El Niño impact.
- **Open work:** Higher spatial and temporal resolution and newer SIF missions for longer records.
- **Issues:** Target data are themselves model products, so errors propagate; coarse 1° monthly resolution; scale mismatch with flux towers.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Evapotranspiration modelling using support vector machines / Modélisation de l'évapotranspiration à l'aide de ‘support vector machines’](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.54.5.918)
Kisi et al. (2009), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 138 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates reference evapotranspiration from limited climate data using machine learning.
- **Architecture:** Support vector machines (SVM) regression compared with empirical evapotranspiration equations.
- **Data:** Daily climatic data from CIMIS weather stations in California with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith estimates as targets.
- **Main result:** SVM models estimate reference evapotranspiration more accurately than empirical methods; specific errors are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing in other climates and with fewer inputs.
- **Issues:** Targets are computed Penman-Monteith values, not lysimeter measurements; few stations.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [The Value of SMAP for Long-Term Soil Moisture Estimation With the Help of Deep Learning](https://doi.org/10.1109/tgrs.2018.2872131)
Fang et al. (2019), *IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing*. 137 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether SMAP satellite soil moisture adds value for long-term soil moisture estimation when extended beyond its lifespan with deep learning.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) network trained to reproduce SMAP from forcings and attributes, combined with the Noah land surface model.
- **Data:** SMAP soil moisture over the contiguous United States, meteorological forcings, Noah land surface model output, and in situ soil moisture networks for evaluation.
- **Main result:** LSTM extrapolates SMAP for several years with little degradation and captures root-zone interannual trends; averaging LSTM and Noah often beats Noah alone.
- **Open work:** Long-term projections and synergistic use with other model-data integration techniques.
- **Issues:** Inherits SMAP limitations such as shallow sensing depth; evaluation limited by sparse in situ sites.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Real-Coded Genetic Algorithm for Rule-Based Flood Control Reservoir Management](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1007900110595)
Chang et al. (1998), *Water Resources Management*. 137 citations.

- **Main goal:** Optimizes rule-based reservoir operation for flood control.
- **Architecture:** Non-neural method: real-coded genetic algorithm compared with binary-coded genetic algorithm for optimizing operating rules.
- **Data:** Historical flood events for a reservoir in Taiwan (Shihmen).
- **Main result:** The real-coded genetic algorithm finds good operating rules faster and more reliably than the binary-coded genetic algorithm.
- **Open work:** Multi-reservoir and real-time application with inflow forecasts.
- **Issues:** Few historical floods are used; results depend on the rule structure and objective weights.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [An exploration of artificial neural network rainfall-runoff forecasting combined with wavelet decomposition](https://doi.org/10.1139/s03-071)
Anctil et al. (2004), *Journal of Environmental Engineering and Science*. 137 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explores whether wavelet decomposition of inputs improves neural network rainfall-runoff forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural networks applied to wavelet-decomposed rainfall and flow components.
- **Data:** Rainfall and streamflow records from a case-study catchment.
- **Main result:** Wavelet preprocessing improves forecasts, especially for some frequency components; numbers are not reported here.
- **Open work:** Choosing decomposition levels and testing on more catchments.
- **Issues:** Few catchments; wavelet boundary effects can contaminate real-time forecasts.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Evaluation and machine learning improvement of global hydrological model-based flood simulations](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ab4d5e)
Yang et al. (2019), *Environmental Research Letters*. 136 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates global hydrological model flood simulations and improves them with machine learning, since GHM-based flood estimates are too inaccurate for most applications.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid physics-ML approach: LSTM post-processor taking basin-averaged meteorology and simulated discharge from GHM-CaMa-Flood chains as inputs to predict observed discharge.
- **Data:** Five GHMs under the ISIMIP2a protocol, 1971–2010, evaluated against 1,032 gauges from the Global Streamflow Indices and Metadata Archive (GSIM).
- **Main result:** GHMs capture peak amplitude reasonably but timing poorly, with large differences across climate zones; the LSTM drastically improves global flood simulations, especially peak magnitude.
- **Open work:** Using hybrid GHM-ML approaches for robust flood risk assessment and projections.
- **Issues:** Post-processing requires gauges and may not transfer to ungauged basins or future climates; inherits forcing biases.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [NEURAL NETWORK-BASED SIMULATION-OPTIMIZATION MODEL FOR RESERVOIR OPERATION](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9496(2000)126:2(57))
Neelakantan et al. (2000), *Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management*. 136 citations.

- **Main goal:** Derives reservoir operating policies efficiently by replacing costly simulation inside optimization.
- **Architecture:** Neural network surrogate of a reservoir simulation model coupled with an optimization search (simulation-optimization).
- **Data:** Reservoir system data for the Chennai city water supply system, India.
- **Main result:** The neural-network-based approach finds improved operating policies at much lower computational cost.
- **Open work:** Extending to stochastic inflows and multi-objective operation.
- **Issues:** Surrogate accuracy limits the policies; single system.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [The Data Synergy Effects of Time‐Series Deep Learning Models in Hydrology](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021wr029583)
Fang et al. (2021), *Water Resources Research*. 135 citations.

- **Main goal:** Examines whether pooling data from heterogeneous regions helps deep learning hydrologic models, challenging the practice of stratified regional models.
- **Architecture:** Time-series deep learning models, LSTM networks, trained on pooled versus region-stratified data.
- **Data:** Two hydrologic examples: soil moisture (SMAP-based) and streamflow (CAMELS) across the contiguous US.
- **Main result:** Models improve when data from characteristically different regions are pooled (data synergy); modest diversity beats homogeneous training sets of similar size.
- **Open work:** Promoting data sharing and building large diverse datasets to better represent extremes and future scenarios.
- **Issues:** Demonstrated for US datasets and LSTM only; mechanisms of synergy are not fully explained.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Runoff and Sediment Yield Modeling using Artificial Neural Networks: Upper Siwane River, India](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2006)11:1(71))
Raghuwanshi et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 135 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts runoff and sediment yield for a small agricultural watershed.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network models (feed-forward) compared with multiple linear regression.
- **Data:** Daily and weekly rainfall, runoff and sediment yield for the Upper Siwane River watershed, India.
- **Main result:** ANN models predict runoff and sediment yield better than regression models.
- **Open work:** Testing on more watersheds and event scales.
- **Issues:** Single watershed; short record.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Using machine learning models, remote sensing, and GIS to investigate the effects of changing climates and land uses on flood probability](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2020.125663)
Avand et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrology*. 134 citations.

- **Main goal:** Investigates how future climate and land use changes alter flood susceptibility in the Tajan watershed, Iran.
- **Architecture:** Random forest and Bayesian generalized linear model for flood susceptibility mapping, with land change modeler (LCM) for land use projection and LARS-WG weather generator for downscaled climate.
- **Data:** 262 historical flood locations and 12 conditioning factors; land use 1990–2019 projected to 2040; climate 1990–2015 projected to 2020–2040 under RCP2.6 and RCP8.5.
- **Main result:** Random forest (AUC 0.91) beats GLMbayes (0.847); elevation, distance from river, land use, slope and rainfall dominate; projected forest and rangeland loss and rainfall increase raise flood probability downstream.
- **Open work:** Using ensembles of climate models and dynamic hydrological modelling to refine projections.
- **Issues:** Susceptibility is static and presence-based; single weather generator downscaling; future factor changes assumed to apply directly to a statistically trained model.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Stream flow forecasting using neuro‐wavelet technique](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.7014)
Kisi (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 133 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves streamflow forecasting by combining wavelet decomposition with neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Neuro-wavelet model: discrete wavelet transform subseries fed into a feed-forward neural network, compared with a single neural network.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow records from stations in Turkey.
- **Main result:** The neuro-wavelet model outperforms the single neural network; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing other wavelets and daily data.
- **Issues:** Few stations; wavelet boundary handling for forecasting.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Can artificial intelligence and data-driven machine learning models match or even replace process-driven hydrologic models for streamflow simulation?: A case study of four watersheds with different hydro-climatic regions across the CONUS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2021.126423)
Kim et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 132 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses whether data-driven machine learning models can match or replace process-based hydrologic models for streamflow simulation.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of an artificial neural network (MLP) and an LSTM against process models SAC-SMA, Xinanjiang and the distributed CREST model.
- **Data:** Four watersheds across the CONUS with different hydro-climatic conditions and input scenarios, including delayed inputs.
- **Main result:** ML models are biased with baseline inputs but reach high accuracy with delayed inputs; ANN excels where rainfall drives runoff; ML is better for high flows, process models for low flows.
- **Open work:** Large-scale tests of transferability and scalability, e.g. in the style of the Distributed Model Intercomparison Projects.
- **Issues:** Only four watersheds; results depend on input lag design; limited generalization claims.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Generalized regression neural network in monthly flow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1080/10286600500126256)
Cigizoglu (2005), *Civil Engineering and Environmental Systems*. 132 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts monthly river flows, where reliable estimates support reservoir operation and water resources planning, using a generalized regression neural network.
- **Architecture:** Generalized regression neural network (GRNN), a kernel-based radial basis type neural network, applied to lagged monthly flow series; compared against other approaches.
- **Data:** Monthly streamflow records from gauging stations; specific rivers and periods are not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the paper presents the GRNN as a viable tool for monthly flow forecasting.
- **Open work:** Testing on more basins, adding climatic predictors and comparing with other neural network types would clarify generality.
- **Issues:** Single-variable data-driven approach with limited record length typical of monthly series; extrapolation beyond observed flows is uncertain.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Deep learning hybrid model with Boruta-Random forest optimiser algorithm for streamflow forecasting with climate mode indices, rainfall, and periodicity](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2021.126350)
Ahmed et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 131 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves long-term forecasting of stream water level using climate mode indices, rainfall and periodicity for water resources planning.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid deep learning: LSTM and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks with Boruta random forest feature selection (BRF-LSTM) applied to lagged predictors.
- **Data:** Six gauging stations in the Murray-Darling Basin, Australia, with lagged climate mode indices, rainfall and a monthly periodicity factor.
- **Main result:** BRF-LSTM outperforms benchmarks, with over 98% of errors within ±0.015 m and RRMSE about 1.30%; periodicity improves skill at four stations.
- **Open work:** Applying the approach to other hydrological variables influenced by low-frequency climate variability.
- **Issues:** Few stations; very low errors may partly reflect water-level persistence; risk of selection bias from feature screening.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Modified K-NN Model for Stochastic Streamflow Simulation](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2006)11:4(371))
Prairie et al. (2006), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 131 citations.

- **Main goal:** Generates synthetic streamflow sequences for water resources planning that reproduce observed statistics, including nonlinear dependence, while allowing values outside the historical record.
- **Architecture:** Nonparametric stochastic method, not a neural network: a local polynomial regression fit combined with K-nearest neighbour (K-NN) resampling of residuals, extending the traditional K-NN bootstrap.
- **Data:** Annual natural streamflow series of the Colorado River at Lees Ferry; observed historical records.
- **Main result:** The modified K-NN model reproduces distributional statistics and dependence of the observed flows and, unlike plain K-NN bootstrap, generates flow values not seen in the historical record.
- **Open work:** Extension to multisite and seasonal or monthly simulation and conditioning on climate information are natural next steps.
- **Issues:** Demonstrated mainly on one basin's annual flows; resampling-based methods depend on record length and stationarity.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Soil moisture retrieval from remotely sensed data: Neural network approach versus Bayesian method](https://doi.org/10.1109/tgrs.2007.909951)
Notarnicola et al. (2008), *IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing*. 130 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves soil moisture from remotely sensed radar data and compares a neural network inversion with a Bayesian retrieval approach.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural network inversion compared against a Bayesian estimation method for inverting backscatter to soil moisture.
- **Data:** Remotely sensed SAR backscatter data with ground measurements of soil moisture; exact sensors and sites not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Both methods retrieve soil moisture with comparable accuracy; the paper discusses their relative strengths, with specifics not reported in the available metadata.
- **Open work:** Combining the two approaches, accounting for vegetation and roughness, and testing on more sites remain open.
- **Issues:** Ground truth is sparse; retrieval performance depends on surface roughness and vegetation conditions represented in the training data.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Explore Spatio‐Temporal Learning of Large Sample Hydrology Using Graph Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021wr030394)
Sun et al. (2021), *Water Resources Research*. 129 citations.

- **Main goal:** Exploits spatial and temporal dependencies across many basins to improve streamflow forecasting in gauged and ungauged basins.
- **Architecture:** Graph neural networks (ChebNet, graph convolutional network, GraphWaveNet) with basins as nodes, compared with an LSTM baseline.
- **Data:** CAMELS large-sample hydrology dataset, with transductive (fixed graph) and inductive (variable graph, ungauged basins) settings.
- **Main result:** GNNs are robust and computationally efficient, matching or beating the LSTM baseline; edge- and node-level analysis interprets learned relations.
- **Open work:** Incorporating river network topology and more data sources into graph learning.
- **Issues:** Graphs built from basin similarity rather than physical connectivity; US-only; gains over LSTM are modest.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Multi-step-ahead neural networks for flood forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.52.1.114)
Chang et al. (2007), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 129 citations.

- **Main goal:** Addresses multi-step-ahead flood forecasting, where errors accumulate with lead time, for real-time flood warning.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of static feedforward neural networks and dynamic recurrent neural networks for multi-step-ahead streamflow prediction.
- **Data:** Hourly rainfall and discharge records from flood events in a Taiwanese catchment; details not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** The recurrent (dynamic) network gives more accurate and stable multi-step-ahead forecasts than static networks.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times, uncertainty quantification and use of rainfall forecasts as inputs remain open.
- **Issues:** Limited number of flood events for training and testing; deterministic forecasts only.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A stochastic nonparametric technique for space‐time disaggregation of streamflows](https://doi.org/10.1029/2005wr004721)
Prairie et al. (2007), *Water Resources Research*. 129 citations.

- **Main goal:** Disaggregates annual streamflows into monthly flows at multiple sites while preserving space-time statistics, for basin-scale water resources simulation.
- **Architecture:** Nonparametric K-nearest neighbour (K-NN) resampling-based disaggregation; a stochastic method, not a neural network.
- **Data:** Naturalized monthly streamflow records at multiple gauges in the Upper Colorado River Basin.
- **Main result:** The technique reproduces monthly and annual statistics and spatial and temporal correlation across sites, and summability of disaggregated flows.
- **Open work:** Combination with paleo-reconstructed or climate-conditioned annual flows for planning scenarios.
- **Issues:** Resampling cannot generate monthly patterns absent from the historical record; assumes stationarity.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### Forecasting groundwater level using artificial neural networks.
Sreekanth et al. (2009), *Current Science*. 129 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts groundwater levels for groundwater management in a hard-rock aquifer setting in India using artificial neural networks.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural network (MLP) trained with backpropagation-type algorithms on groundwater level and related inputs.
- **Data:** Observed groundwater levels and associated hydrometeorological data from an Indian watershed; details not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** The neural network forecasts groundwater levels with acceptable accuracy, according to the authors.
- **Open work:** Including pumping and recharge information and testing at more wells and longer horizons.
- **Issues:** Short records and site-specific training limit transferability; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Prévision hydrologique par réseaux de neurones artificiels : état de l'art](https://doi.org/10.1139/l98-069)
Coulibaly et al. (1999), *Canadian Journal of Civil Engineering*. 128 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews the use of artificial neural networks for hydrological forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Review of artificial neural network applications (mainly multilayer perceptron) to rainfall-runoff, streamflow and other hydrological forecasting.
- **Data:** Review of published studies; no new data.
- **Main result:** Neural networks are found to be promising for hydrological forecasting but practice in input selection, training and validation is inconsistent.
- **Open work:** Standardized methodology, uncertainty estimation and physical interpretation of networks.
- **Issues:** Review written in French; reflects literature up to the late 1990s.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### Daily River Flow Forecasting Using Artificial Neural Networks and Auto-Regressive Models
Kisi (2005), *Turkish Journal of Engineering and Environmental Sciences*. 128 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts daily river flows and compares artificial neural networks with classical auto-regressive time-series models.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (feedforward MLP) compared with auto-regressive (AR) models using lagged flows as inputs.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow records from a river in Turkey; period not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** The neural network models perform better than the auto-regressive models for daily flow forecasting, according to the author.
- **Open work:** Adding precipitation inputs and testing on more rivers and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single-river, flow-only inputs; extrapolation to extreme flows is uncertain.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Comparison of artificial neural network models for hydrologic predictions at multiple gauging stations in an agricultural watershed](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.7136)
Mutlu et al. (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 128 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts streamflow and related hydrologic variables at multiple gauging stations in an agricultural watershed and compares different artificial neural network models.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of artificial neural network model types for multi-station hydrologic prediction; the specific network types are not specified in the available metadata.
- **Data:** Hydrologic observations at multiple gauging stations in an agricultural watershed in the United States; details not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the comparison identifies which network configuration predicts best across stations.
- **Open work:** Extension to water quality variables and to ungauged locations is a natural next step.
- **Issues:** Watershed-specific training; limited data for extreme events.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Neural networks and non-parametric methods for improving real-time flood forecasting through conceptual hydrological models](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-6-627-2002)
Brath et al. (2002), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 128 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves real-time flood forecasts from a deterministic lumped rainfall-runoff model by forecasting short-term rainfall and updating the predicted discharge.
- **Architecture:** Time-series techniques: linear stochastic ARMA and ARIMA models compared with nonlinear artificial neural networks (ANNs) and the nearest-neighbours non-parametric regression method, used for rainfall forecasting and discharge updating.
- **Data:** Rainfall and discharge records for a catchment with a conceptual rainfall-runoff model; catchment details not given in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Rainfall forecasting, discharge updating, and both in cascade improve discharge forecasts; ANN-based techniques give a remarkable improvement over heuristic rainfall prediction and the non-updated model.
- **Open work:** Testing on more catchments and longer lead times, and quantifying forecast uncertainty.
- **Issues:** Single conceptual model and catchment; rainfall forecasting from time series alone has limited skill beyond short horizons.

### [COMPARISON OF ANNS AND EMPIRICAL APPROACHES FOR PREDICTING WATERSHED RUNOFF](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9496(2000)126:3(156))
Anmala et al. (2000), *Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management*. 128 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts watershed runoff and compares artificial neural networks with empirical approaches commonly used in practice.

- **Issues:** Data-driven models trained on limited watersheds and events; transferability uncertain.

### [Simulation and prediction of suprapermafrost groundwater level variation in response to climate change using a neural network model](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2015.09.038)
Chang et al. (2015), *Journal of Hydrology*. 127 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates and predicts suprapermafrost groundwater level variation in response to climate change in a permafrost region.

### [A deep learning approach for hydrological time-series prediction: A case study of Gilgit river basin](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12145-020-00477-2)
Hussain et al. (2020), *Earth Science Informatics*. 127 citations.

### [Uncertainties in real‐time flood forecasting with neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.6184)
Han et al. (2007), *Hydrological Processes*. 127 citations.

Aytek et al. (2008), *Journal of Earth System Science*. 127 citations.

### [NeuralHydrology - A Python library for Deep Learning research in hydrology](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.04050)
Kratzert et al. (2022), *Journal of Open Source Software*. 126 citations.

Misra et al. (2009), *Biosystems Engineering*. 126 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates runoff and sediment yield from a watershed, which are difficult to model physically, using support vector machines.
