Jeong et al. (2018), *Journal of Hydrology*. 123 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates groundwater table levels with data-driven models and a preprocessing procedure, to support groundwater monitoring and early detection of stressed aquifers.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of NARX deep neural network, LSTM, GRU and a linear ARX reference model, with detrending and deseasonalization (DTDS) preprocessing.
- **Data:** Water table level series from the Jindo Uisin and Pohang Gibuk monitoring wells, South Korea, 2005–2014.
- **Main result:** All models are reasonably accurate; NARX and LSTM are best with or without DTDS, and DTDS makes 2014 drought-related aquifer stress easier to detect.
- **Open work:** Testing on more wells and aquifer types and using forecasts for groundwater management.
- **Issues:** Only two wells; quantitative metrics are not reported in the abstract; site-specific results.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Drought prediction based on SPI and SPEI with varying timescales using LSTM recurrent neural network](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00500-019-04120-1)
Poornima et al. (2019), *Soft Computing - A Fusion of Foundations, Methodologies and Applications*. 123 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts drought using the SPI and SPEI indices at several timescales.
- **Architecture:** LSTM recurrent neural network, as stated in the title.
- **Data:** Not reported (no abstract); SPI and SPEI series at varying timescales.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata.
- **Open work:** Not reported.
- **Issues:** No abstract; region, data period, baselines and skill could not be verified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [An Artificial Neural Network model for generating hydrograph from hydro-meteorological parameters](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.03.032)
Ahmad et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrology*. 123 citations.

- **Main goal:** Generates flood hydrographs, including peak flow, time to peak and shape, from hydro-meteorological parameters for flood management.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward artificial neural network (MLP) trained with backpropagation, mapping hydro-meteorological inputs to hydrograph characteristics.
- **Data:** Hydro-meteorological and streamflow data for the Red River basin, Manitoba, Canada.
- **Main result:** The neural network reproduces peak flow, timing and hydrograph shape with good accuracy, according to the authors.
- **Open work:** Incorporating further hydrological processes and uncertainty; application to other basins.
- **Issues:** Snowmelt-driven single-basin application; limited flood events.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Groundwater Estimation from Major Physical Hydrology Components Using Artificial Neural Networks and Deep Learning](https://doi.org/10.3390/w12010005)
Afzaal et al. (2019), *Water*. 121 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates groundwater levels from physical hydrology components with neural networks, as an alternative to periodic manual well measurements.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of a multilayer perceptron (MLP), an LSTM and a convolutional neural network (CNN) with four input combinations.
- **Data:** Stream level, streamflow, precipitation, humidity, temperature, evapotranspiration and related variables, 2011–2015 training and 2016–2017 validation, Baltic River and Long Creek watersheds, Prince Edward Island, Canada.
- **Main result:** MLP performs best in validation (RMSE 0.471 and 1.15); stream level explains about half of GWL variance; more inputs reduce RMSE by 11% and 1.6%.
- **Open work:** Testing on more watersheds and extending to forecasting.
- **Issues:** Two small watersheds and a short record; hyperparameters chosen by trial and error.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Real‐time recurrent learning neural network for stream‐flow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.1015)
Chang et al. (2002), *Hydrological Processes*. 121 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts streamflow in real time using a recurrent neural network that adapts online to new observations.
- **Architecture:** Real-time recurrent learning (RTRL) recurrent neural network trained online, compared with conventional approaches.
- **Data:** Hourly streamflow and rainfall data from a river in Taiwan; details not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** The RTRL network provides accurate real-time streamflow forecasts and adapts to changing conditions, according to the authors.
- **Open work:** Multi-step-ahead forecasting and application to flood events at other basins.
- **Issues:** Single basin; one-step-ahead focus; online learning can be unstable.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Weekly soil moisture forecasting with multivariate sequential, ensemble empirical mode decomposition and Boruta-random forest hybridizer algorithm approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.catena.2019.02.012)
Prasad et al. (2019), *CATENA*. 120 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts weekly soil moisture for environmental, agricultural and hydrological applications.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid of ensemble empirical mode decomposition (EEMD), Boruta random forest feature selection and an extreme learning machine (ELM); compared with MARS and plain ELM.
- **Data:** Thirteen weekly hindcast predictors from the Australian Water Availability Project (AWAP) WaterDyn model at four sites in the Murray-Darling Basin.
- **Main result:** The EEMD-Boruta-ELM model gives the lowest errors and best performance among compared models.
- **Open work:** Use in near-real-time soil moisture forecasting and testing at more sites.
- **Issues:** Targets are model-derived (WaterDyn) rather than observed; EEMD on full series can leak future information if not applied carefully; few sites.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Rainfall runoff modelling based on genetic programming](https://doi.org/10.2166/nh.2002.0012)
Babovic et al. (2002), *Hydrology Research*. 119 citations.

- **Main goal:** Uses genetic programming to induce rainfall-runoff models directly from data as an alternative to conceptual and neural network models.
- **Architecture:** Genetic programming (symbolic regression) evolving explicit rainfall-runoff expressions.
- **Data:** Catchment rainfall and runoff records; the specific catchment is not reported here.
- **Main result:** Genetic programming yields compact runoff models with accuracy comparable to or better than the benchmarks used. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Combining evolved expressions with physical knowledge and testing on more catchments.
- **Issues:** Evolved formulas may overfit and lack physical interpretability; single-catchment evidence.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Application of neural network and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems for river flow prediction](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.54.2.247)
Pramanik et al. (2009), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 119 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts river flow at a downstream location from upstream flows, comparing two data-driven approaches for operational flow forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural network (ANN) compared with an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS).
- **Data:** Daily flow records from gauging stations in the Mahanadi River system, India.
- **Main result:** ANFIS gives somewhat better flow predictions than the ANN, with both performing acceptably. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Adding rainfall and catchment inputs and testing on extreme flood events.
- **Issues:** Single river system; limited treatment of high flows and no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Machine-learning methods for stream water temperature prediction](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-25-2951-2021)
Feigl et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops and benchmarks machine learning models for daily river water temperature prediction to support water management under climate change.
- **Architecture:** Six models: stepwise linear regression, random forest, XGBoost, feed-forward neural networks (MLP) and two recurrent neural networks, tuned by Bayesian optimization, versus linear regression and air2stream.
- **Data:** 10 Austrian catchments (200 to 96,000 km2) with daily air temperature, runoff, precipitation and global radiation.
- **Main result:** Mean RMSE of 0.55 °C versus 1.55 °C for linear regression and 0.98 °C for air2stream; FNN and XGBoost each best in 4 of 10 catchments, RNNs best in the largest.
- **Open work:** Regional multi-catchment models and applications to future climate; R package wateRtemp released.
- **Issues:** High sensitivity to hyperparameters (FNN RMSE standard deviation 1.60 °C); single-catchment models; Austrian setting only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A novel approach to parameter uncertainty analysis of hydrological models using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-13-1235-2009)
Shrestha et al. (2009), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Replaces time-consuming Monte Carlo parameter uncertainty analysis of hydrological models with a fast emulator usable in real time.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (MLP) trained to map model inputs to uncertainty descriptors (prediction quantiles) derived from Monte Carlo realizations.
- **Data:** Monte Carlo simulations of the lumped conceptual HBV model for the Brue catchment, United Kingdom.
- **Main result:** The ANN reproduces Monte Carlo prediction intervals reasonably accurately on verification data.
- **Open work:** Applying the emulator to complex distributed models and to real-time forecasting with short lead times.
- **Issues:** Only parametric uncertainty is considered; single catchment and model; the emulator inherits the Monte Carlo setup assumptions.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Application of fuzzy logic to forecast seasonal runoff](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.1359)
Mahabir et al. (2003), *Hydrological Processes*. 118 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts seasonal spring runoff volumes in snowmelt-dominated basins where regression methods are unreliable.
- **Architecture:** Fuzzy logic (rule-based fuzzy inference) model using snowpack, soil moisture and precipitation indices.
- **Data:** Historical seasonal runoff and snow and climate indices for basins in Alberta, Canada.
- **Main result:** The fuzzy model categorises runoff (e.g. low, average, high) more reliably than regression-based forecasts.
- **Open work:** Extending to more basins and integrating climate signals into the rule base.
- **Issues:** Coarse categorical output; rule base partly expert-defined; short records.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Performance Evaluation of Artificial Neural Networks for Runoff Prediction](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2000)5:4(424))
Elshorbagy et al. (2000), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates how well artificial neural networks predict runoff and how their performance should be assessed.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural networks compared with regression-based alternatives.
- **Data:** Streamflow and hydrometeorological records from a Canadian basin (Red River, Manitoba).
- **Main result:** ANNs predict runoff competitively, and the study highlights the need for multiple performance measures. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Better evaluation criteria for peak flows and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single basin; standard performance measures may hide poor peak-flow performance.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Forecasting of hydrologic time series with ridge regression in feature space](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2006.07.003)
Yu et al. (2007), *Journal of Hydrology*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts hydrologic time series with a kernel method that is faster to train than support vector regression.
- **Architecture:** Kernel ridge regression in feature space combined with phase-space (chaos-based) reconstruction of the time series.
- **Data:** Daily river flow series from benchmark catchments. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Ridge regression in feature space matches support vector machine accuracy at lower computational cost. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Automated selection of embedding and kernel parameters and tests on more catchments.
- **Issues:** Results depend on embedding and kernel choices; univariate inputs only.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Division-based rainfall-runoff simulations with BP neural networks and Xinanjiang model](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2008.12.032)
Ju et al. (2009), *Neurocomputing*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves rainfall-runoff simulation by combining a conceptual model with neural networks applied to divided parts of the flow regime.
- **Architecture:** Back-propagation (BP) neural networks combined with the Xinanjiang conceptual model in a division-based scheme.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from a Chinese catchment. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** The division-based hybrid improves simulations over a single model. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Testing other division criteria and catchments.
- **Issues:** Single-catchment evidence; division thresholds are subjective.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Forecasting flows in Apalachicola River using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.1492)
Huang et al. (2004), *Hydrological Processes*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river flows in the Apalachicola River, Florida, with data-driven models to support water management.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural networks using upstream flows and antecedent observations.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow records from gauging stations on the Apalachicola River system.
- **Main result:** Neural networks forecast flows accurately at short lead times. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Including rainfall forecasts and extending lead times.
- **Issues:** Single river; skill expected to decline at longer leads and for extreme flows.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A Neural Networks Approach for Deriving Irrigation Reservoir Operating Rules](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1015563820136)
Cancelliere et al. (2002), *Water Resources Management*. 117 citations.

- **Main goal:** Derives monthly operating rules for an irrigation reservoir that approximate optimal release policies.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network trained on optimal releases from dynamic programming to form operating rules.
- **Data:** Inflow, storage and demand data for an irrigation reservoir in Sicily, Italy, with optimised releases as targets.
- **Main result:** ANN-based rules reproduce optimal releases better than linear rules and reduce irrigation shortages in simulation.
- **Open work:** Extending to multireservoir systems and including inflow forecasts.
- **Issues:** Depends on deterministic optimisation of historical inflows; single reservoir.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Hydrologically Informed Machine Learning for Rainfall‐Runoff Modeling: A Genetic Programming‐Based Toolkit for Automatic Model Induction](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr026933)
Chadalawada et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Automates the construction of physically meaningful rainfall-runoff models from flexible modelling frameworks, avoiding time-consuming manual trial of configurations.
- **Architecture:** Genetic programming (evolutionary computation) model induction toolkit (ML-RR-MI) that searches SUPERFLEX and FUSE building blocks to build lumped conceptual models.
- **Data:** Rainfall-runoff data for the Blackwater River basin, Alabama, USA.
- **Main result:** Evolved model configurations are consistent with fieldwork and previous research findings; quantitative skill is not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Extending to semi-distributed models (later done in MIKA-SHA) and other building-block libraries.
- **Issues:** Single basin; computational cost of the search; no comparison with deep learning in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Challenges in Applying Machine Learning Models for Hydrological Inference: A Case Study for Flooding Events Across Germany](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr025924)
Schmidt et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether machine learning models can be used for hydrological inference, not just prediction, using flood events across Germany.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural networks (MLP) and random forest compared with multiple linear regression, interpreted using permuted feature importance.
- **Data:** Large dataset of flood events across Germany with catchment and event predictors.
- **Main result:** ML models beat linear regression and reflect basic hydrological principles, but feature importances differ across algorithms, revealing equifinality that hampers inference.
- **Open work:** Using multiple algorithms and interpretation methods within cross-validation when doing ML-based inference.
- **Issues:** Inference conclusions depend on chosen algorithms; correlated predictors complicate importance estimates.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Modelling groundwater levels in an urban coastal aquifer using artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.6686)
Krishna et al. (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models groundwater levels in an urban coastal aquifer to support groundwater management under pumping and seawater intrusion risk.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural networks trained with back-propagation variants (e.g. Levenberg-Marquardt).
- **Data:** Observed groundwater levels, rainfall and related records from wells in a coastal city aquifer in India.
- **Main result:** Neural networks reproduce observed groundwater level fluctuations well. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Adding pumping data and longer forecasts for management scenarios.
- **Issues:** Few wells and short records; no physical constraints on groundwater dynamics.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A split-step particle swarm optimization algorithm in river stage forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2007.09.004)
Chau (2007), *Journal of Hydrology*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Speeds up and improves training of neural networks used for river stage forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural network trained by a split-step particle swarm optimization algorithm (PSO followed by Levenberg-Marquardt).
- **Data:** Water level records from the Shing Mun River, Hong Kong.
- **Main result:** The split-step PSO trains faster and gives more accurate stage forecasts than standard back-propagation or PSO alone.
- **Open work:** Applying the hybrid training to other hydrological problems and lead times.
- **Issues:** Single river; gains depend on optimiser settings.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [A non-linear neural network technique for updating of river flow forecasts](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-5-577-2001)
Shamseldin et al. (2001), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 116 citations.

- **Main goal:** Updates conceptual model river flow forecasts using recent errors to improve real-time accuracy.
- **Architecture:** Non-linear auto-regressive exogenous-input (NARX) updating procedure built on a multilayer neural network, compared with linear ARX updating.
- **Data:** Daily discharge forecasts from the SMAR conceptual model on five catchments with different climatic conditions.
- **Main result:** The NARX neural network updating procedure outperforms the linear ARX procedure.
- **Open work:** Testing at sub-daily time steps and with other conceptual models.
- **Issues:** Daily data only; updating limited to output correction rather than model states.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Artificial neural networks for streamflow prediction](https://doi.org/10.1080/00221680209499899)
Dolling et al. (2002), *Journal of Hydraulic Research*. 115 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts streamflow with artificial neural networks as an alternative to conceptual and statistical models.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward artificial neural networks.
- **Data:** Streamflow and hydrometeorological records from a mountain basin. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Neural networks give accurate streamflow predictions. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Testing on more basins and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Limited data; no uncertainty quantification.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Evaluation of artificial neural network techniques for flow forecasting in the River Yangtze, China](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-6-619-2002)
Dawson et al. (2002), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 115 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates neural networks for six-hourly flow forecasting on the River Yangtze and compares them with conventional statistical techniques.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) and radial basis function (RBF) networks with alternative RBF transfer functions.
- **Data:** Six-hourly rainfall-runoff data for the River Yangtze at Yichang, upstream of the Three Gorges Dam, 1991-1993.
- **Main result:** Both networks simulate flows beyond the training range, and the Gaussian function is not necessarily the best RBF; comparisons are made with stepwise regression, ARMA and zero-order forecasts.
- **Open work:** Longer records and assessing other transfer functions and lead times.
- **Issues:** Short three-year record; single gauge.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Reconstruction of GRACE Total Water Storage Through Automated Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020wr028666)
Sun et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Fills the roughly 1-year gap between GRACE and GRACE-FO total water storage records to maintain data continuity.
- **Architecture:** Automated machine learning (AutoML) workflow selecting and tuning six ML model types (including tree ensembles and neural networks) per grid cell, with model combination.
- **Data:** GRACE/GRACE-FO total water storage anomalies over CONUS with meteorological and climatic predictors.
- **Main result:** Mean gridwise NSE about 0.85, correlation about 0.95 and normalized RMSE about 0.09 on test data; skill holds in the mission gap and GRACE-FO period; no single algorithm is best everywhere.
- **Open work:** Applying AutoML to larger-scale hydrological prediction systems and global reconstructions.
- **Issues:** Gridwise models ignore spatial dependence; reconstruction in the gap cannot be directly verified; CONUS only.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Temporal Fusion Transformers for Streamflow Prediction: Value of Combining Attention with Recurrence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12335)
Koya et al. (2023), *arXiv*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether combining recurrence and attention improves streamflow prediction over LSTM and transformer models.
- **Architecture:** Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), combining LSTM recurrence with attention, compared with LSTM and transformer models.
- **Data:** Caravan dataset, 2,610 globally distributed catchments.
- **Main result:** TFT exceeds the LSTM and transformer benchmarks and offers interpretability of streamflow generation drivers.
- **Open work:** Further testing in ungauged settings and deeper analysis of the learned attention.
- **Issues:** Improvement margins are not quantified in the abstract; preprint.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Application of adaptive fuzzy rule-based models for reconstruction of missing precipitation events](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626660009492339)
Abebe et al. (2000), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs missing precipitation records from neighbouring gauges to complete hydrological datasets.
- **Architecture:** Adaptive fuzzy rule-based models compared with neural networks and linear regression.
- **Data:** Daily precipitation records from nearby rain gauges. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Fuzzy rule-based models reconstruct missing values with accuracy comparable to neural networks. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Applying to other gauge networks and handling extreme events.
- **Issues:** Performance depends on correlation between gauges; rule generation is data-hungry.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Retrieving surface roughness and soil moisture from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.5589/m02-066)
Baghdadi et al. (2002), *Canadian Journal of Remote Sensing*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves surface roughness and soil moisture from SAR backscatter for bare agricultural soils.
- **Architecture:** Neural network inversion of SAR backscatter trained on backscatter simulated by the integral equation model (IEM).
- **Data:** IEM-simulated backscatter for training and SAR data with field measurements over agricultural fields for testing.
- **Main result:** Neural networks retrieve soil moisture and roughness with useful accuracy, especially with multi-angle or multi-polarisation data.

- **Issues:** Relies on IEM accuracy; bare soils only; limited field validation.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Neural network modelling of non-linear hydrological relationships](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-11-1563-2007)
Abrahart et al. (2007), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether neural networks can model non-linear hydrological relationships, responding to claims that they offer no improvement over linear transfer functions.
- **Architecture:** Eight neural network models emulating a non-linear rainfall-runoff equation and a runoff coefficient relationship, compared with multiple linear regression.
- **Data:** Synthetic random inputs with uniform distribution generated from a recognised non-linear hydrological model; no temporal component.
- **Main result:** Neural networks reproduce the non-linear relationships and outperform least squares multiple linear regression.

### [Retrieving soil moisture and agricultural variables by microwave radiometry using neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0034-4257(02)00105-0)
Frate et al. (2003), *Remote Sensing of Environment*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves soil moisture and agricultural variables from microwave radiometry over vegetated fields.
- **Architecture:** Neural network inversion trained on simulations from a discrete electromagnetic emission model.
- **Data:** Simulated brightness temperatures for training and experimental radiometer measurements over agricultural fields for testing.
- **Main result:** Neural networks retrieve soil moisture and vegetation variables with good accuracy. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Applying to satellite radiometers such as SMOS.
- **Issues:** Depends on the forward model; experimental validation limited to few sites.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Runoff prediction using an integrated hybrid modelling scheme](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2009.03.034)
Remesan et al. (2009), *Journal of Hydrology*. 114 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves runoff prediction with a hybrid scheme combining input selection and data-driven models.

- **Main result:** The hybrid wavelet-based models outperform conventional neural network and ANFIS models. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Testing on more catchments and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; added complexity of the hybrid scheme.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [GENETIC PROGRAMMING: A NEW PARADIGM IN RAINFALL RUNOFF MODELING 1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-1688.2002.tb00991.x)
Liong et al. (2002), *JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association*. 113 citations.

- **Main goal:** Introduces genetic programming as a paradigm for rainfall-runoff modelling.
- **Architecture:** Genetic programming (symbolic regression) for rainfall-runoff.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from a catchment in Singapore. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Genetic programming performs well and yields explicit models. Not reported in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Testing at longer lead times and other catchments.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; risk of overfitting evolved expressions.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Stochastic optimization of multireservoir systems via reinforcement learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006wr005627)
Lee et al. (2007), *Water Resources Research*. 113 citations.

- **Main goal:** Optimises operation of multireservoir systems under inflow uncertainty.
- **Architecture:** Reinforcement learning (Q-learning) compared with stochastic dynamic programming.
- **Data:** Inflow and operating data for a multireservoir system in Korea (Geum River basin).
- **Main result:** Q-learning produces operating policies competitive with or better than stochastic dynamic programming.
- **Open work:** Scaling to larger systems and continuous state spaces.
- **Issues:** Discretised states; simulation-based evaluation only.

### [Mitigating Prediction Error of Deep Learning Streamflow Models in Large Data‐Sparse Regions With Ensemble Modeling and Soft Data](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021gl092999)
Feng et al. (2020), *Geophysical Research Letters*. 112 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies and reduces error of deep learning streamflow models when predicting in large contiguous ungauged regions.
- **Architecture:** LSTM deep network with integration of soft data and a novel input-selection ensemble.

### [Distributed long-term hourly streamflow predictions using deep learning - A case study for State of Iowa](https://doi.org/10.31223/osf.io/vs4x8)
Xiang et al. (2020), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 112 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves long-lead hourly streamflow forecasting with deep learning across a state-wide gauge network.

Hosseiny et al. (2020), *Scientific Reports*. 112 citations.

- **Main goal:** Speeds up large-scale flood depth and extent simulation by coupling a hydraulic model with machine learning.

### [A Short-term Flood Prediction based on Spatial Deep Learning Network: A Case Study for Xi county, China](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.127535)
Chen et al. (2022), *Journal of Hydrology*. 111 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts short-term floods in Xi county, China using spatial deep learning.
- **Architecture:** Spatial deep learning network; the specific network family is not specified in the available metadata.

- **Issues:** No abstract; data, architecture and skill could not be verified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Bayesian training of artificial neural networks used for water resources modeling](https://doi.org/10.1029/2005wr004152)
Kingston et al. (2005), *Water Resources Research*. 111 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies uncertainty in artificial neural network predictions for water resources modelling, where deterministic training gives single weight sets and no prediction intervals.
- **Architecture:** Bayesian training of a multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network, sampling the weight posterior with Markov chain Monte Carlo instead of point-estimate backpropagation.
- **Data:** Water resources case study; a River Murray (South Australia) salinity forecasting application is the known example. Details of periods and inputs not reported here.
- **Main result:** Bayesian training yields weight distributions and prediction intervals with accuracy comparable to standard training, giving more informative and interpretable network outputs.
- **Open work:** Extending Bayesian treatment to input and architecture uncertainty and reducing the computational cost of MCMC sampling.
- **Issues:** MCMC sampling is computationally demanding and convergence is hard to check for high-dimensional weight spaces; prior choice affects results.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Improving generalization of artificial neural networks in rainfall–runoff modelling / Amélioration de la généralisation de réseaux de neurones artificiels pour la modélisation pluie-débit](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.50.3.439.65025)
Giustolisi et al. (2005), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 111 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves the generalization of artificial neural networks in rainfall-runoff modelling, where overfitting to short calibration records degrades predictions.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural networks trained with strategies to improve generalization; specific regularization variants are not detailed here.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from a catchment case study; catchment and periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** Generalization-improving strategies yield more robust runoff predictions than plain training; quantitative gains not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing across more catchments and combining with input selection and uncertainty estimation.
- **Issues:** Single case study; behaviour for extreme floods outside the calibration range is untested.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Exploring the exceptional performance of a deep learning stream temperature model and the value of streamflow data](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/abd501)
Rahmani et al. (2020), *Environmental Research Letters*. 110 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models daily stream water temperature at continental scale and examines the value of streamflow data as input.
- **Architecture:** LSTM deep learning model, basin-centric lumped, including a two-stage setup using streamflow simulated by a pretrained LSTM.
- **Data:** 118 data-rich US basins without major dams, with forcing, catchment attributes and observed streamflow.
- **Main result:** Median RMSE 0.69 °C, NSE 0.985 and correlation 0.994; observed or simulated streamflow inputs improve performance.
- **Open work:** Extending to dammed and data-poor basins.
- **Issues:** Only data-rich undammed basins; performance in poorly gauged settings is uncertain.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Global optimization techniques for the calibration of conceptual rainfall-runoff models](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626669809492137)
Franchini et al. (1998), *Hydrological Sciences Journal-journal Des Sciences Hydrologiques*. 110 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares global optimisation techniques for automatic calibration of conceptual rainfall-runoff model parameters.
- **Architecture:** Global optimisation algorithms including genetic algorithm and shuffled complex evolution (SCE-UA), combined with local search, applied to a conceptual rainfall-runoff model.
- **Data:** Synthetic and observed rainfall-runoff series for test catchments; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** Algorithms differ in efficiency and reliability; SCE-UA is generally the most efficient and robust for finding the global optimum.
- **Open work:** Treating parameter uncertainty and equifinality and multi-objective calibration.
- **Issues:** Results depend on the chosen model and objective function; computational cost of genetic algorithms is high.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [A neural network model of rainfall-runoff using radial basis functions](https://doi.org/10.1080/00221689609498476)
Mason et al. (1996), *Journal of Hydraulic Research*. 110 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models the rainfall-runoff transformation with a neural network as an alternative to conceptual hydrological models.
- **Architecture:** Radial basis function (RBF) neural network.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff series, possibly including synthetic data from a catchment model; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** RBF networks reproduce runoff with useful accuracy and train faster than backpropagation networks; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Testing on more catchments and longer real records.
- **Issues:** Limited evaluation; black-box model with uncertain extrapolation to extreme events.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Application of neural approaches to one-step daily flow forecasting in Portuguese watersheds](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2006.06.015)
Pulido-Calvo et al. (2007), *Journal of Hydrology*. 110 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts daily river flow one step ahead in Portuguese watersheds to support water management.

- **Data:** Daily flow records from Portuguese watersheds; stations and periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** Neural approaches provide accurate one-step daily flow forecasts, generally improving on conventional models; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times and inclusion of rainfall forecasts.
- **Issues:** One-step-ahead forecasts are dominated by persistence; regional transferability unclear.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [COMPARISON OF PROCESS‐BASED AND ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORK APPROACHES FOR STREAMFLOW MODELING IN AN AGRICULTURAL WATERSHED 1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-1688.2006.tb04475.x)
Srivastava et al. (2006), *JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association*. 110 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares a process-based watershed model with an artificial neural network for streamflow simulation in an agricultural watershed.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network compared with the process-based SWAT hydrologic model.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow and meteorological data from an agricultural watershed in the United States; periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** The neural network reproduces streamflow at least as well as, and in parts better than, the process-based model; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Combining process-based and data-driven models and testing under land-use change.
- **Issues:** The neural network lacks physical interpretability and cannot simulate scenarios outside the training conditions.

### [Modelling of the monthly and daily behaviour of the runoff of the Xallas river using Box-Jenkins and neural networks methods](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2004.03.011)
Castellano-Méndez et al. (2004), *Journal of Hydrology*. 110 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models monthly and daily runoff of the Xallas river (Galicia, Spain) to support hydropower and water management.
- **Architecture:** Box-Jenkins ARIMA time series models compared with artificial neural networks; the network type is not specified here.
- **Data:** Monthly and daily runoff and rainfall records of the Xallas river basin; periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** Both approaches reproduce runoff; the neural networks capture nonlinear daily behaviour better in the reported comparison, details not given here.

- **Issues:** Single river basin; conclusions on relative performance may not generalize.

### [NeuralHydrology - Interpreting LSTMs in Hydrology](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-28954-6_19)
Kratzert et al. (2019), *Explainable AI*. 109 citations.

- **Main goal:** Interprets LSTM rainfall-runoff models to address the opacity that limits their acceptance in environmental sciences.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory network (LSTM) analysed by inspecting internal memory cell states and gradients.
- **Data:** Two catchments, one snow-influenced and one without, from the CAMELS US dataset.
- **Main result:** The trained LSTM internally learns patterns consistent with hydrological understanding, e.g. cell states resembling snow storage and dynamic reservoirs.
- **Open work:** Systematic interpretability tools for larger samples of basins and other hydrologic variables.
- **Issues:** Only two catchments; qualitative interpretation; links between cells and physical stores are not unique.

### [Regional flood inundation nowcast using hybrid SOM and dynamic neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2014.07.036)
Chang et al. (2014), *Journal of Hydrology*. 108 citations.

- **Issues:** No abstract; study region, lead times and skill could not be verified.

### [Peak-flow forecasting with genetic algorithm and SWMM](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)0733-9429(1995)121:8(613))
Liong et al. (1995), *Journal of Hydraulic Engineering*. 108 citations.

### [Comparison of four updating models for real-time river flow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1080/02626660209492964)
Xiong et al. (2002), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 108 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares output updating procedures that correct real-time river flow forecasts from rainfall-runoff models using recent observed errors.
- **Architecture:** Four updating models compared, including autoregressive error-correction schemes and a neural network-based updating model; also includes a fuzzy-rule-type variant in the known study.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall and river flow data from several catchments; catchments and periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** Updating markedly improves forecast accuracy over non-updated simulations; the neural network updating performs competitively, details not given here.

- **Issues:** Gains decrease with lead time; results depend on the underlying rainfall-runoff model.

### [Application of tank, NAM, ARMA and neural network models to flood forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1002/1099-1085(20001015)14:14<2473::aid-hyp109>3.0.co;2-j)
Tingsanchali et al. (2000), *Hydrological Processes*. 108 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares conceptual, statistical and neural network models for flood forecasting.
- **Architecture:** Conceptual tank and NAM models, ARMA time series model and an artificial neural network compared; the network type is not specified here.

### [Physics‐Informed Neural Networks With Monotonicity Constraints for Richardson‐Richards Equation: Estimation of Constitutive Relationships and Soil Water Flux Density From Volumetric Water Content Measurements](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020wr027642)
Bandai et al. (2021), *Water Resources Research*. 107 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates soil water retention and hydraulic conductivity functions and water flux from volumetric water content measurements alone.
- **Architecture:** Physics-informed neural network (PINN) of three linked feedforward neural networks, two constrained to be monotonic, solving the Richardson-Richards equation inversely.
- **Data:** Synthetic volumetric water content data with artificial noise from numerical solutions for three soil textures.
- **Main result:** Reconstructs water content dynamics and recovers retention and conductivity functions nonparametrically, except at wet and dry extremes.
- **Open work:** Applying to field measurements and improving behaviour at the extremes.
- **Issues:** Synthetic data only; poor reconstruction at wet and dry ends.

### [Assessing the Physical Realism of Deep Learning Hydrologic Model Projections Under Climate Change](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022wr032123)
Wi et al. (2022), *Water Resources Research*. 106 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses whether deep learning hydrologic models produce physically realistic streamflow projections under warming.
- **Architecture:** Regional LSTM benchmarked against process models HYMOD, SAC-SMA and VIC; hybrid variants with process-model outputs as extra targets (multi-output LSTM) or input features.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow in 15 California watersheds forced with warming scenarios, plus an LSTM trained on over 500 US watersheds.
- **Main result:** LSTM reproduces hydrograph shifts but in some basins unrealistically increases the runoff ratio; SAC-SMA ET as input fixes this, but not with VIC or HYMOD; the 500-basin LSTM gives more realistic responses.
- **Open work:** Hybrid modelling and large diverse training sets to make LSTM climate projections trustworthy.
- **Issues:** Synthetic warming scenarios rather than full climate projections; hybrid benefit depends on process model fidelity.

Landeras et al. (2009), *Journal of Irrigation and Drainage Engineering-asce*. 106 citations.

### [Potential assessment of the support vector regression technique in rainfall forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-006-9026-2)
Hong et al. (2007), *Water Resources Management*. 106 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses support vector regression for rainfall forecasting, a nonlinear problem poorly handled by linear models.

- **Main result:** SVR forecasts rainfall more accurately than the benchmark models; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Hybrid parameter optimization and additional meteorological predictors.
- **Issues:** Limited data and stations; parameter tuning sensitivity.
- *Basis: assessment*

Kao et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrology*. 105 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts regional flood inundation depths several hours ahead to support emergency management.

### [Improving hydrologic models for predictions and process understanding using neural ODEs](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-26-5085-2022)
Höge et al. (2022), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 105 citations.

- **Main goal:** Combines deep learning predictive power with conceptual model interpretability in hydrology.
- **Architecture:** Neural ordinary differential equation (neural ODE) model where internal processes of a conceptual bucket model are replaced by neural networks (MLPs).

Leahy et al. (2008), *Journal of Hydrology*. 105 citations.

Yang et al. (2009), *Journal of Arid Environments*. 104 citations.

Clair et al. (1998), *Water Resources Research*. 103 citations.

Sivapragasam et al. (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 103 citations.

Wang et al. (2024), *Water Resources Research*. 102 citations.

- **Main goal:** Combines deep learning accuracy with physical mechanisms in distributed hydrological modelling for very large basins.

Chauhan et al. (2009), *Water Resources Management*. 102 citations.

### [Improving Snow Water Equivalent Maps With Machine Learning of Snow Survey and Lidar Measurements](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018wr024146)
Broxton et al. (2019), *Water Resources Research*. 101 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reduces uncertainty in snow water equivalent (SWE) mapping from aerial lidar snow depth, which lacks spatially explicit snow density, in semiarid Arizona mountain forests that supply surface water.

Cigizoglu (2003), *Environmetrics*. 101 citations.

Firat et al. (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 101 citations.

### [Simulation of Runoff and Sediment Yield using Artificial Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biosystemseng.2006.02.014)
Agarwal et al. (2006), *Biosystems Engineering*. 100 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates runoff and sediment yield in a catchment to support soil and water management where physically based models are data-demanding.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural networks (MLP, backpropagation) at daily, weekly and monthly time scales, compared with linear models.
- **Data:** Rainfall, runoff and sediment observations from a river basin in India; exact basin and period not confirmed here.
- **Main result:** The neural networks simulate runoff and sediment yield satisfactorily and generally better than the linear models.
- **Open work:** Test at other basins and include land-use and erosion drivers.
- **Issues:** Single-catchment empirical model; sediment observations are sparse and extremes may be underestimated.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Estimating propagation probability from meteorological to ecological droughts using a hybrid machine learning copula method](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-559-2023)
Jiang et al. (2023), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 99 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies the probability that meteorological drought propagates into ecological (vegetation) drought of different magnitudes in northwestern China, to support ecological conservation.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid of machine learning classifiers and a four-dimensional C-vine copula; 11 classifiers compared, with quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA) best; drought events identified with a three-dimensional spatiotemporal clustering method.
- **Data:** Meteorological and ecological drought indices over northwestern China, 1982–2020; 130 meteorological and 184 ecological drought events, 46 paired propagation events. Specific input products not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** QDA performs best among 11 models; ecological droughts last longer but have smaller area and severity than meteorological droughts; the hybrid method handles large regions better than traditional propagation methods.
- **Open work:** Applying the framework to other regions and drought types, and to future climate scenarios to project propagation risk.
- **Issues:** Only 46 paired propagation events for training; results depend on the event-pairing overlap rule and drought index choices; skill metrics not given in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Physics‐Informed Neural Networks of the Saint‐Venant Equations for Downscaling a Large‐Scale River Model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022wr033168)
Feng et al. (2022), *Water Resources Research*. 99 citations.

- **Main goal:** Downscale coarse large-scale river model output to subgrid scale near the river-ocean interface, where coarse meshes misrepresent tidal flow and flood inundation.
- **Architecture:** Physics-informed neural network (PINN) solving the 1-D Saint-Venant equations and assimilating observations, with a new Fourier-feature embedding to encode periodic tidal boundary conditions.
- **Data:** Synthetic floodplain and open-channel cases, evaluated against analytical solutions and numerical models, plus storm-surge and tide-driven flood wave cases.
- **Main result:** PINN water depths are satisfactorily accurate with limited observations and outperform linear interpolation in resolving subgrid topography and flow regimes.
- **Open work:** Extending the approach to 2-D flows, real river networks and coupling with operational large-scale river models.
- **Issues:** Tested only on synthetic 1-D cases; PINN training cost and convergence on complex real geometries are not established.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Drought monitoring by downscaling GRACE-derived terrestrial water storage anomalies: A deep learning approach](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.128838)
Foroumandi et al. (2023), *Journal of Hydrology*. 99 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improve drought monitoring by downscaling coarse GRACE-derived terrestrial water storage anomalies to finer spatial resolution.
- **Architecture:** Deep learning downscaling model; the specific network family is not specified in the available metadata.
- **Data:** GRACE terrestrial water storage anomalies with higher-resolution hydroclimatic predictors; region and products not reported.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the title implies downscaled TWSA supports finer-scale drought assessment.
- **Open work:** Validation against in situ groundwater and drought indicators and extension to other regions and GRACE-FO periods.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; downscaled storage cannot be fully validated at fine scales and inherits GRACE errors and gaps.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [PREDICTION OF TWO‐YEAR PEAK STREAM‐DISCHARGES USING NEURAL NETWORKS 1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-1688.1997.tb03537.x)
Muttiah et al. (1997), *JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association*. 99 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts two-year peak stream discharges for ungauged basins from basin characteristics.

### [Genetic Programming‐Based Empirical Model for Daily Reference Evapotranspiration Estimation](https://doi.org/10.1002/clen.200800009)
Guven et al. (2008), *Clean-soil Air Water*. 99 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates daily reference evapotranspiration from limited meteorological data with an explicit empirical formula.

- **Data:** Daily meteorological data from weather stations (California CIMIS network), with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ET0 as reference.
- **Main result:** The genetic programming formula estimates ET0 closely matching Penman-Monteith and better than several empirical methods.
- **Open work:** Test the derived equations in other climates.
- **Issues:** Equations may not transfer to other climates; reference is a model estimate rather than lysimeter measurements.

### [Evaluation of artificial intelligence models for flood and drought forecasting in arid and tropical regions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2021.105136)
Adikari et al. (2021), *Environmental Modelling & Software*. 98 citations.

- **Issues:** Abstract missing; details of models, data and results not verified.

### [Regional Flood Frequency Analysis using Support Vector Regression under historical and future climate](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2016.04.041)
Gizaw et al. (2016), *Journal of Hydrology*. 98 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimate flood quantiles at ungauged sites through regional flood frequency analysis, under both historical and projected future climate.
- **Architecture:** Support vector regression (SVR) relating flood quantiles to catchment and climate descriptors.
- **Data:** Gauged streamflow records and catchment descriptors, with future climate from climate model projections; region and products not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the title implies SVR-based regional estimates of flood quantiles for current and future climate.

### Predicting Runoff from Rainfall Using Neural Networks
Halff et al. (1993), *Engineering Hydrology*. 98 citations.

- **Main result:** The neural network reproduces storm hydrographs reasonably well; numbers not reported here.

- **Issues:** Small dataset and limited validation; extrapolation to extreme storms is uncertain.

### [Streamflow simulation in data-scarce basins using Bayesian and physics-informed machine learning models](https://doi.org/10.1175/jhm-d-20-0082.1)
Lu et al. (2021), *Journal of Hydrometeorology*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses LSTM streamflow prediction in poorly monitored, data-scarce watersheds and addresses overfitting, uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution prediction.
- **Architecture:** LSTM networks with L2 and dropout regularization, a Bayesian LSTM for uncertainty quantification, and a physics-informed hybrid LSTM coupled with a hydrologic model for out-of-distribution prediction.
- **Data:** Daily streamflow in two diverse sets of catchments with and without snow influence, with calibration records as short as two years.
- **Main result:** With similar hydrologic variability, LSTM reaches NSE above 0.8 from two years of data; under shifted variability the hybrid model generalizes better; Bayesian and hybrid LSTMs do not overfit and the Bayesian LSTM gives useful uncertainty.
- **Open work:** Applying the approaches to more data-scarce regions and combining Bayesian and physics-informed components.
- **Issues:** Small number of case-study catchments; out-of-distribution skill depends on the process model in the hybrid; quantitative uncertainty calibration not reported in the abstract.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A two‐step‐ahead recurrent neural network for stream‐flow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.1313)
Chang et al. (2004), *Hydrological Processes*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves multi-step streamflow forecasting with recurrent networks for flood warning.
- **Architecture:** Recurrent neural network trained with real-time recurrent learning to forecast two steps ahead, compared with a feedforward network.
- **Data:** Streamflow and rainfall records from a river in Taiwan.
- **Main result:** The two-step-ahead recurrent network forecasts streamflow more accurately than the comparison models.
- **Open work:** Extend to longer lead times and other catchments.
- **Issues:** Single-basin study; performance on extreme floods not quantified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Generalisation for neural networks through data sampling and training procedures, with applications to streamflow predictions](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-8-940-2004)
Anctil et al. (2004), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares generalisation techniques for neural network streamflow models to give practitioners guidelines for building models that infer behaviour beyond the training data.
- **Architecture:** Multi-layer perceptron neural networks trained by Levenberg-Marquardt, with five generalisation approaches: stop training, Bayesian regularisation, stacking, bagging and boosting.
- **Data:** Streamflow modelling in six catchments with diverse hydrological behaviours.
- **Main result:** All approaches beat standard networks; stacking, bagging and boosting improve most, stacking slightly best but inconsistent across catchments.
- **Open work:** Authors recommend combining stop training or Bayesian regularisation with bagging or boosting; further testing in other catchments remains.
- **Issues:** Gains from stacking are small and catchment-dependent; ensemble methods increase computational cost.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Knowledge Extraction from Trained Neural Network River Flow Models](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2005)10:4(264))
Sudheer (2005), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Extracts physically interpretable knowledge from trained neural network river flow models to address their black-box nature.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural network (MLP) river flow models analysed with sensitivity and input-contribution techniques.
- **Data:** River flow and rainfall records from a catchment; details not reported in the available information.
- **Main result:** The analysis shows the trained networks capture physically plausible relations between inputs and flow.
- **Open work:** Develop general interpretability methods for hydrological neural networks.
- **Issues:** Interpretation techniques are approximate and case-specific.

### [Optimal tree-based release rules for real-time flood control operations on a multipurpose multireservoir system.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2008.11.038)
Wei et al. (2009), *Journal of Hydrology*. 97 citations.

- **Main goal:** Derives real-time reservoir release rules for flood control in a multipurpose multireservoir system.
- **Architecture:** Decision tree models learning release rules from optimal releases computed by an optimization model.
- **Data:** Historical typhoon flood events and multireservoir operation data from a river basin in Taiwan.
- **Main result:** Tree-based release rules approximate optimal operations and reduce flood peaks compared with conventional rules.
- **Open work:** Incorporate forecast uncertainty in inflows and test on new events.
- **Issues:** Limited number of flood events for rule learning; performance depends on optimization targets.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Continental-scale streamflow modeling of basins with reservoirs: Towards a coherent deep-learning-based strategy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2021.126455)
Ouyang et al. (2021), *arXiv*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Determines which dam-influenced basins can be modeled by deep learning for continental-scale daily streamflow prediction using readily available information.
- **Architecture:** Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks trained on basin groups defined by reservoir degree of regulation (dor), purpose and diversion, in a divide-and-conquer strategy.
- **Data:** 3,557 basins over the contiguous United States (83% dammed), extending reference-basin datasets with reservoir attributes (e.g. GAGES-II-type information).
- **Main result:** Training on all basins gives median NSE 0.74; pooled training yields median NSE 0.73, 0.78 and 0.71 for zero-, small- and large-dor basins; reference-trained models transfer poorly and migrating models between dor groups fails.
- **Open work:** Separately modeling reservoirs for irrigation, fire protection, hydropower and flood control, and explicit representation of large-dor reservoirs.
- **Issues:** Large-dor basins with irrigation dams remain poorly simulated; no explicit reservoir operation data; dammed basins must be in the training set.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A graph neural network (GNN) approach to basin-scale river network learning: the role of physics-based connectivity and data fusion](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-26-5163-2022)
Sun et al. (2022), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a fast basin-scale river network model for streamflow forecasting, since high-resolution vector-based river network models are computationally demanding.
- **Architecture:** Multistage physics-guided graph neural network (GNN) pretrained to emulate a vector-based river routing model, fine-tuned on gauge observations, with graph-based data fusion for bias correction and graph coarsening for scalability.
- **Data:** Outputs of a high-resolution vector-based river network model and streamflow gauge observations in a snow-dominated western US watershed and a larger basin.
- **Main result:** The GNN surrogate reproduces the process model with median KGE above 0.97; data fusion improves KGE by up to 50% at cross-validation gauges; coarsened graphs give comparable skill at a fraction of training cost.
- **Open work:** Scaling to continental river networks and determining the degree of physical realism needed in large-scale GNN river models.
- **Issues:** Surrogate inherits biases of the process-based model; tested in a limited number of basins; forecasting skill under extremes not detailed.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Intelligent control for modeling of real‐time reservoir operation, part II: artificial neural network with operating rule curves](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.5582)
Chang et al. (2005), *Hydrological Processes*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models real-time reservoir operation decisions by learning from operating rule curves.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network (specific type not specified in the available information) incorporating reservoir operating rule curves; part II of a study on intelligent control.
- **Data:** Reservoir operation records from a reservoir in Taiwan.
- **Main result:** The neural network with rule curves reproduces operator decisions and improves operation performance.
- **Open work:** Combine with inflow forecasts and multi-objective optimization.
- **Issues:** Single reservoir; learned rules reflect historical operating practice.

Antar et al. (2006), *Hydrological Processes*. 96 citations.

### [Comparison of Artificial Intelligence Techniques for river flow forecasting](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-12-123-2008)
Firat (2008), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 96 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares artificial intelligence methods for daily river flow forecasting to identify the most suitable approach.

### [Machine-learning- and deep-learning-based streamflow prediction in a hilly catchment for future scenarios using CMIP6 GCM data](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-1047-2023)
Singh et al. (2023), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 95 citations.

- **Main goal:** Projects future streamflow in the Himalayan Sutlej River basin under climate change for water resource planning.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of Gaussian linear regression, generalized additive model, MARS, artificial neural network (MLP), random forest and a 1D convolutional neural network; random forest selected for projections.
- **Data:** Daily data 1979–2009 at Kasol for training; bias-corrected CMIP6 output from six GCMs downscaled to 0.25° under SSP245 and SSP585 for 2041–2070 and 2071–2100.
- **Main result:** Random forest performs best (test R2 0.78, NSE 0.71, KGE 0.82); mean annual streamflow rises about 0.8–1.4%, monsoon flow increases ~10–13%, while pre-monsoon and winter flows decline (winter ~-22%).
- **Open work:** Incorporating glacier and snowmelt dynamics and land-use change, and assessing downstream agricultural water impacts.
- **Issues:** Statistical models trained on historical relationships may not hold under future climate; GCM and downscaling uncertainty; glacier retreat not explicitly modeled.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Surrogate optimization of deep neural networks for groundwater predictions](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10898-020-00912-0)
Müller et al. (2019), *Journal of Global Optimization*. 95 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provide accurate, cheap groundwater level predictions for water managers who cannot run complex mechanistic models, and find good hyperparameters efficiently.

Goswami et al. (2005), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 95 citations.

### [A spatial–temporal graph deep learning model for urban flood nowcasting leveraging heterogeneous community features](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-32548-x)
Farahmand et al. (2021), *Scientific Reports*. 94 citations.

- **Main goal:** Nowcasts urban flood inundation during extreme weather events by combining physics-based and human-sensed data to improve situational awareness.

### [Deep learning for cross-region streamflow and flood forecasting at a global scale](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100617)
Zhang et al. (2024), *Innovation (Cambridge (Mass.))*. 93 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecast streamflow and floods globally, including ungauged catchments where physically based models are hard to calibrate.
- **Architecture:** ED-DLSTM, an encoder-decoder double-layer long short-term memory (LSTM) network with a spatial attribute encoding module.

- **Main result:** Mean NSE of 0.75 across the 2,000+ catchments; in Chile 76.9% of ungauged catchments reach NSE > 0 in the best case; cell states show emergent hydrological regionalization.

### [MC-LSTM: Mass-Conserving LSTM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.05186)
Hoedt et al. (2021), *International Conference on Machine Learning*. 93 citations.

- **Main goal:** Build recurrent networks that obey conservation laws, since many physical and economic systems redistribute conserved quantities.
- **Architecture:** Mass-Conserving LSTM (MC-LSTM), a long short-term memory variant whose gating redistributes stored mass so inputs are conserved exactly.
- **Data:** Arithmetic tasks, traffic forecasting, a pendulum, and a large hydrology benchmark (CAMELS-US rainfall-runoff).
- **Main result:** Sets a new state of the art for neural arithmetic units and for peak-flow prediction in the hydrology benchmark; its states correlate with real-world processes.
- **Open work:** Handling non-conserved fluxes and unobserved sinks, and extension to spatially distributed systems.
- **Issues:** Strict mass conservation can hurt when data have biases or unmeasured losses such as evapotranspiration; overall streamflow skill is not clearly above a standard LSTM.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

Si et al. (2021), *Scientific Reports*. 92 citations.

- **Main goal:** Extend lead times of monthly streamflow and flood prediction on the Yangtze River, beyond the roughly one month of physically based models, using ENSO information.

- **Data:** Monthly Yangtze River streamflow and ENSO indices, 1952–2018; tested on two extreme flood years and one small flood year.
- **Main result:** ConvLSTM improves stability and flood accuracy; adding ENSO better times flood peaks and flows; ConvLSTM + encoder-decoder GRU performs best.
- **Open work:** Adding other climate indices and quantifying uncertainty for longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Very few flood years tested and a single monthly series, so results may not generalize; no uncertainty estimates.
- *Basis: abstract*

Shrestha et al. (2005), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 92 citations.

Rahimikhoob (2008), *Irrigation science*. 92 citations.

### [Prediction of coastal flooding risk under climate change impacts in South Korea using machine learning algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aba5b3)
Park et al. (2020), *Environmental Research Letters*. 91 citations.

### [Rapid spatio-temporal flood modelling via hydraulics-based graph neural networks](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-4227-2023)
Bentivoglio et al. (2023), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 89 citations.
