### [Over-parameterisation, a major obstacle to the use of artificial neural networks in hydrology?](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-7-693-2003)
Gaume et al. (2003), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 75 citations.

- **Main goal:** Questions whether feed-forward neural networks are worthwhile for streamflow forecasting given their tendency to over-parameterise and fit noise.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural network (MLP) with structure chosen by a validation-based model selection method, compared with a linear model and the GR4J conceptual rainfall-runoff model.
- **Data:** Two case studies: river flow prediction from upstream flows and rainfall-runoff modelling; catchment details not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Selected networks have only two or three hidden neurons, perform close to the linear model, and are outperformed by GR4J for rainfall-runoff.
- **Open work:** Broader case studies and evaluation methods to settle the usefulness of neural networks in hydrology.
- **Issues:** Conclusions rest on two case studies and one evaluation method; networks of the period were small and trained on limited data.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Soil moisture estimation using an artificial neural network: a feasibility study](https://doi.org/10.5589/m04-041)
Jiang et al. (2004), *Canadian Journal of Remote Sensing*. 75 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether a neural network can estimate soil moisture from surface and atmospheric variables observable by remote sensing.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network for soil moisture estimation; network type and configuration not reported here.
- **Data:** Training and test data from simulations and/or observations; exact sources not reported here.
- **Main result:** The feasibility study shows that a neural network can estimate soil moisture with useful accuracy.
- **Open work:** Applying the approach to real satellite observations and other regions.
- **Issues:** Feasibility-level study with limited evaluation; performance under real retrieval noise is uncertain.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Empirical comparison of various methods for training feed‐Forward neural networks for salinity forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1029/1999wr900150)
Maier et al. (1999), *Water Resources Research*. 74 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares methods for training feed-forward neural networks for forecasting river salinity, to guide practical model development.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural networks (multilayer perceptron) trained with various algorithms, including backpropagation variants with different parameters and second-order methods.
- **Data:** River salinity, flow and level time series for the River Murray, South Australia, with a multi-week forecast horizon.
- **Main result:** Training methods differ mainly in training speed, while generalization ability is broadly similar; specific numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Guidance on network geometry and input selection is needed alongside training methods.
- **Issues:** Single river case study; findings on training algorithms may not transfer to other problems.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Reservoir operation using the neural network and fuzzy systems for dam control and operation support](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0965-9978(02)00015-7)
Hasebe et al. (2002), *Advances in Engineering Software*. 74 citations.

- **Main goal:** Supports reservoir and dam operation decisions with neural network and fuzzy systems that emulate operator rules.
- **Architecture:** Neural network and fuzzy system models for reservoir release decisions; configuration not reported here.
- **Data:** Reservoir inflow, storage and release records from Japanese dams; periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** Neural network and fuzzy approaches reproduce operator decisions and can support dam control, with differing strengths between the two.
- **Open work:** Combining the approaches with inflow forecasts and testing in real-time operation.
- **Issues:** Limited case studies; learning from past operations can reproduce past suboptimal decisions.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Evaluation and interpretation of convolutional long short-term memory networks for regional hydrological modelling](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-26-795-2022)
Anderson et al. (2022), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 73 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assessing and interpreting a spatiotemporal deep learning architecture for regional streamflow modelling.
- **Architecture:** Convolutional long short-term memory network (ConvLSTM) with perturbation-based interpretation experiments.
- **Data:** Gridded reanalysis climate forcing (ERA5) and observed daily streamflow at 226 gauges in southwestern Canada, 1980-2015.
- **Main result:** Median NSE 0.68 with 35% of stations above 0.8; the model focuses on in-basin inputs and responds physically to temperature perturbations, including glacier-dependent August sensitivity.
- **Open work:** Further interpretable deep learning hydrology and climate change scenario use.
- **Issues:** Moderate median skill; sensitivity tests are not proof of physical process learning.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Modelling of river discharges and rainfall using radial basis function networks based on support vector regression](https://doi.org/10.1080/00207720310001640241)
Choy et al. (2003), *International Journal of Systems Science*. 73 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models river discharge and rainfall time series with radial basis function networks designed via support vector regression.
- **Architecture:** Radial basis function network whose centers and weights are obtained from support vector regression.
- **Data:** River discharge and rainfall time series; locations and periods not reported here.
- **Main result:** The SVR-based RBF networks model the discharge and rainfall series accurately with compact structures.
- **Open work:** Applying the method to longer-lead forecasting and more catchments.
- **Issues:** Limited data sets; kernel and parameter selection influence results.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Multi-objective performance comparison of an artificial neural network and a conceptual rainfall—runoff model](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.52.3.397)
Vos et al. (2007), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 73 citations.

- **Main goal:** Compares an artificial neural network and a conceptual rainfall-runoff model using multiple performance criteria rather than a single score.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural network (MLP) compared with the HBV conceptual rainfall-runoff model under multi-objective evaluation.
- **Data:** Daily rainfall, evaporation and discharge for the Geer River basin, Belgium.
- **Main result:** The neural network scores well on some criteria but shows timing errors and weaker performance on others, while HBV is more balanced across criteria.
- **Open work:** Multi-objective training of neural networks and improved input selection.
- **Issues:** Single basin; neural network performance is sensitive to inputs and training objective.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Spatiotemporal deep learning rainfall-runoff forecasting combined with remote sensing precipitation products in large scale basins](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.128727)
Zhu et al. (2022), *Journal of Hydrology*. 72 citations.

- **Main goal:** Rainfall-runoff forecasting in large-scale basins with a spatiotemporal deep learning model that uses remote sensing precipitation products as forcing.
- **Architecture:** Spatiotemporal deep learning model combined with remote-sensing precipitation; the exact architecture is not available.
- **Data:** Satellite remote sensing precipitation products and observed streamflow for large basins; specific products and basins are not available because the abstract is missing.
- **Main result:** Not reported; the abstract is unavailable.
- **Open work:** Comparison across precipitation products and transfer to other large basins would follow naturally.
- **Issues:** Abstract missing, so the card is based on the title only; satellite precipitation errors propagate into runoff forecasts.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Real‐Time Flood Forecasting Using Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1111/0885-9507.00090)
Thirumalaiah et al. (1998), *Computer‐Aided Civil and Infrastructure Engineering*. 72 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts stream flows during storms in real time to support operational flood management.
- **Architecture:** Neural networks trained with error backpropagation, conjugate gradient and cascade correlation, using past flood values as inputs.
- **Data:** Sequences of past observed flood values at a specific river location; site details not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Flood forecasts with lead times of one or more hours are satisfactory, especially at the shortest warning times.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times and inclusion of rainfall inputs are natural extensions.
- **Issues:** Uses only past flow values at one location; skill declines with lead time and no uncertainty is provided.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Optimal functional forms for estimation of missing precipitation data.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2009.06.014)
Teegavarapu et al. (2009), *Journal of Hydrology*. 72 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates missing precipitation records at rain gauges using optimal functional forms for spatial weighting.
- **Architecture:** Optimization-based functional forms for weighting neighbouring gauges in missing precipitation estimation; machine-learning type not specified here.
- **Data:** Daily precipitation records from a network of rain gauges; region and period not reported here.
- **Main result:** Optimal functional forms improve missing precipitation estimates compared with traditional weighting methods such as inverse distance.
- **Open work:** Applying the approach to other networks and climates and to temporal resolutions.
- **Issues:** Calibrated weights are network specific; extreme events and zero-precipitation cases are challenging.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Robust Runoff Prediction With Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Meteorological Variables From Deep Learning Ensemble Model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023wr035676)
Wu et al. (2023), *Water Resources Research*. 71 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts runoff at three hydrological stations for flood warning while accounting for meteorological drivers beyond precipitation and making the model interpretable.
- **Architecture:** Decomposition-ensemble pipeline: TVF-EMD and robust local mean decomposition of runoff, bidirectional gated recurrent unit (BiGRU) and extreme learning machine sub-models, combined nonlinearly by a random forest; SHAP for explanation.
- **Data:** Runoff series from three hydrological stations with meteorological variables selected by the Relief algorithm and variance inflation factor; station locations and periods not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Outperforms comparison models on various evaluation metrics, and SHAP quantifies each meteorological variable's contribution to the long-term runoff trend; no specific numbers are given in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Testing on more basins and longer lead times, and checking whether the decomposition is applied without future information leakage, are natural next steps.
- **Issues:** Very complex multi-stage pipeline with risk of overfitting and decomposition leakage in operational use; only three stations evaluated.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Explainable AI in drought forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mlwa.2021.100192)
Dikshit et al. (2021), *Machine Learning with Applications*. 71 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasting drought and explaining how input variables drive the forecasts.
- **Architecture:** Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model interpreted with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).
- **Data:** SPI-12 from monthly SILO rainfall, 1901-2018 (train 1901-2000, test 2001-2018), in four regions of New South Wales, Australia.
- **Main result:** SPI-12 forecasts at 3-month lead evaluated with R2, NSE and RMSE; SHAP shows variable impacts vary strongly in time and space, including during the Millennium Drought.
- **Open work:** Region- and period-specific interpretation of drought forecasting models.
- **Issues:** Limited to four regions; SHAP explanations are model-dependent.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Modelling evapotranspiration using discrete wavelet transform and neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.7448)
Partal (2009), *Hydrological Processes*. 71 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models evapotranspiration using wavelet-transformed inputs and neural networks to capture multiscale variability.
- **Architecture:** Discrete wavelet transform of input time series combined with an artificial neural network (wavelet-neural network); network type not specified.
- **Data:** Meteorological station data with reference evapotranspiration estimates from Turkey; period not reported here.
- **Main result:** The wavelet-neural network model estimates evapotranspiration more accurately than conventional neural networks and empirical methods.
- **Open work:** Testing at more stations and climates and studying input selection.
- **Issues:** Targets are computed rather than measured evapotranspiration; boundary effects of wavelet decomposition.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Advance flood forecasting for flood stricken Bangladesh with a fuzzy reasoning method (Copies of English Papers by the Center Staff Published in the Fiscal Year of 1999)](https://doi.org/10.1002/(sici)1099-1085(20000228)14:3<431::aid-hyp947>3.0.co;2-0)
Liong et al. (2000), *Venue not recorded*. 71 citations.

- **Main goal:** Provides advance flood forecasts for Bangladesh using a fuzzy reasoning method to extend warning lead time.
- **Architecture:** Fuzzy reasoning (fuzzy rule-based) forecasting method.
- **Data:** Upstream and downstream river water level records in Bangladesh; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The fuzzy reasoning method gives useful multi-day advance water level forecasts.
- **Open work:** Longer lead times and comparison with neural networks and hydrodynamic models.
- **Issues:** Limited events and stations; details not available.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Data Assimilation for Streamflow Forecasting Using Extreme Learning Machines and Multilayer Perceptrons](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019wr026226)
Boucher et al. (2020), *Water Resources Research*. 70 citations.

- **Main goal:** Using neural networks for data assimilation in streamflow forecasting by learning the mapping from streamflow to model states.
- **Architecture:** Ensemble-based data assimilation with extreme learning machines (ELM) and multilayer perceptrons (MLP) applied to the GR4J lumped hydrological model.
- **Data:** International testbed of four hydrologically dissimilar catchments.
- **Main result:** Neural network assimilation noticeably improves over OpenLoop simulation in all catchments, evaluated with CRPS.
- **Open work:** Applying to models with more state variables.
- **Issues:** Proof of concept with only two state variables and four catchments.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Improving long-term streamflow prediction in a poorly gauged basin using geo-spatiotemporal mesoscale data and attention-based deep learning: A comparative study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.128608)
Ghobadi et al. (2022), *Journal of Hydrology*. 70 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improving long-term streamflow prediction in a poorly gauged basin, as implied by the title.
- **Architecture:** Attention-based deep learning compared with other models; specific network family not specified in the available metadata.
- **Data:** Geo-spatiotemporal mesoscale data for a poorly gauged basin; details not available.
- **Main result:** Not reported; the title implies attention-based deep learning improves long-term streamflow prediction.
- **Open work:** Not reported; likely transfer to other poorly gauged basins.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; details unverified.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Multiobjective training of artificial neural networks for rainfall‐runoff modeling](https://doi.org/10.1029/2007wr006734)
Vos et al. (2008), *Water Resources Research*. 70 citations.

- **Main goal:** Trains artificial neural networks for rainfall-runoff modelling with multiple objectives to improve balanced performance across hydrograph aspects.
- **Architecture:** Feed-forward neural network (MLP) trained with a multi-objective evolutionary optimization algorithm instead of single-objective back-propagation.
- **Data:** Rainfall, evaporation and discharge records for the Geer River basin, Belgium.
- **Main result:** Multi-objective training yields networks with better balanced performance across criteria, including timing and peak flows, than single-objective training.
- **Open work:** Combining multi-objective training with improved input selection and comparing with conceptual models.
- **Issues:** Single basin; computational cost and choice of objectives affect results.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Statistical forecasting of regional avalanche danger using simulated snow-cover data](https://doi.org/10.3189/002214309790152429)
Schirmer et al. (2009), *Journal of Glaciology*. 70 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts regional avalanche danger levels statistically and tests whether snow-cover variables simulated by a snowpack model add skill beyond meteorological predictors.
- **Architecture:** Statistical classification models (classification trees and nearest-neighbour methods) using meteorological variables and SNOWPACK-simulated snow-cover variables as predictors.
- **Data:** Swiss avalanche danger levels issued for the Davos region, with weather station data and SNOWPACK simulations; exact period not reported here.
- **Main result:** Models reach moderate accuracy for the danger level; adding simulated snow-stratigraphy variables gives only a limited improvement over meteorological predictors alone.
- **Open work:** Better snow-instability parameters from snowpack simulations and extension to other regions are natural next steps.
- **Issues:** Single region; target is a human-issued danger level with its own inconsistencies; moderate accuracy limits operational use.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Retrieving soil moisture from simulated brightness temperatures by a neural network](https://doi.org/10.1109/36.942544)
Liou et al. (2001), *IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing*. 69 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves soil moisture from passive microwave brightness temperatures, a nonlinear inversion problem for land remote sensing.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural network trained to invert brightness temperatures to soil moisture.
- **Data:** Brightness temperatures simulated by a coupled land surface process and radiobrightness model, not real satellite observations.
- **Main result:** The neural network retrieves soil moisture accurately from the simulated brightness temperatures, particularly for near-surface layers.
- **Open work:** Testing on real radiometer observations and with vegetation and roughness effects.
- **Issues:** Simulation-only study; retrieval error on real data with noise and model mismatch is not assessed.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [Constraints of artificial neural networks for rainfall-runoff modelling: trade-offs in hydrological state representation and model evaluation](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-9-111-2005)
Vos et al. (2005), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 69 citations.

- **Main goal:** Examines constraints of ANN rainfall-runoff models, especially timing errors caused by using lagged discharge to represent catchment state.
- **Architecture:** Multilayer feedforward neural networks (MLP) with alternative state inputs: moving averages of discharge and rainfall and the GR4J soil moisture component.
- **Data:** Daily and hourly rainfall and runoff data from the Geer catchment, Belgium.
- **Main result:** Daily forecasts are good, but hourly forecasts show lagged predictions from the autoregressive input; alternative state representers fix timing but reduce overall fit.
- **Open work:** Use of multiple performance measures during ANN training to balance timing and fit.
- **Issues:** Single catchment; trade-off between timing and goodness of fit unresolved; multi-objective training only suggested.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Transformer Versus LSTM: A Comparison of Deep Learning Models for Karst Spring Discharge Forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022wr032602)
Pölz et al. (2024), *Water Resources Research*. 68 citations.

- **Main goal:** Evaluates whether the transformer improves forecasts of karst spring discharge up to 4 days ahead for drinking-water management.
- **Architecture:** Transformer compared with a long short-term memory (LSTM) network and a common baseline model, in discharge-based and non-discharge-based input scenarios, with uncertainty analysis.
- **Data:** Extensive hourly database for an Austrian karst spring (LKAS2) plus two further karst springs with diverse discharge characteristics; inputs include rainfall, electrical conductivity and temporal information.
- **Main result:** Transformer beats the LSTM by 9% mean difference for the spring with the longest response time but is 4% worse for the shortest; both reach NSE 0.64-0.92 and sMAPE 10.8-28.7% at LKAS2 and the transformer better captures snowmelt.
- **Open work:** Testing on more springs and longer horizons, and exploiting attention for process understanding, are natural next steps.
- **Issues:** Only three springs; performance depends on spring response time; prediction intervals are widest during snowmelt.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Robust Meteorological Drought Prediction Using Antecedent SST Fluctuations and Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020wr029413)
Li et al. (2021), *Water Resources Research*. 68 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts meteorological drought robustly by exploiting the full antecedent global sea surface temperature fluctuation pattern rather than signals from a few ocean regions.
- **Architecture:** Antecedent SST fluctuation pattern (ASFP) predictors fed to support vector regression, random forest and extreme learning machine models for ensemble, probabilistic and deterministic predictions.
- **Data:** Antecedent global SST fields and the standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI) at 1°x1° for the Colorado, Danube, Orange and Pearl River basins; SST product not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** ASFP-ELM effectively predicts the space-time evolution of drought events at 1- and 3-month lead times and outperforms ASFP-SVR and ASFP-RF; no skill numbers in the abstract.
- **Open work:** Extending to longer leads and more basins, and integrating into drought early warning systems, are suggested.
- **Issues:** Short lead times only; SST-only predictors ignore land-surface memory; skill numbers and physical interpretation are not given in the abstract.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Development of a Distributed Physics‐Informed Deep Learning Hydrological Model for Data‐Scarce Regions](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023wr036333)
Zhong et al. (2024), *Water Resources Research*. 68 citations.

- **Main goal:** Simulates streamflow in data-scarce regions, including ungauged internal sub-basins, where large-sample deep learning and transfer learning generalize poorly.
- **Architecture:** Distributed physics-informed deep learning model: differentiable hydrological models for each sub-basin with neural network parameterization, coupled with a differentiable Muskingum channel routing scheme.
- **Data:** Streamflow from the downstream-most gauge for training and upstream held-out stations for testing, with meteorological forcing; basin and data products are not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** Trained only on the outlet station, it outperforms a distributed hydrological model at both training and held-out upstream stations, and beats transfer-learning models while needing fewer gauges.
- **Open work:** Testing in more regions with distinct hydrological processes and adding further process modules are natural extensions.
- **Issues:** Equifinality in sub-basin parameters when constrained only by outlet flow; no quantitative scores in the abstract; evaluated on a limited number of basins.
- *Basis: assessment*

### River flow forecasting using neural networks and wavelet analysis
Cannas et al. (2005), *European geosciences union general assembly*. 68 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river flow by combining wavelet analysis with neural networks to handle multiscale variability.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural network (MLP) fed with wavelet-decomposed flow series, compared with networks using raw data.
- **Data:** Monthly river flow records from a catchment in Sardinia, Italy.
- **Main result:** Wavelet pre-processing improves neural network flow forecasts compared with networks on undecomposed data.
- **Open work:** Choice of wavelet and decomposition levels and operational testing.
- **Issues:** Conference abstract with limited detail; possible information leakage from non-causal wavelet decomposition.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Artificial neural network models for estimating regional reference evapotranspiration based on climate factors](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.7153)
Dai et al. (2009), *Hydrological Processes*. 68 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates regional reference evapotranspiration from limited climate factors where full Penman-Monteith inputs are unavailable.

- **Data:** Climate station data with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference ET as target in a Chinese (arid/semi-arid) region; details not confirmed.
- **Main result:** ANN models with a few climate variables approximate Penman-Monteith ET0 well and outperform simpler empirical equations.
- **Open work:** Spatial transferability across stations and climates.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; targets are computed ET0, not lysimeter measurements.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Timing error correction procedure applied to neural network rainfall—runoff modelling](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.52.3.414)
Abrahart et al. (2007), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 68 citations.

- **Main goal:** Corrects timing errors (lagged predictions) common in neural network rainfall-runoff forecasts.
- **Architecture:** Neural network rainfall-runoff model (feedforward) with a timing error correction procedure applied to training/outputs; exact network type is not specified here.
- **Data:** Rainfall and river flow records from a UK catchment; details not reported.
- **Main result:** The correction procedure reduces timing errors in forecast hydrographs relative to the uncorrected network.
- **Open work:** Integrating timing-aware objectives into training and testing on more catchments.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; specifics are uncertain, and evaluation on a single catchment would limit generality.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Neuro-fuzzy river ice breakup forecasting system](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coldregions.2006.08.009)
Mahabir et al. (2006), *Cold Regions Science and Technology*. 68 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts river ice breakup severity, where ice jams cause flooding and physically based models are limited.

- **Data:** Historical breakup records and hydrometeorological data for the Athabasca River at Fort McMurray, Canada.
- **Main result:** The neuro-fuzzy system classifies breakup severity better than existing approaches and provides an interpretable early-warning tool.

- **Issues:** Small number of breakup events; site-specific rules.
- *Basis: abstract+knowledge*

### [USE OF A GENETIC ALGORITHM AND MULTI-OBJECTIVE PROGRAMMING FOR CALIBRATION OF A HYDROLOGIC MODEL](https://doi.org/10.13031/2013.17229)
Balascio et al. (1998), *Transactions of the ASABE*. 67 citations.

- **Main goal:** Calibrates a hydrologic model automatically, balancing several objectives such as volume and peak flow errors.
- **Architecture:** Genetic algorithm combined with multi-objective programming for parameter optimisation of a hydrologic model.
- **Data:** Observed rainfall and streamflow for a watershed; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The genetic algorithm finds parameter sets that fit observed hydrographs well under multiple objectives; numbers not reported here.

### [Neuro-dynamic programming for designing water reservoir network management policies](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.conengprac.2006.02.011)
Castelletti et al. (2007), *Control Engineering Practice*. 67 citations.

- **Main goal:** Designs operating policies for water reservoir networks, where dynamic programming suffers from the curse of dimensionality.
- **Architecture:** Neuro-dynamic programming: approximate dynamic programming with neural networks approximating the value function; not a forecasting model.
- **Data:** Simulated operations of a multi-reservoir network in Italy (Piave river system) driven by hydrological inflow records.
- **Main result:** Neuro-dynamic programming yields policies comparable to stochastic dynamic programming at much lower computational cost for larger networks.

### [The extrapolation of artificial neural networks for the modelling of rainfall-runoff relationships](https://doi.org/10.2166/hydro.2005.0025)
Hettiarachchi et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydroinformatics*. 67 citations.

- **Main goal:** Addresses the poor extrapolation of ANN rainfall-runoff models to floods larger than those in the training data.
- **Architecture:** Feedforward neural network (MLP) with modified input/output scaling to allow extrapolation beyond the training range.
- **Data:** Rainfall-runoff records from a catchment; details not reported.
- **Main result:** Adjusting the scaling range improves predictions of flows exceeding the training range compared with standard scaling.
- **Open work:** Physically informed constraints for extreme flows.
- **Issues:** Abstract not available; few extreme events to verify extrapolation.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Rainfall‐Runoff Modeling Based on Genetic Programming](https://doi.org/10.1002/0470848944.hsa017)
Babovic et al. (2006), *Venue not recorded*. 67 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models rainfall-runoff relations with interpretable data-driven equations.
- **Architecture:** Genetic programming (symbolic regression) evolving rainfall-runoff model equations.
- **Data:** Rainfall and runoff records from a catchment; details not reported.
- **Main result:** Genetic programming produces compact rainfall-runoff models with accuracy comparable to or better than conventional models.

- **Issues:** Abstract not available; evolved expressions may overfit.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Flash Drought: Review of Concept, Prediction and the Potential for Machine Learning, Deep Learning Methods](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022ef002723)
Tyagi et al. (2022), *Earth's Future*. 66 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reviews the flash drought concept, the sources of uncertainty in its prediction, and the potential of machine learning and deep learning to improve it.
- **Architecture:** Review of 121 articles covering flash drought definitions, key indicators, characteristics, and monitoring, prediction and impact-assessment methods, including ML and DL approaches.
- **Data:** Literature corpus of 121 relevant articles; no new data.
- **Main result:** Flash drought prediction is limited by inconsistent definitions and indicators, low subseasonal-to-seasonal predictability, input-data errors, parameter uncertainty and nonlinear, non-stationary indicator interactions; combining traditional methods and multisource data with ML/DL shows promise.
- **Open work:** Calls for consistent definitions, better physical understanding, and ML/DL models that fuse multisource data for S2S flash drought prediction.
- **Issues:** A review, so no new quantitative evaluation; conclusions about ML potential are largely prospective.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Karst spring discharge modeling based on deep learning using spatially distributed input data](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-2021-403)
Wunsch et al. (2021), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 66 citations.

- **Main goal:** Models karst spring discharge where few climate stations exist in the catchment, by learning directly from gridded meteorological data.
- **Architecture:** 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) processing gridded meteorological inputs followed by a 1D CNN for discharge simulation, compared with 1D models using station data; spatial input sensitivity analysis.
- **Data:** Gridded meteorological data (product not named in the abstract) and discharge for three karst spring catchments in the Alpine and Mediterranean regions.
- **Main result:** The 2D models simulate karst spring discharge excellently, rivalling existing modeling studies in the regions, and the sensitivity analysis highlights relevant input areas useful for catchment delineation.
- **Open work:** Using spatial sensitivity to localize and delineate karst catchments and testing more springs are suggested directions.
- **Issues:** Only three catchments; no quantitative scores in the abstract; performance tied to the quality of gridded meteorological products.
- *Basis: abstract*

### A flood forecasting neural network model with genetic algorithm
Wu (2006), *Venue not recorded*. 66 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts floods using a neural network whose training is improved by a genetic algorithm.
- **Architecture:** Neural network (feedforward) with a genetic algorithm used for weight or parameter optimization.
- **Data:** River flow and rainfall data; details not reported.

### [On the need for physical constraints in deep learning rainfall–runoff projections under climate change: a sensitivity analysis to warming and shifts in potential evapotranspiration](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-28-479-2024)

- **Main goal:** Assesses whether deep learning rainfall-runoff models produce physically plausible streamflow projections under warming and changes in potential evapotranspiration.
- **Architecture:** Sensitivity analysis comparing three conceptual process-based models with LSTM, mass-conserving LSTM (MC-LSTM) and a new MC-LSTM-PET variant, plus a national LSTM.
- **Data:** 212 watersheds in the Great Lakes basin and a national LSTM fit to 531 US watersheds (CAMELS); warming scenarios with Hamon and Priestley-Taylor PET.
- **Main result:** DL models beat process models historically, but the LSTM shows unrealistic water losses under warming (-20% to -25%), whereas MC-LSTM-PET reproduces the expected PET-dependent responses of process models.
- **Open work:** Physical constraints on architecture and inputs are needed for credible DL climate projections; further constraint designs are open.
- **Issues:** Sensitivity experiments with idealized scenarios; no ground truth for future responses; process models are used as the plausibility reference.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Using Convolutional Neural Networks for Streamflow Projection in California](https://doi.org/10.3389/frwa.2020.00028)
Duan et al. (2020), *Frontiers in Water*. 51 citations.

- **Main goal:** Develops a temporal convolutional network for long-term streamflow projection in California under climate change.
- **Architecture:** Temporal convolutional neural network (TCNN) with causal convolution blocks, compared with other machine learning models.
- **Data:** CAMELS watersheds in California for training; LOCA downscaled climate projections for future streamflow.
- **Main result:** TCNN captures physically plausible input–streamflow relationships, remains stable under an idealized extreme test (4x precipitation, +5 °C), and produces future projections.
- **Open work:** Further evaluation of extrapolation under climate change and comparison with process-based projections.
- **Issues:** Extrapolation beyond observed climate is inherently uncertain; inherits biases of the LOCA forcing.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [FloodGNN-GRU: a spatio-temporal graph neural network for flood prediction](https://doi.org/10.1017/eds.2024.19)
Kazadi et al. (2024), *Environmental Data Science*. 51 citations.

- **Main goal:** Emulates physics-based inundation models for fast spatio-temporal flood prediction.
- **Architecture:** FloodGNN-GRU: graph neural network (GNN) combined with gated recurrent unit (GRU), with velocities as vector features.
- **Data:** LISFLOOD-FP simulation of Hurricane Harvey (2017) in Houston, Texas.
- **Main result:** Outperforms data-driven alternatives on several metrics; trains 100x faster and tests 1000x faster than a comparable simulation.
- **Open work:** Generalizing to other events and domains and longer lead times.
- **Issues:** Single simulated event; skill degrades for longer predictions; trained on model output, not observations.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Coupling Machine Learning Into Hydrodynamic Models to Improve River Modeling With Complex Boundary Conditions](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022wr032183)
Huang et al. (2022), *Water Resources Research*. 50 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves river hydrodynamic modeling with complex lake and uncontrolled downstream boundary conditions for flood management.
- **Architecture:** Coupled framework of a gated recurrent unit (GRU) network with a 1-D hydrodynamic model (GRU-HD), using ML-predicted water levels as downstream boundary conditions.
- **Data:** Water levels and streamflow on the middle and lower Yangtze River with Poyang and Dongting lakes; periods not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** GRU-HD simulates water levels, streamflow and river-lake exchange with most KGE above 0.90, and ML boundary conditions beat the rating-curve approach.
- **Open work:** Applying to other river-lake systems and to forecasting mode with predicted inflows would follow.
- **Issues:** Single river system; ML boundary predictions may not extrapolate to unprecedented floods.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [A Machine Learning Framework for Predicting and Understanding the Canadian Drought Monitor](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022wr033847)
Mardian et al. (2023), *Water Resources Research*. 50 citations.

- **Main goal:** Automates prediction of the expert-produced Canadian Drought Monitor (CDM) maps and explains drought dynamics in near real time.
- **Architecture:** Machine learning framework (tree-based gradient boosting type model, not named in the abstract) with SHAP variable importance for interpretation.
- **Data:** Nearly two decades of CDM expert analyses with climate, hydrological and remote sensing predictors including GRACE groundwater signals.
- **Main result:** Effectively predicts CDM maps and drought evolution; SHAP links the 2015 Prairie drought to a strong El Nino and reduced groundwater detected by GRACE.
- **Open work:** Streamlining CDM operations and retrospectively extending the CDM to evaluate drought events historically.
- **Issues:** Learns expert judgments, which embed subjectivity; skill metrics and model type are not detailed in the abstract.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Rainfall-runoff modelling using adaptive neuro-fuzzy systems](https://doi.org/10.2166/hydro.2001.0002)
Gautam et al. (2001), *Journal of Hydroinformatics*. 50 citations.

- **Data:** Observed rainfall and runoff data from a catchment; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** ANFIS simulates runoff well and is competitive with neural network and conceptual approaches; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Test on more catchments and longer lead forecasting.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; rule base grows with inputs; limited physical interpretability.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Applying fuzzy theory and genetic algorithm to interpolate precipitation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2005.03.034)
Chang et al. (2005), *Journal of Hydrology*. 50 citations.

Garbrecht (2006), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 50 citations.

### [Development and Validation of GANN Model for Evapotranspiration Estimation](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)1084-0699(2009)14:2(131))
Kumar et al. (2009), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 50 citations.

- **Main result:** The GANN model estimates evapotranspiration accurately and compares favourably with conventional methods; numbers not reported here.

### [Forecasting Palmer Index Using Neural Networks and Climatic Indexes](https://doi.org/10.1061/(asce)he.1943-5584.0000028)
Cutore et al. (2009), *Journal of Hydrologic Engineering*. 50 citations.

Chidthong et al. (2009), *Hydrological Processes*. 50 citations.

### [From RNNs to Transformers: benchmarking deep learning architectures for hydrologic prediction](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-29-6811-2025)
Liu et al. (2025), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 49 citations.

- **Main goal:** Benchmarks attention-based models against LSTM across diverse hydrologic prediction tasks to guide model choice in the era of large models.
- **Architecture:** Benchmark framework comparing 11 transformer architectures with an LSTM baseline, plus pretrained large language models and time series attention models for zero-shot forecasting.
- **Data:** Multi-source datasets for daily runoff (including a global streamflow dataset), soil moisture, snow water equivalent and dissolved oxygen.
- **Main result:** LSTM is best for regression (median KGE 0.75 on global streamflow, 0.11 above the best transformer), while attention models overtake LSTM as tasks move to autoregression and zero-shot prediction.
- **Open work:** Provides a platform for developing large-scale hydrologic models; scaling foundation models for hydrology remains open.
- **Issues:** Results depend on hyperparameter tuning per architecture; zero-shot evaluation of LLMs is limited.

Han et al. (1997), *Journal of Arid Environments*. 49 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates daily soil water evaporation from weather and soil variables in arid conditions.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network relating meteorological and soil moisture inputs to soil evaporation.
- **Data:** Field measurements of soil evaporation and weather in a dry region; specifics not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** The neural network estimates daily evaporation with good accuracy; exact metrics not reported here.

Aytek et al. (2008), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 49 citations.

### [Non-parametric Methods for Soil Moisture Retrieval from Satellite Remote Sensing Data](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs1010003)
Lakhankar et al. (2009), *Remote Sensing*. 49 citations.

- **Main goal:** Retrieves soil moisture from active microwave satellite data, where physical backscatter models are complex and poorly constrained.

- **Data:** Active microwave backscatter data with NDVI and soil characteristics; evaluation against ESTAR soil moisture and field measurements.
- **Main result:** Adding soil characteristics and NDVI reduces retrieval RMSE by about 30%; RMSE about 4.0% vs ESTAR and 6.5% vs field measurements; vegetated areas less accurate.

- **Issues:** Lower accuracy over vegetated areas; limited study area and period.

### [Toward improving the reliability of hydrologic prediction: Model structure uncertainty and its quantification using ensemble‐based genetic programming framework](https://doi.org/10.1029/2007wr006451)
Parasuraman et al. (2008), *Water Resources Research*. 49 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies model structure uncertainty in hydrologic prediction to improve reliability.
- **Architecture:** Ensemble-based genetic programming framework producing multiple model structures.
- **Data:** Hydrologic observations from a case study; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The ensemble genetic programming framework quantifies structural uncertainty and provides prediction intervals; numbers not reported here.

### [Development of a low-flow forecasting model using the M5 machine learning method](https://doi.org/10.1623/hysj.52.3.466)
Štravs et al. (2007), *Hydrological Sciences Journal*. 49 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts low flows of rivers to support water management during dry periods.
- **Architecture:** M5 model trees (piecewise linear regression trees).
- **Data:** Discharge and precipitation records from Slovenian rivers; details not reported here.
- **Main result:** The M5 model trees provide accurate low-flow forecasts with interpretable models; numbers not reported here.
- **Open work:** Extend lead times and compare with neural networks.
- **Issues:** Abstract unavailable; regional application; limited extremes.

### [Unveiling the limits of deep learning models in hydrological extrapolation tasks](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-29-5871-2025)
Baste et al. (2025), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 48 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether LSTM rainfall-runoff models can extrapolate to extreme precipitation beyond the training range, a key concern for flood design and climate change.
- **Architecture:** Stand-alone LSTM compared with a hybrid model combining a conceptual hydrological model with an LSTM, probed with synthetic design precipitation events of increasing intensity and duration.
- **Data:** 196 catchments in Switzerland for training; synthetic design storms of varying intensity and duration for the extrapolation experiments.
- **Main result:** The LSTM cannot predict discharge above a theoretical limit of 73 mm/d, below the 183 mm/d training maximum, and shows concave runoff response; gating, not only cell-state saturation, blocks new extreme information.
- **Open work:** More robust training strategies, larger and more diverse training sets, and architectures that preserve extrapolation capacity for extremes.
- **Issues:** Synthetic design events rather than observed extremes; a single region; larger hidden states or more data do not guarantee better extrapolation.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Hybrid Physically Based and Deep Learning Modeling of a Snow Dominated, Mountainous, Karst Watershed](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021wr030993)
Xu et al. (2022), *Water Resources Research*. 48 citations.

- **Main goal:** Predicts streamflow in a snow-dominated mountainous karst watershed, where physically based and conceptual models struggle with complex terrain, snowmelt and matrix-conduit flow duality.
- **Architecture:** Hybrid model coupling a physically based, spatially distributed snow model with a ConvLSTM (convolutional long short-term memory) deep learning model that maps spatiotemporal recharge to outlet streamflow.
- **Data:** Meteorological forcing and simulated snowmelt for a single watershed in northern Utah with seasonal snow and variably karstified carbonate bedrock; observed outlet streamflow. Exact periods not reported in the abstract.
- **Main result:** The hybrid ConvLSTM simulates outlet streamflow with high accuracy and outperforms reference models; learned spatial recharge and discharge patterns are consistent with known hydrogeology.
- **Open work:** Test transferability to other karst watersheds and extend interpretation of learned recharge and storage patterns.
- **Issues:** Single-watershed study, so generalization is unproven; skill metrics are not quantified in the abstract and snow-model errors propagate into the deep learning component.
- *Basis: abstract*

### [Integrating hydrometeorological information for rainfall‐runoff modelling by artificial neural networks](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.7299)
Chiang et al. (2009), *Hydrological Processes*. 48 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves rainfall-runoff forecasting by integrating different hydrometeorological information sources as inputs to data-driven models.
- **Architecture:** Artificial neural network rainfall-runoff models fed with combined hydrometeorological inputs; the specific network type is not specified here.
- **Data:** Rainfall and streamflow records from a Taiwanese watershed; other details not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the title implies that integrating hydrometeorological information improves ANN runoff forecasts.
- **Open work:** Testing longer lead times, additional catchments and forecast rainfall inputs.
- **Issues:** Single-region application and black-box model; generalization to other basins and extreme typhoon floods is uncertain.
- *Basis: assessment*

### [Improved Understanding of How Catchment Properties Control Hydrological Partitioning Through Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2021wr031412)
Cheng et al. (2022), *Water Resources Research*. 47 citations.

- **Main goal:** Identifies how catchment properties control the Budyko parameter omega (Fu's equation) governing long-term partitioning of precipitation into evapotranspiration and runoff.
- **Architecture:** Boosted regression tree and CUBIST rule-based regression models interpreted with feature importance, accumulated local effects (ALE) and LIME explainable AI methods.
- **Data:** 15 catchment properties for 443 Australian catchments; continental omega and evapotranspiration mapped at 0.05° resolution.
- **Main result:** Root zone storage capacity, vapor pressure, vegetation coverage, precipitation depth, seasonality-asynchrony index and water use efficiency dominate omega, with nonlinear, non-monotonic and regionally varying effects.
- **Open work:** Applying the interpretable parameterization to other continents and to nonstationary climate and land-cover conditions.
- **Issues:** Long-term static framework ignores temporal change; interpretation methods reflect model associations rather than causality; Australia-only.
- *Basis: abstract*

Maity et al. (2008), *Hydrological Processes*. 47 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts basin-scale streamflow using information from large-scale atmospheric circulation phenomena to extend lead time.

- **Data:** Streamflow from an Indian river basin with large-scale circulation indices such as ENSO; other details not reported in the available metadata.
- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the title implies circulation information improves streamflow forecasts.

### [Counterpropagation fuzzy–neural network for streamflow reconstruction](https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.102)
Chang et al. (2001), *Hydrological Processes*. 47 citations.

- **Main goal:** Reconstructs missing streamflow records, needed for water resources planning, using a hybrid fuzzy-neural approach.

- **Main result:** Not reported in the available metadata; the title implies the network reconstructs streamflow with useful accuracy.
- **Open work:** Applying to other basins and comparing with conventional regression and backpropagation networks.
- **Issues:** Reconstruction quality depends on correlated neighbouring stations; uncertainty is not quantified.

### [Towards interpreting machine learning models for predicting soil moisture droughts](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/acdbe0)
Huang et al. (2023), *Environmental Research Letters*. 46 citations.

- **Main goal:** Explains what drives machine learning predictions of soil moisture during drought events to assess reliability of AI-based drought modelling.
- **Architecture:** Site-specific random forest models interpreted with permutation importance, accumulated local effects, SHAP, LIME and individual conditional expectation explainable AI tools.
- **Data:** Observations from 30 flux sites covering 8 vegetation types (soil temperature, aridity, latent heat flux and related variables).
- **Main result:** Soil temperature, atmospheric aridity, time variables and latent heat flux dominate globally; grass sites depend more on temperature, aridity and latent heat, forest sites on time-dependent variables.
- **Open work:** Using interpretations to guide operational drought prediction, irrigation and water management, and extending to more sites.

### [Robustness of Process-Based versus Data-Driven Modeling in Changing Climatic Conditions](https://doi.org/10.1175/jhm-d-20-0072.1)
O et al. (2020), *Journal of Hydrometeorology*. 46 citations.

- **Main goal:** Assesses how robust process-based and data-driven rainfall-runoff models are when applied under climate conditions different from their calibration period.
- **Architecture:** Comparison of the ECMWF physically based land surface model, the conceptual Simple Water Balance Model and an LSTM (long short-term memory) runoff model, using differential split-sample tests.
- **Data:** Streamflow from 161 European catchments, with calibration in a reference period (e.g., wet years) and evaluation in a climatically contrasting period (e.g., dry years).
- **Main result:** All models lose performance as conditions depart from the reference climate; the physically based model is the most robust, while the LSTM shows relatively low robustness in this setup.
- **Open work:** Train data-driven models on diverse spatial and temporal variability to improve robustness, and improve physics-based parameterizations.
- **Issues:** The split-sample setup restricts LSTM training data, which disadvantages data-driven models; the authors note results may not generalize.
- *Basis: abstract*

Yakowitz et al. (1987), *Venue not recorded*. 46 citations.

### [Long-term drought prediction using deep neural networks based on geospatial weather data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06212)
Grabar et al. (2023), *arXiv*. 45 citations.

- **Main goal:** Forecasts drought up to a year ahead for agricultural planning and insurance, a problem still unsolved with reasonable accuracy.
- **Architecture:** End-to-end spatio-temporal neural networks compared, including the EarthFormer transformer and convolutional LSTM, predicting the Palmer Drought Severity Index.
- **Data:** Open monthly gridded climate data as input; five distinct environmental regions as testbeds for PDSI prediction.

### [Quantifying cascading uncertainty in compound flood modeling with linked process-based and machine learning models](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-28-2531-2024)
Muñoz et al. (2024), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 45 citations.

- **Main goal:** Quantifies how uncertainty from initial conditions, forcing, parameters and model structure cascades through compound flood modeling chains.
- **Architecture:** Linked process-based hydrodynamic model and machine learning model (PB-ML) compared with multiple linear regression to attribute uncertainty contributions over time.
- **Data:** Hydrodynamic model scenario ensembles for Hurricane Harvey in Galveston Bay, Texas, evaluated through maximum water level residuals.
- **Main result:** The PB-ML model captures hidden nonlinear interactions and outperforms MLR; model structure and forcing are the main uncertainty sources, contributing 56% of variance reduction in maximum water level residuals.

Liu et al. (2023), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 34 citations.

- **Main goal:** Fills gaps in daily ESA CCI satellite soil moisture caused by poor coverage, snow, frozen soil and radio-frequency interference, to provide spatiotemporally continuous data for hydrological and ecological research.
- **Architecture:** Spatiotemporal machine learning gap-filling approach combining satellite observations with model-driven knowledge (bias-corrected model diurnal temperature range) and a residual calibration step; tree-based ML regression.

### [Causality-Structured Deep Learning for Soil Moisture Predictions](https://doi.org/10.1175/jhm-d-21-0206.1)
Li et al. (2022), *Journal of Hydrometeorology*. 34 citations.

### [The suitability of a seasonal ensemble hybrid framework including data-driven approaches for hydrological forecasting](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-501-2023)

### [Hydrological Projections in the Third Pole Using Artificial Intelligence and an Observation‐Constrained Cryosphere‐Hydrology Model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023ef004222)
Long et al. (2024), *Earth's Future*. 21 citations.

### [Accelerating Urban Flood Inundation Simulation Under Spatio‐Temporally Varying Rainstorms Using ConvLSTM Deep Learning Model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025wr040433)
Liao et al. (2025), *Water Resources Research*. 21 citations.

### [Towards Interpretable Physical‐Conceptual Catchment‐Scale Hydrological Modeling Using the Mass‐Conserving‐Perceptron](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024wr037224)
Wang et al. (2024), *Water Resources Research*. 20 citations.

### [Assessing the adequacy of traditional hydrological models for climate change impact studies: a case for long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-29-2811-2025)

### [Demonstrating a Hybrid Machine Learning Approach for Snow Characteristic Estimation Throughout the Western United States](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023wr035805)
Steele et al. (2024), *Water Resources Research*. 18 citations.

- **Main goal:** Improves estimates of snow water equivalent (SWE) and snow density across the western United States by combining physical modelling with machine learning.

### [Interrogating process deficiencies in large-scale hydrologic models with interpretable machine learning](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-29-4457-2025)
Husic et al. (2025), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 18 citations.

- **Main goal:** Diagnoses process deficiencies in large-scale operational hydrologic models by identifying catchment attributes that control their performance.

### [Exploring the ability of LSTM-based hydrological models to simulate streamflow time series for flood frequency analysis](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-29-4951-2025)
Martel et al. (2025), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 17 citations.

### [Synergizing Intuitive Physics and Big Data in Deep Learning: Can We Obtain Process Insights While Maintaining State‐Of‐The‐Art Hydrological Prediction Capability?](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024wr037582)
He et al. (2024), *Water Resources Research*. 17 citations.

### [A Quantum-Empowered SPEI Drought Forecasting Algorithm Using Spatially Aware Mamba Network](https://doi.org/10.1109/tgrs.2025.3583578)

- **Main goal:** Corrects orographic quantitative precipitation estimate (QPE) errors in headwater basins to improve flood simulation and nowcasting.

- **Issues:** Limited number of flood events; error climatology depends on the hydrologic inverse correction method.

### [An explainable deep learning model based on hydrological principles for flood simulation and forecasting](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-29-7217-2025)
Xiang et al. (2025), *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*. 12 citations.

### [Global Flood Projection and Socioeconomic Implications Under a Deep Learning Framework](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024wr037139)
Kang et al. (2025), *Water Resources Research*. 12 citations.

- **Main goal:** Projects global changes in bivariate flood risk (peak and volume) and their socioeconomic exposure under climate change, and identifies drivers of streamflow change.

- **Data:** Bias-corrected outputs of 20 CMIP6 global climate models under four SSPs; global catchment streamflow; population and GDP exposure data.
- **Main result:** Under SSP3-7.0 the median joint return period of a 50-year flood falls to about 27.6 years, exposing 186 trillion USD and 4 billion people; downwelling shortwave radiation is the dominant driver of daily streamflow changes.

### [Improved 30‐m Evapotranspiration Estimates Over 145 Eddy Covariance Sites in the Contiguous United States: The Role of ECOSTRESS, Harmonized Landsat Sentinel‐2 Imagery, Climate Reanalysis, and Deep Neural Network Postprocessing](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023wr036313)

- **Main result:** 30 m ET reaches r = 0.8, RMSE 1.736, KGE 0.466 versus r = 0.485, KGE -0.841 for 70 m ECOSTRESS ET; DNN postprocessing raises test-site performance to r = 0.842, KGE 0.792. Radiation input biases drive most errors.

### [Evaluating the Functional Realism of Deep Learning Rainfall‐Runoff Models Using Catchment Hydrology Principles](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025wr040076)
Bayati et al. (2025), *Water Resources Research*. 9 citations.

- **Main goal:** Tests whether accurate LSTM rainfall-runoff models rely on hydrologically plausible internal mechanisms (functional realism).

- **Data:** 672 North American catchments with strong LSTM predictive skill; forcings of precipitation, temperature and potential evapotranspiration.
- **Main result:** High accuracy often masks implausible reasoning: in over 70% of rain-dominated basins temperature rises increase simulated streamflow without rain, and in snow basins PET is misattributed as a snowmelt driver.
- **Open work:** Use the diagnostic to constrain or regularize LSTM training and test robustness under climate shifts and extremes.
- **Issues:** Diagnosis only, no remedy proposed; IRF extraction depends on perturbation design; limited to North America.

Jahangir et al. (2025), *Water Resources Research*. 8 citations.

- **Main goal:** Produces streamflow forecasts that are consistent across timescales (daily and weekly) for decision-making.

### [Global Runoff Partitioning Based on Budyko‐Constrained Machine Learning](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025wr039863)
Cheng et al. (2025), *Water Resources Research*. 8 citations.

- **Main goal:** Estimates global partitioning of runoff into baseflow and quickflow by combining a physical framework with machine learning.

- **Data:** 1,461 catchments worldwide for training and testing; applied globally at 0.25° grid.
- **Main result:** Test R2 of 0.96 for runoff and 0.91 for baseflow; globally 35.3% of precipitation becomes runoff (19.6% baseflow, 15.7% quickflow); vegetation controls Budyko alpha and soil controls baseflow parameters.
